A guest (atithi) is defined as one who comes unexpected, and he is to be honoured, whether liked or not, learned or foolish. Several kinds of "fallen" Brahmin are named, and the text says not to eat food from certain people (a Shudra, one who cooks for a Shudra, food in an iron vessel, or at a death-impurity), with atonements such as the Chandrayana and Santapana fasts. Aruna cites Narada's teaching that one must not pass over a nearby Brahmin, even a poor or foolish one, in favour of one who is far away, and the sun agrees: do not test a Brahmin, since he is made of all gods, but honour him for his birth. The last part lists atonements for a dog bite, for worms in the body, and for eating the food of the dead, and sets rules for cleansing.

01-185.json.summary: The sun (Aditya) continues to Aruna (Anuru) on ancestor rites. A shraddha must not be done at night or at the twilights; it is called a demoness's hour. Before a shraddha one must first do the mothers' rite. Aruna asks how the mothers' rite goes and who the mothers are, and the sun tells it: feed eight Brahmins, and a ninth, with sweet food (jaggery, sweets, no bitter tastes), then offer six rice balls, with curds, unbroken rice and jujube, to the mother, grandmother, great-grandmother and the father's mother and her line, facing east. In the growth rite (vriddhi) five Brahmins stand for the "Nandimukha" ancestors. The chapter sets out how to seat the Brahmins (two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north), the three pure things in a shraddha (the daughter's son, kusha grass, sesame) and three praised habits (cleanliness, no anger, no haste), the need for an upper cloth, and a warning against rinsing the mouth in a careless way. It ends with the shraddha blessing: may our givers grow, may the Vedas and our line grow, may our faith not leave us, and may we have much to give.

01-186.json.summary: The sun (Bhaskara) speaks, still on household and ritual duty. In Shravana a snake offering is made with mantras, and the bed is taken up and put down at set months. He sorts rites into daily, wish-based and occasional ones, saying daily ones need no reward and wish-based ones must be done for their fruit, and lists the Vedic sacrifices (agnihotra, new and full moon rites, Soma sacrifices). Virtues named: kindness to all, freedom from envy, patience, cleanliness, freedom from greed. The Brahmin's ways of living are listed, and it is said that one should be clean, sweet-smelling, kind in speech and should not look at the sun or at a naked woman. The chapter lists foods to avoid (garlic, onion, mushrooms and similar; stale food; food touched by dogs or liquor), the days of impurity after a birth or death (ten days for a Brahmin, with shorter periods for other classes), ways of purifying objects, and bathing rules. The last verses speak of a wife's duty to serve her husband and to please her elders, and of rules for widows. These are the text's own social rules, reported as stated.

01-187.json.summary: Aruna (called Anuru) asks the sun which good deeds take people to heaven. He lists five great sacrifices (of action, penance, study, meditation and knowledge) and asks which is best, how many kinds of duty and wrong there are, and how people cross the ocean of rebirth. The sun answers that faith (shraddha) is the root of all duty; without faith, even great gifts bring nothing. He then speaks of his own six-syllable mantra, "Om namah Khasholkaya", saying whoever holds it in the heart has read, heard and done everything. Sumantu narrates that Garuda's elder brother, bowing, asks the sun what these words mean, and a speaker called Saptashvatilaka ("ornament of the seven-horse [chariot]") replies, praising the sun's words as authoritative, saying the teacher who explains the sun-duty is to be honoured like the sun, and that such knowledge is above other scriptures. The chapter ends with a long passage on the five cow products (dung, urine, milk, curds, ghee, with the bile-stone gorochana), five cows born from the milk-ocean (Nanda, Subhadra, Surabhi, Sumana, Shobhanavati) and the bathing and worship of the sun with them, with a promise of heaven and a stay in the sun's world. Gifts to those who recite and meditate (japa) are called the best gifts, and feeding a bhojaka at a shraddha brings the sun's own place.

01-188.json.summary: The chapter title is "honouring the bhojakas" and the speaker is marked as Saptashva ("seven-horse"). Cooked food should first be offered to the sun and fire and then eaten; one who eats without offering it to the sun, fire, teacher and Brahmins eats sin. Farming, trade, anger and untruth increase sin, and the five household "slaughter places" (grinder, pounder, hearth, water-pot, broom) harm the householder; worship of the sun, fire and teacher clears these sins. Offerings of food are rewarded by the number of grains, and with ghee-cakes, relishes, fragrant rice and sixty-day rice the reward is multiplied ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand times. Looking at the sun gives the merit of a Ganga bath and bowing gives the merit of bathing in all holy places. The ancestors are pleased by a mantra-reciting Brahmin fed at a shraddha, and they come as guests to test one's faith, so every guest, whether handsome or ugly, clean or dirty, must be received with welcome, seat, foot-water and food. The sun is always present in the bodies of bhojakas, so one who abandons them or listens to slander against Brahmins suffers in hell. The chapter ends by calling the mantra-reciter the best of worthy recipients.

01-189.json.summary: The speaker is marked as Saptashvatilaka. Giving to one who does not recite mantras is useless, like pouring offerings on ashes. True giving is done with kindness and faith, and gifts to the poor, blind, wretched, children, old and sick bring endless fruit. A beggar helps the giver, since the giver rises and the receiver stays below; a giver should welcome a guest, treat him courteously, and not give with anger or rude words. Five things make a gift great (generosity, welcome, friendliness, compassion, no jealousy). Holy places are named (Varanasi, Kurukshetra, Prayaga, Pushkara, the Ganga bank, the sea, Naimisharanya, Mulasthana, Pundarikasvamika, Kalapriya, Kshirikavasa) with all sun-hermitages, and favourable times (eclipses, the northern turning, equinox, sankranti). Faith is called the root of all this, and a ten-fold list of duty is given: non-violence, patience, truth, modesty, faith, self-control, giving, worship, penance and meditation. The chapter lists the five great sins and their companions, and the lesser sins that equal them (such as giving up the sun-knowledge after learning it, which is like drinking liquor). It ends by saying that people reach different worlds according to the faith with which they worship the sun: demons' world, ghosts' world, sages' world, the Gandharvas' world, Indra's, Prajapati's, and Vishnu's own world for nine-fold worship, and beyond that the sun's own highest place.

01-190.json.summary: The speaker is marked as Saptashvatilaka, and the heading calls this a talk between the sun and Aruna (Anuru). It opens with the end of a list of the goals of sun-devotees (countless star-like chariots), then turns to sins. Sins that lead to hell are listed in short by mind, speech and body: setting fire in a cattle path, forest, town or village; seizing property, or stealing sandal, aloe, camphor, silks and a trust; pulling away girls fit to marry; going with a son's or friend's wife or with a sister; violence to a girl; sex with outcaste women. Then the "minor sins" are given: not paying a Brahmin as promised, leaving a good wife, taking land, gold or cloth, troubling sun-devotees, selling a wife or child, selling pools and gardens, taking women's property, not protecting women, speaking ill of gods, fire, good people, cows and Brahmins, giving up one's own duty, and disbelief. Several more wrongs are named, such as breaking up the dining row.

01-191.json.summary: The speaker is marked as Saptashvatilaka, and the heading calls this a talk between him and Aruna. It goes on with the list of wrongdoing that leads to hell: those who slander cows, Brahmins, crops, good people and ascetics; who foul wells, groves, temples and cool places with filth; who drink liquor and are driven by lust, anger and pride; who follow false teachings; who make false deeds or documents; who sell weapons; who are cruel to servants, beat or overload cattle and oxen, or do not feed the weak; who abandon wife, children, guests and the hungry; who cook for themselves alone without giving food to a Brahmin; and who break vows they took. Many kinds of theft are listed, even to a mustard seed, and all are said to lead to hell. After death the sinner gets a body for punishment and is led by Yama's messengers to Yama's realm, where Dharmaraja punishes the unseen wrongdoer, as a king punishes wrongdoers on earth. The chapter ends by saying atonement must be done, since sin is not otherwise destroyed even in a hundred crore ages, and that one who does good by body, mind and speech, or has it done, gets high happiness.

01-192.json.summary: The speaker is marked as Saptashvatilaka, and the heading calls this a talk between him and Aruna. It describes the journey of the dead to Yama's city, where all beings must go and face the good and bad they have done, as reported by Chitragupta and others. Good people, gentle and kind, go by an easy road; one who gave sandals, wooden sandals or an umbrella to Brahmins goes in comfort. The wicked go by the fearful southern road, 86,000 yojanas long, with sharp thorns, razor-edged stones, burning sand, forests of swords, fire, ice, wild animals, snakes, insects, rain of stones and burning coals, thunder and darkness, with no rest, no water and no help. The text says those who have worshipped the sun even once in the mind never see Yama's face, and that sinners become ghost-kings for a time by the order of the bird (Garuda, whom the speaker addresses) and then reach the sun's city. People who worship the sun are not touched by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wet. The chapter ends by urging devotion to the sun for one who wants great wealth.

01-193.json.summary: The speaker is marked as Saptashvatilaka, and the title is "rules for the tooth-stick". Aruna is told of the seven "seventh-day" (saptami) vows, the highest secret of sun-worship, to be done on the bright seventh in Magha or Margashirsha, or on days such as the solstice, equinox, sankranti, Sunday or an eclipse. The seven are called after what is used: mustard seeds, the leaf-cups of the arka plant, pepper, sesame, and rice, and so on. The tooth-stick is cut from a chosen tree, each giving its own gift: mahua (a son), bilva (wealth), khadira (savings), kadamba (loss of enemies), ashvattha (fame), karavira (steady knowledge), shirisha (fortune), priyangu (good luck). The user sits quietly, thinks of the wish, says a prayer to the stick three times, chews it, washes and throws it down. If it falls upright or faces him, success is near; if it falls facing away three times, the saptami is not to be taken up. That night he sleeps on a clean bed, wearing clean cloth, and in the morning he washes, prays to the sun, does japa and fire offering, and bathes in the afternoon. He then worships the sun and sleeps in front of the god while reciting the Gayatri.

01-194.json.summary: The speaker is marked as Saptashvatilaka, in a talk about dreams (svapna) in the sun-vow. After the rites are done, the worshipper lies on the ground and thinks of the god, and the dream seen that night is read as an omen. Good signs include seeing the sun, Indra's banner or the moon; gold ornaments, mirrors and whisks; bleeding or loss of hair; milking a buffalo, lioness or cow; eating the flesh of a sheep or a lion; drinking liquor; eating milk-rice from a gold, silver or lotus-leaf dish; winning in a gamble or a fight; one's own body burning; garlands and white cloth; horses, animals and birds; riding a horse or chariot; climbing a mountain, horse, lion, bull or elephant; seeing gods, Brahmins, teachers and ascetics, and their blessings; and being beheaded, which means a kingdom. Also dreamt as good are drinking from the sea or river and crossing a sea. The chapter ends by saying that if a dream shows kingship or wealth for a fixed number of saptamis (four to eight), the fruit grows by the count: sons, long life, wealth, many wishes, fame.

01-195.json.summary: Aruna (Anuru) asks for the highest method of the saptami vows, and Saptashvatilaka answers. On a bright Sunday in the northern turning one takes the vow for sons, wife, wealth and land. Seven saptamis are named by what is eaten: arka leaf-cups, pepper, neem leaves, fruit, and one called "kamika". The rule is: on the fifth a single meal, little food, no sex, no honey, meat or sour; on the sixth, ghee-rice in leaf-cups; on the seventh no other food; in some versions only pepper or neem leaves; a fast on air for a day and night is the "victory saptami". The names of the seven are written on leaves and placed in a pot with white sandal, garlands, seven grains and gold, with ashvattha and ashoka leaves and curds and rice; the worshipper then sleeps, and the dream seen is the sign. At dawn he tells the dream to wise bhojaka Brahmins and friends, bathes at noon, worships the sun, does japa and fire offering, and gives to a bhojaka. The fruit is the reward of ten horse sacrifices, burning of hard sin, and cure of even the worst skin disease, "as Garuda carries off snakes".

01-196.json.summary: Saptashvatilaka continues, speaking on conduct and offerings. On the seventh one should be friendly to all, not touch oil, wear blue cloth, sleep with a woman or gamble, weep, strike any creature or harm others; entering the sun's temple while doing wrong brings the sin of killing a Brahmin. A bhojaka who lends money at interest out of greed goes to hell; one who sets up another god's image must do atonement and the Santapana fast before worshipping the sun again. The sun must be offered fresh, clean, scented flowers, not stale or spoiled ones, and a bhojaka who snatches flowers out of greed goes to the great Raurava hell. A long section lists incense and pastes and their rewards: sandal incense and aloe give a boon, guggulu health and a wife, saffron luck, red sandal everything, musk great wealth, camphor lordship over kings; plastering the sun's temple frees from disease and leprosy. The seven saptamis are said to bring wealth (arka leaves), love (pepper), cure (neem), sons (fruit), and success to men and women alike. Results of keeping the vow are praised (no blindness, leprosy or poverty; sons, enjoyment, rewards of all sacrifices), and a broken vow can be repaired by atonement. Finally the "twelve-named" bright seventh is taught: a different name of the sun each month from Magha on (Vibhavasu, Vivasvan, Bhaskara, Vikartana, Pataṅga, Sahasramshu and others), with simple fasts. The secret is not to be given to the faithless, the unteachable or the sinful, except to a Brahmin to cure disease.

01-197.json.summary: The speaker is marked as Saptashvatilaka. He goes on to the wish-fulfilling use of flowers, incense and lamps. Each flower is paired with a reward: jasmine gives the sun's nearness; oleander health and lasting wealth; mallika the god's favour; white lotus good fortune; lotus, blue lotus and kunda fame, learning and strength; mandara (coral tree) cures all skin disease; bilva leaves give great wealth; arka garlands make the sun a ready giver; bakula garlands a beautiful bride; champaka the same; ashoka freedom from worry. Worship with a set of twelve bows, each with a name (bhur, bhuvah, svah, mahah, janah, tapah, satyam, and so on, ending "Om namah Khasholkaya"), is described as the way to give a full circle of worship. Lamps: ghee gives good eyesight, mustard oil brings enemies' loss, mahua oil good fortune. The best offerings are named: jati flowers, sandal incense, saffron among scents, and sweet cakes as food. After worship, circumambulation and bowing, the worshipper goes by a fine chariot to the sun's world. A "water-handful" saptami is described, and there is a rule for any saptami not named: eat what one gets for a small coin (a cowry), whether eatable or not.

01-198.json.summary: Shatanika asks which one god is highest in the world, who is worshipped by Brahma and others, and which duty is best of all. Sumantu answers by retelling a talk between Bhishma and Vyasa on the bank of the Ganga. Bhishma, bowing, asks Vyasa who the sun is, where he was born, and why men bow first to him and then to others. Vyasa says the sun is the first of all the gods, the one who destroys darkness, the best of duties and the best to be worshipped, and is called Aditya because he is the first maker (and the son of Aditi and Kashyapa); the world, gods, demons and all beings come from him. Brahma came from his mouth, Rudra from his chest, Upendra (Vishnu) from his right hand, Dhatri from his left hand, Daksha from his left foot and Kashyapa from his right. Bhishma asks why the sun is attacked by rakshasas at the three twilights and seized by Rahu; Vyasa explains that the sun burns them, that the three gods are in his disc at the twilights, and that an eclipse is only the disc being covered. The chapter closes by saying there is no night, day, offering, or good or bad action without the sun, and he protects and makes all.

01-199.json.summary: Bhishma asks how one can please the sun so that he gives boons quickly, and Vyasa answers. By worship, recitation, fire offering, meditation and concentration, after receiving initiation and the rules of the circle, one who worships with a single mind soon gets the sun's favour: strength, wealth, grain, gold, beauty, health, long life, fame, sons, duty, wealth, desire, knowledge and liberation. Bhishma then asks for the sun-bathing rite with its secret, and Vyasa teaches it: take clay with a mantra in a clean place, divide it in three (one part for washing off dirt, one to be charged with the weapon-mantra, one with the sun's mantra), recite over the water, bathe at a sun-holy place to the sound of conch and horn while thinking of the sun, rinse the mouth, and then do the "king of mantras" in its letters (given as syllable parts), the water-offering to gods, sages and ancestors, the twilight prayer, and the gift of water in cupped hands to the sun. The arghya is made with red oleander, sesame, rice and kusha water in a copper vessel with red sandal incense, and is offered kneeling with the vessel on the head. The fruit is said to equal gifts at eclipses, solstices and Pushkara; even an uninitiated person gets the fruit in a year, and an initiated one is not born again but merges into the sun.

01-200.json.summary: Bhishma asks for the right method of worshipping the sun, and Vyasa answers. The worshipper seeks a quiet, pleasant place, sits facing east on a good seat with a straight body, and places mantra syllables on his body (nyasa): on the fingers from thumb to little finger, on the heart, head, topknot, body as armour, eyes and hands as weapon; the "eye-seed" and the three-syllable sun-mantra and the "armour" mantra are given by their letters. He then does breath control with the first seed-syllable, purifies himself with three fierce mantras, and regards himself as the sun. Placing the sun on his own limbs this way, he is said to be bound by nothing, enemies turn into friends, and what he lacks he gains. He then sets up a prepared ground, a flower basket on his right and a copper pot of water on his left, washed with the weapon-mantra, covers it with the "armour" mantra, and sprinkles all the offerings. The chapter ends with Bhishma saying that he knows the method taught with Puranic mantras, but asks Vyasa to tell the full method with Vedic mantras. (The answer is not in this chapter.)

01-201.json.summary: The chapter begins with an unmarked narrator, who says he will tell a talk between the eldest god (Brahma, the four-faced one, seated in Manovati) and Keshava (Vishnu). Vishnu, bowing, asks Brahma how to worship the sun in his disc, and Brahma praises the question and answers. The worshipper sets the "Khasholka" seat by placing seed-syllables in the east, centre, south-east and on round to the north-east, and over it a mantra-made lotus of eight petals with filaments and a seed-pod, in five colours. Eight powers (Dipta, Sukshma, Jaya, Bhadra, Vibhuti, Vimala, Amogha, Vidyuta) are placed round it with a ninth in the middle, called Sarvatomukhi. The sun is then called and set on the seed-pod, and the Vedic verses "Ud u tyam jatavedasam", "Agnim dutam", "Akrishnena rajasa", "Hamsah shuchishad" and others are used to worship him and the powers in turn. Seven seed-syllables are set out with their verses. The chapter ends by giving the sun's form for meditation: red, very bright, standing on a white lotus, two-armed, with one wheel, calm, holding a lotus, and round in the disc at the centre.

01-202.json.summary: Vishnu asks Brahma how a man should worship the sun set in an image. (The source leaves the speaker mark for the reply blank, but it answers Vishnu.) The reply, "well asked", gives the rite of worship with named Vedic verses for each step, beginning with "Ise tva" for the head and "Agnim ile" for the right hand and "Agna ayahi" for the feet, then a garland, a handful of loose flowers, and the sun's bath in this order: water, "Imam me Ganga", herbal washings, milk, curds, ghee, herb water, rubbing with a paste, perfumed water, gold-water arghya and foot-water. After this come the sacred thread, cloth, flower garland, incense with guggulu, collyrium, red-tilak and a long-life mark, and a lotus-eyed touch, with a verse for each. The chapter closes with the hymn "Sahasrashirsha Purusha" and "Vishvatashchakshuh", and a verse to Shri and Lakshmi.

01-203.json.summary: The chapter begins with a missing first verse; someone asks the four-faced Brahma for a short account of the worship of the "sky" (vyoma) with eight points (the eight-cornered sun-figure), and Brahma, addressing Krishna (Vishnu), answers. The eight-cornered figure can be made of gold, silver, copper or stone. The sun is first worshipped in the centre with flowers and the verse "Mahisha vo mahan", then the corners one by one with Vedic verses to Indra, the lord of rakshasa-killers and others, covering the east, south-east, south-west and north-east, and finally the whole with "Namo astu sarvapapebhyah". In the morning the Rudras and Vasus are worshipped, and in the afternoon "Hamsah shuchishad". The worshipper then gives clean cloth, sandals and a gold ring to the teacher, with scent, flowers and food. Reward: many sons and wealth; a fast and worship on the northern turning gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice; the same at the equinox, and at eclipses of the sun and moon, which leads to Brahma's world. One who hears this is later born on earth as a king, rich, with many sons and unbeaten in battle.

01-204.json.summary: Sumantu teaches the way to worship the sun in a jewelled or image form. The worshipper first honours the Earth with scent, flowers and rice, and calls the sun with the mantra "Om Khasholkam avahayami, Om bhur bhuvah svah". Water is charged with the Gayatri and the verses "Apo hishtha" and "Hiranyagarbhah samavartata", and the offerings follow in order, each with a named Vedic verse: the vessel shown to the sun, foot-water ("Hamsah shuchishad"), a bath with milk and with water verses, circumambulation, flowers, scented powders, rice grains, incense, sandal paste, lamp, saffron, a cloth, white garments, food, a sacred thread, and a crown. Five verses of praise close the worship, and the eight powers of the god are worshipped in order. The chapter says Brahma first taught this to Vishnu, and that one who worships so gets all wishes here and hereafter: a son, wealth, a daughter, Vedic learning or, with no wish at all, liberation. Brahma and others reached success by this method.

01-205.json.summary: Vyasa speaks again to Bhishma, giving another method of worshipping the sun. The seat is prepared by placing seed-syllables in the east, south-east, south-west and on round to the north-east, with an eight-petalled lotus in five colours above it and the eight powers (Dipta and so on) round it, with the ninth in the middle. The sun is called and set on the seed-pod; then foot-water, rinsing water, a seat, cloth, scent, ornaments, flowers, offering and incense are given with faith. After this the limbs of the sun (heart, head, armour, eye, weapon) are worshipped in their places, the planets are worshipped on the outer ring in the eight directions (for example Mercury in the south, Venus in the north and Mars in the south-east), and the eight guardians of the directions, Indra and the rest, are worshipped with scents, flowers and incense. The text says that where the sun is worshipped this way there is no fear of thieves, fire, hell, hail or poison, and there is comfort, health, plenty and lasting wealth. It says the sun should be worshipped as the one in the middle of the disc of light, not as a chariot and horses, and that at the end the worshipper gives the sun leave to go with the heart-seed.

01-206.json.summary: Bhishma asks Vyasa for the "taking out" (uddhara) of the Puranic mantras, with hand-gestures (mudras), powers, forms and colours; Vyasa answers. He gives the three-syllable sun-mantra by its letters, each belonging to a god (Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra), and says one who recites it with faith reaches the highest state. Then the hand-gestures: a lotus-shaped one (the "vimudra") that makes the sun pleased and protects like a mother in great fear; the "heart", "head", "topknot" and "armour" gestures; the weapon gesture named "Trasani" that frightens obstacles; and the "eye" gesture, for each limb of the sun. The eight-syllable lore of the sun and one-syllable armour and weapon mantras are described by their letters. The nine powers (Dipta, Sukshma, Jaya, Bhadra, Vibhuti, Vimala, Amogha, Vidyuta, Sarvatomukhi) are given their seed-syllables and a common gesture. The planets, from the Moon to Ketu, have their own seeds, with "Om" at the start, "namah" at the end for worship and recitation and "svaha" for fire offering. Last come the forms to meditate on: the sun as red as a hibiscus on a white lotus, two-armed, holding lotuses, and the planets each in their colour (white Moon, red Mars, yellow Jupiter, and so on). One who meditates on the sun three times a day becomes rich as Kubera and strong, and one who worships by this rule is freed even from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

01-207.json.summary: Bhishma exclaims at the greatness of the sun, and Vyasa agrees: there is no god, refuge, Veda, offering, duty, wealth, friend, relative, mother, teacher or holy place equal to the sun. Worshippers of the sun get the highest goal and cross the ocean of rebirth; kings, thieves, planets, snakes, poverty and sorrow cannot hurt one when the sun is pleased. Even a sinner who worships the sun on Sundays reaches the highest state. Ways of worship are listed: a night meal on Sunday; offering five jewels with a mantra; a shraddha on sankranti or at the solstice to please the sun; a fast on the sixth and the seventh with a shraddha. A man or woman who worships the sun on the seventh gets all wishes, especially on his day and at eclipses. Vyasa compares sun worship to climbing a mountain of jewels, where each takes jewels according to his own strength: a seeker of wealth gets wealth, of sons gets sons, of liberation gets liberation. Sumantu then closes: Vyasa disappeared, Bhishma worshipped the sun as taught, and he tells the king (Shatanika) to worship him too, as Vyasa and Bhishma did after worshipping him once on a seventh.

01-208.json.summary: Shatanika asks again for the seventh-day (saptami) vow that pleases the sun. Sumantu says the seven saptamis, spoken by the sun himself to Aruna, are named by what is used: arka leaf-cups, pepper, neem leaves, fruit, the "no-rice" one (anodana), the "victory" one and the "wish" one (kamika). They are taken up on a Sunday in the bright half, at the solstices or at an eclipse; the worshipper is celibate, clean and self-controlled, with japa and fire offering. The rules are: a single meal on the fifth, no sex or honey or meat on the sixth, then the seventh with the thing named; the "victory" one is a day-and-night fast on air only. The names of the seven are written on leaves and put in a new pot, and one leaf is drawn by the worshipper; the "wish" one is done monthly for seven months. Fruits: lasting wealth to the seventh generation (arka leaves), meeting loved ones (pepper), cure of all disease (neem), sons and grandsons (fruit), and victory over enemies. The chapter says no vow or penance equals this one, that men and women who keep it reach the highest state, and that none in the family is blind, leprous, impotent, maimed or poor. If the vow is broken, one fasts for three nights or shaves the head and starts again. It ends with gifts of gold to Brahmins on the seventh.

01-209.json.summary: Sumantu continues the saptami teaching, now for twelve bright sevenths of a year. One may eat cow dung, barley gruel, fallen leaves, milk, a single meal, alms or only water, and worships the sun with flowers (lotus and others), perfumes, incense (guggulu, sandal), dark milk-rice and ornaments, and honours the best Brahmins with gold and food. This gives the fruit of sacrifices with large gifts, a stay in the sun's world in a fine chariot, and later birth in a great family. Each month a different name of the sun is said: Vishnu in Chaitra, Aryaman in Vaishakha, Vivasvan in Jyeshtha, Divakara in Ashadha, Parjanya in Shravana, Varuna in Bhadrapada, Martanda, Bhargava, Mitra, Pusha in Pausha, Bhaga in Magha and Tvashta in Phalguna. The teaching is a great secret: it is not to be given to an unteachable, faithless, sinful, ungrateful, atheist or cruel person. One who hears or reads it daily with faith finds happiness here, a place in the sun's world, and later rebirth as a king.

01-210.json.summary: Sumantu says the short account of the saptami vows is done and now gives more detail. In Phalguna's bright half the worshipper fasts on the sixth and worships the sun with scent, flowers (arka and white oleander), guggulu and sandal, offers jaggery water, and sleeps before him at night reciting the best recitation. The sun's six-syllable mantra and the Gayatri (said a hundred thousand times first) are the highest practice. Shatanika asks who should be fed on the seventh. The sun's rule: feed a "ghati" Brahmin (one who has the "pot" of the three Vedas), and sun devotees; do not feed those who do not follow the sun, or one with a low-caste wife, a leper, a devotee of another god, an astrologer who tells stars, a slanderer, a paid temple worker (devalaka), a stage performer or a story-teller who lives by it. Shatanika objects that astronomy is the sixth limb of the Veda, and Sumantu replies that it is the use of it for a living and to tell the stars to others that is barred. Offerings are listed (rice, mung beans, cakes, milk, curds) and foods to avoid (horse-gram, lentils, beans and the like). The chapter describes the "arka-puta" rite (taking leaf-cups from the arka plant at a clean place in the north-east) with a prayer, and lists sages, kings and others who reached success by this vow, including Kauthumi, who was cured of leprosy. Shatanika ends by asking who Kauthumi was and how he got leprosy and worshipped the sun; the answer is not in this chapter.

01-211.json.summary: Sumantu, answering the king's question, tells an old story of a learned Brahmin, Hiranyanabha, who went with his son Kauthumi to the sage Janaka's hermitage. There a dispute with other Brahmins began, and Kauthumi in anger killed a Brahmin. His father gave him up, and his brothers and others also turned him away. He went to holy places and temples but was not freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin, and a severe disease came on him: no ears or nose, oozing pus and blood. He came home and begged his father for an easy remedy. Hiranyanabha said that Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and others all rejoice in heaven by relying on the sun, so Kauthumi should worship the sun with devotion, repeat mantras, sing Sama chants and hear the Itihasas and Puranas. Kauthumi named the chants he knew, and his father taught him two higher ones, a special Jyeshtha-sama and a hymn said to be given by the sun-god himself. Kauthumi did this at the three twilights before the sun and heard the Puranas; the sin and the disease left him, and by the sun's grace he entered the sun's disc and never returns. Sumantu calls this the first saptami (the arka-leaf cup one), which gives wealth.

01-212.json.summary: Sumantu says that the first saptami, with arka-leaf cups, has been told, and now teaches the second, with pepper, to be kept on the bright sixth of Chaitra with a fast and sun-worship. Shatanika asks for the sacred mantras, including the sun's heart mantra and the body-touching (nyasa) rites. Sumantu, as Brahma once told it, gives the seed-syllable "Om vam phat" and says that one who remembers it, eats sweet food, drinks milk, keeps silence and repeats it can see the sun in person within a year, and 1,200,000 repetitions bring him to heaven in his body. He then gives the sun's heart, armour and weapon mantras with their letters, the placing of the sun's parts on head, heart and throat, and the worship of the one-syllable sun: hand-sign (mudra) at the heart, offering water in a vessel with flowers, bathing the god with the heart mantra, a lotus hand-sign, food offering and silent repetition, then sending the god away with the heart mantra. The text promises that no obstacle or sin will come to one who does this. The mantra syllables are given in obscure, coded form.

01-213.json.summary: Sumantu continues the worship rite from the previous chapter. After seeing the fire god and the sun within the fire, the worshipper protects the group with the syllable "ghu". This purifies the fire. He then offers into a lotus-shaped place or into the fire of the heart, and the god is truly invoked. With the syllable Om he gives a hundred offerings while fixing his mind on the eyes, then five offerings to please the limbs, and finally sends the god away with the heart mantra. It is a short chapter.

01-214.json.summary: Sumantu names twelve hand-signs (mudras) of sun-worship: padmini, madhyama, arkini, jvalini, tejani, gabhastini, shankha, suryavaktra, sahasrakirana and others. For each he gives its use: offering water, seeing the sun after a certain number of days (seven, three, twelve), repeating a mantra ten thousand or a hundred thousand times, standing in water up to the navel, and so on. The hand positions are described one by one, for example hands joined with thumbs up, hands spread, palms back to back, forefingers bent. Results named are freedom from disease, fear and death, destruction of sin including the sin of killing a Brahmin, power over enemies, and reaching the sun's place. Sumantu says Brahma worships the sun by this rule and urges the king to do the same, then to feed Brahmins and, on the seventh, eat a peppercorn with a mantra; this gives a meeting with a loved one at once. This is the pepper saptami. Indra with Shachi, Nala with Damayanti and Rama with Sita are said to have fasted on it and been united with their loved ones.

01-215.json.summary: Sumantu begins the third saptami, the one with neem leaves, said to be the best for curing disease, and says he will give the worship rules and the mantras. The chapter is a short list of mantras in coded form: a root mantra to the sun under the name Khasholka, mantras for the head and for the "weapon", a mantra to the thousand-rayed one, the sun's Gayatri, and a series of names (Dharmatma, Ananta the thunder-holder, Shyamapingala, Budha, Vagishvara, Shukra, Ishvara, Rahu, Dhruva and others) each placed in a direction. It ends with the mantra to call the god and the one to send him away. Little explanation is given beyond the mantras.

01-216.json.summary: Sumantu continues the neem saptami rite. The worshipper sprinkles mantra-purified water, places mantras on his body and thinks of himself as the sun. He draws an eight-petalled lotus, calls the sun with a hand-sign, bathes the image, and places the parts of the sun, the planets, the twelve Adityas (Bhaga, Surya, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuna, Savita, Dhata, Vivasvan, Tvashta, Pusha, Rudra, Vishnu), the direction guardians and a list of goddess-powers around it. He offers a lamp, food, ornaments, cloth and flowers, and eats a neem leaf with a mantra ("you are neem, bitter, home of the sun, remove all disease"). Brahmins are fed and paid, and he eats sweet food without salt or alkali, keeping the vow for a year; it frees him from all disease. A bright Bhadrapada seventh is added: fast, worship in the Maheshvara way, and on the eighth give date, coconut, citron and mango fruits. Shatanika then asks how the Purana and the Bharata should be heard. Sumantu, repeating what Brahma said, teaches the rules. Hearing at dawn, evening or night pleases Brahma, Hari or Shiva. The reciter (vachaka) sits on Vyasa's seat, which hearers must not use; he must be a Brahmin, and hearing from a reciter of another class leads to hell. He should speak clearly, with feeling and in the proper voice; reciters and hearers are ranked as good, passionate or dull. Hearers give a monthly fee in gold mashas (one to four, by class) and more on festival days; the text says a hearer who does not pay falls in class. The chapter praises the reciter highly as Vyasa, guru and father, and closes with the glory of the sun and of the reciter.

02-001.json.summary: Opening of the Madhyama Parva. After salutations, the sages ask Suta, son of Romaharshana, for the Purana, and Suta bows to Vyasa and agrees. He lists the contents of this section: consecration of images, praise of dharma and of Brahmins, rules for times of distress, the making of images, time and creation, the signs of a Purana, geography, the lunar days, shraddha, the gifts of a dying man, the duties of each age and atonements. He then begins teaching: the householder's stage is the source of the other three, and dharma gives wealth, desire and liberation, so one should hold to it and give up wealth or desire that goes against it. He teaches the three qualities (sattva rises, rajas stays in the middle, tamas goes down), action with and without desire, and a list of virtues for all classes: calm, self-control, kindness, giving, honesty, non-violence. The text lists the heavenly place for each group: Brahmins who keep their rites, Kshatriyas who do not flee battle, Vaishyas who keep their duty, Shudras who serve, sages, forest-dwellers, ascetics and yogis. The chapter has an odd line saying not to build a tank, water-shed or monastery where one already stands.

02-002.json.summary: Suta teaches creation. All was dark and unknown, and Rudra alone was the supreme cause. He formed mind, then the sense of "I", then the five elements, eight natures and sixteen changes, and the three qualities. From him came Brahma and Vishnu; Shambhu bewildered the world with his power, and Vasudeva is said to be bodiless and unborn. Brahma and Vishnu are called his sons who make and withdraw the world in each age. Time is counted: seventy-two yugas make a manvantara, fourteen make a kalpa, which is one day of Brahma. The seven upper worlds (Bhur to Satya) and seven lower ones (Patala, Vitala, Atala, Talatala, Sutala, Rasatala and so on) are named, and Rudra is at their beginning, middle and end. Brahma, born from Prakriti together with Vishnu, made the classes in order: Brahmins first, then Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, and a fourth class described as lacking a "foot" and kept outside certain observances. He then made earth, sky, directions, islands, seas, rivers, holy places, clouds, thunder, rainbows and meteors. The last verse is broken.

02-003.json.summary: Suta describes the worlds. Above Dhruva lies Maharloka, then Janaloka where Sanandana and the other sons of Brahma live, then Tapoloka with gods free from burning, then Brahmaloka (Satyaloka), where Brahma and the yogis dwell. Vishnu's city there and, above Brahma's seat, a shining place where Shiva lives with Devi are described, reached by ascetics who have given up pride, desire and anger; this is called Rudra's world. Seven lower worlds follow, from Mahatala and Haimatala to Rasatala, filled with palaces, temples and nagas, with kings such as Mucukunda and Bali named. Beneath them are crores of hells such as Raurava, where sinners are thrown. At the very bottom is Shesha, called Ananta, a form of Vishnu as Kalagni Rudra and Narasimha, who bears everything and destroys the world at its end with a flame of poison.

02-004.json.summary: Suta teaches the geography of the earth. There are seven great islands (Jambu, Plaksha, Shalmala, Kusha, Krauncha, Shaka and Pushkara), each ringed by an ocean: of salt, sugarcane juice, ghee, curds, milk, sweet water and others. Jambudvipa is in the middle, with golden Mount Meru at its center, 84,000 yojanas high. The ring of mountains (Himavan and others) divides the nine regions (varsha) such as Bharata, Kimpurusha, Harivarsha, Ilavrita (the middle one around Meru) and the northern Kuru land. Four mountains stand around Meru (Mandara, Gandhamadana, Vipula, Suparshva). The great Jambu tree gives the island its name; its huge fruits fall and form the Jambu river, whose water brings freedom from sorrow, age and bad smell, and whose river-bank gold is called Jambunada. Above Meru are named the places of Brahma, Indra, Shankara, Vishnu and Durga, then a shining place beyond form, and the sun god turning on the wheel of the zodiac. The chapter then gives the sun's yearly path north and south, the order of the sun, moon, stars and planets in the sky, with the seven sages and Dhruva highest, and rules about the rising and setting of Venus, in which the lengths of its "setting" are tied to the four classes. The last verses are unclear.

02-005.json.summary: Suta praises Brahmins and teaches how to recognise worthy and unworthy ones. The text says the Brahmin is by birth the lord of the three other classes, made first by austerity; gods and ancestors eat the offerings through his mouth, rites done without a Brahmin bear no fruit, and a house without Brahmin foot-water, Vedic sound and the sacred calls is like a cremation ground. Greeting a Brahmin brings long life; Brahmins are said to be purified by rites, the Veda, learning and pilgrimage. Then a long list names 26 kinds of faulty people (adhama, vishama, pashu, kripana, papishtha, nashta, kashta, rushta, dushta, pushta, hrishta, kuntha, andha, kana, chanda, khanda, vachala, kadarya, chapala, malimasa, steyi and others), with 85 subtypes. Examples: one who wears sandals before his teacher, one sweet in speech and poisonous at heart, one who bathes elsewhere though Prayaga is near, one who ignores his parents, one who eats in a Shudra's house or has relations with a Shudra woman, a thief, one who does not repay a helper. The chapter then values the astrologer who knows the horoscope (a land or king without one is as lost as a night without a lamp), and names four kinds of Brahmin: bhojaka, kathaka, Shiva-Brahmin and sun-Brahmin, of whom the sun-Brahmin is best and the Shiva-Brahmin who worships the lingam is called blameworthy. Parts of the last verses are unclear.

02-006.json.summary: Suta teaches respect for parents and teachers. The text says no one but the father is a relative to all four classes, that father, teacher and elder are three high gurus, and that the mother is above them. It lists gurus: the mother, the father, the visible gods (sun, fire, moon), the giver of the mantra, and others. Gifts of cloth and jewels are to be given on the twelfth, the new moon and at the sun's change of sign, and feeding on eclipses and solstices. Short verses of salutation to the father, mother, teacher and Brahmin are given. The order of salutation is the grandfather, mother, teacher, maternal grandfather, teacher of rites and priest. The elder brother is like a father; the father is like Meru. The chapter says that giving up the visible gods for the unseen is sinful, and praises bathing in the foot-water of the grandfather and honoring the grandmother.

02-007.json.summary: Suta repeats Brahma's rules for hearing the Purana (hear pure, at dawn, evening or night) and goes on to rules of reciting, copying and keeping books. Each book has a god: Shiva for the Agamas, Sharada for the Tantras, Ganapati for the Jamalas, Indra for the Damaras, Narayana for the Bharata and Ramayana, Brahma for the first Purana. Food offerings (bali) are given in the rite, and the seating directions of reciter and hearer are set. Eating meat after hearing the Purana, or praising one god in front of another's temple in the wrong way, is said to bring rebirth as a donkey. Parents' honor comes before one's own teachers. The text lists which works are incomplete without others (for example the Bhagavata without the Narasimha, the Bharata without its first book) and says a book must not be sold or stolen: taking a book or six letters brings Raurava hell or leprosy. The size of a good book (32, 24 or 8 fingers) and the writing material are given, and the copyist must be a Brahmin, pure, skilled, calm and fasting; times and directions to avoid for copying are listed, with warnings and rewards by number of letters. Pay for the copyist is stated, and the style of reading in seven notes is described. The order in which the classes sit to hear is also set out. The text says a Shudra must not teach dharma, that hearing from his mouth makes it unfit (like dog's milk), and that a Shudra who preaches dharma is to be put to death, or his tongue cut by the king. The chapter ends praising the reciter as Vyasa, and a town without him as dull as a day without the sun.

02-008.json.summary: Suta gives the order of the Puranas (Shaiva third, Bhagavata, Matsya fifth, Bhavishya sixth) and rules for study. Study is stopped for set numbers of days when certain animals pass between teacher and pupil (cat, mongoose, snake, horse, elephant and so on). Knowledge is to be given to the teacher's son and to the learned, pure, devoted and calm, and not to the deceitful, angry, greedy or dishonest. Teaching to the unworthy brings quick death to one of the two. Works by mlecchas are not to be studied. The text sets rules for compiling summaries of the sacred texts, forbids them in some months and at some hours, and says a book made impure is purified at once by the Narasimha mantra. A woman, an outcast or even a mleccha reaches the highest goal in this way; one who sees a fault in it is reborn as a donkey. The last part is a numbered list of identifications: one is Brahman, two is nature, nine is Bhairava, ten Janardana, eleven Rudra, twelve the sun, and so on up to a hundred, a thousand, a lakh and a crore, ending with the claim that the pure Brahman is reached in a moment.

02-009.json.summary: Suta explains two kinds of religious work: the "inner altar" (acts done through knowledge, without desire) and the "outer altar" (installing gods, building temples, tanks, wells and shelters, feeding Brahmins and serving teachers), the second being recommended for the Dvapara and Kali ages and depending on the king's support. Consecration rites are of three grades. The best takes three days, with 28 deities, sixteen reciters and four priests, and gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice. The middle takes one day, and the lowest only honours Ganesha, the planets, the direction guardians, Varuna and Shiva. Sizes are given: a temple of 61 hands is the best, half that the middle; ponds and lakes have measures by hands; wrong directions bring illness, death or fear. Works left without consecration give little fruit. Merit grows with the material: clay, grass or wood, brick, stone, copper or silver, gold, jewels. A builder of Vishnu's house lifts a hundred and one generations of his own and related families; rebuilding a ruined temple gives double the fruit; water standing through the dry season takes one to heaven. The chapter also says a Shiva lingam must not be moved, gives rules for the posts (yupa) of tanks and wells, and says no house should be built over water or over a temple.

02-010.json.summary: Suta gives the rules for preparing land and planting. The ground is measured and ploughed three days, with white bulls for a temple and black bulls for a garden, and five kinds of grain are sown. Gold-coloured earth is taken, the Vastu offering is made, and the digging is done with a mantra; one who gives up a tank without the Vastu rite loses half his merit. The post (yupa) takes a shape for each work: a snake for a tank, a jar for a well, a lotus for a garden, a mace in Vishnu's house, a horse for the horse sacrifice. Trees are planted after the seed is treated with Vishnu and other mantras, in a rite compared to conception, and the text says a man without a son gets a son by planting. The chapter lists what different trees give: ashvattha (merit for thousands), ashoka (removes sorrow), bilva (long life), jambu (wealth), banyan (liberation), mango (desire), and others, and trees not to plant (such as thorny or certain bitter ones). Tulasi is to be planted by month, with results for each. Cutting a peepal, banyan or sacred tree is said to equal killing a Brahmin. The last part gives mixtures for feeding and healing trees (milk, meat, fish-water, grains and others) and ends with gilding and cloth-wrapping of trees.

02-011.json.summary: Suta begins the tantra rule for consecration, to be done on a very holy day. It says one type of work is not to be released as part of another's rite: a well is not released in a tree rite, nothing else is done in a Tulasi rite, a lingam consecration is not mixed with another god's. Each is done in its own land, by its own method, and doing the reverse is said to shorten life. A pond, tank or garden whose measure is short is no fault if it is ten hands; larger ones, and groves of ten or twelve trees, are consecrated as before. The bilva tree has its own rite; parched grain and unbroken rice are then given on the head. The chapter is very short and rather broken.

02-012.json.summary: Suta teaches the marks of an image. An image lacking its marks must not be worshipped. Images may be of stone, wood, copper or clay and one to one and a half hands tall; an image eight fingers high is not to be worshipped at home. Exact finger measures are given for face, chin, forehead, nose, ears, eyes, neck, head, hands, feet and toes. The figure should have large eyes, rich ornaments and a halo, and hold a golden garland. The heights are named in "tala" units: Vishnu nine, Vasudeva three, Narasimha five, Hayagriva five, Narayana eight, Maheshvara five, Durga nine, Lakshmi and Vani three, Savita (sun) seven. Vasudeva holds the disc, conch, mace and lotus with the Shrivatsa mark, with Subhadra and Rukmini, Narada, Kapila, Dharma and Adharma at his sides. Images are set at a holy place, hill, tank, in town or in an assembly of Brahmins. In Kali, wood is advised, or clay if one cannot afford it, and sandal, aloe, bilva and padma wood are named.

02-013.json.summary: Suta teaches the fire-pits (kunda) for sacrifice. Ten shapes are named: square, round, quarter, half-moon, yoni-shaped, eight-part and others. The ground is cleaned of husks and hair, sown with sprouts for seven days, dug, wetted and measured with a cord, and its sides and lotus-shaped pit are marked in fractions of the area. Uses are given: a square pit for the rites of the twice-born, installation of a god and the house; an eight-sided lotus pit for Soma, the man and horse sacrifices; a half-moon for Shiva and Devi birth rites; a yoni-shaped pit for Shakti rites, wishes and the cure of fever; a six-sided pit for pilgrimage and entering war; others for killing, driving away, disease, treasure, kingship and winning a bride. The ridges (mekhala) and the sloping of the pit are measured by the size of the pit and the number of offerings. The pit is said to be the body of Nature, with a "womb" and "navel", and Shiva and Shakti are united in it. A pit missing a part is a bad sign. A mandala is drawn to the south and worshipped by the earlier measures. The chapter is cut off.

02-014.json.summary: Suta teaches the size of fire offerings (homa). Each sacrifice must keep its own measure, since a rite done without the right measure is spoiled. The usual counts of offerings are fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand and ten million. A rich man or king who does less than he can does not gain the fruit. Rites for peace and well-being are tied to the planets, and ten thousand offerings are advised for omens. The king may do the hundred-thousand and ten-million offerings, others a hundred or ten thousand; in Kali the planetary hundred-thousand and ten-million offerings, treasure-rites and rites to harm others are not for a householder. The text gives the daily count of offerings over three, five, nine or more days, and says on which day to install the gods, give the food offering and close the rite. A rite changed from these rules gives no fruit.

02-015.json.summary: Suta teaches the preparation of the fire-pit and the fire. A pit has eighteen preparatory steps: looking at the place, sprinkling it with kusha water, marking it with three cords, setting pegs with the Narasimha mantra, and shaping the "tongue". Fire must not be taken from the house of a mleccha or a Shudra, from a river, mountain or hall, or from a woman's hand; it is purified and brought three times. The fire has seven tongues for each kind of offering: Hiranya (gold) for ghee, Bahurupa for flowers, Krishna for rice-milk, Padmaraga for sugarcane, Suvarna and Lohita for lotus, Shveta for bilva leaf, Dhumini for sesame, Karalika for wood, and Manojava for offerings to ancestors; a few are for cruel rites. The chapter then says which part of the pit is the fire's head, eyes, ears and belly, and where each kind of offering goes. A wrong placing brings disease, sickness of the eyes, pain of mind or death. Good and bad signs of the flame are described: a sweet scent like sandal, aloe and camphor and a flame turning right are good; a broken or smoking flame means death or loss. The remedy is to give up 28 offerings, feed Brahmins, give 25 ghee offerings with the root mantra, and bathe and worship Hari three times.

02-016.json.summary: Suta gives the worship of the fire god at the close of a sacrifice. After the offerings the worshipper recites the sixteen services, calls the fire, draws the seat, and meditates on him: golden, three-eyed, seated on a lotus, with matted hair, holding a spear and the sign of fearlessness. Kamadeva, Indra, Varaha and the six-faced Skanda are worshipped at the doors. Eight hand-signs are shown. Then twelve short verses are given, one for each service: seat, welcome, water for the feet, water of honour, bathing, ornaments, scent, flowers, incense, lamp, food and a closing bow. The fire is addressed as Vaishvanara, Havyavahana, Dhananjaya, Jatavedas and Hutashana, and as Narayana's own light. The chapter closes by saying he is given an offering with these verses.

02-017.json.summary: Suta lists the names of the fire for each kind of sacrifice. The fire is called Agni at fifty offerings, Kashyapa at fifty again, Vishnu in a ghee-lamp rite, Vanaspati in a sesame rite, Brahmana at a thousand, Hari at ten thousand, Vahni at a hundred thousand and Hutashana at ten million. It has other names for peace rites (Varuna), killing rites (Aruna), daily rites (Anala), atonement, installing the gods, house rites, great gifts, cow gifts (Rudra), giving a bride, the weighing gift (Dhata), the release of a bull (Surya) and so on. Many life-cycle rites are listed with the fire's name: conception (Maruta), parting of the hair (Pingala), the rite for a son (Indra), naming, the first outing, first feeding, hair-cutting (Shanmukha), initiation (Vitihotra) and returning from study (Dhananjaya). It also names fires of the body and the world: the stomach fire, the undersea fire, the horse, elephant and chariot fires, the fire in water, hill fire, forest fire, lamp fire and the funeral fires.

02-018.json.summary: Suta gives the measure of materials used in the fire rite; the rite is fruitless if the measure is wrong or ignored. Ghee is given by a "karsha" (a small weight) and milk by a "shukti" (a small cup). Curds, milk, honey and the five cow products are given in the same amounts; parched grain, flat rice and sugar by a handful; jaggery by three tolas. Leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, lotus, sesame, rice, mustard, pepper and aromatic woods each get a size, for example fruit pieces cut in eight or ten parts, sticks a hand-span long and three-leaved durva grass. Bilva leaves are offered with the stalk removed, three leaves at a time and unbroken, and a Rakshasa takes the fruit of a rite if the stalk is dipped. The offerer sits facing east for most rites and north for a peace rite. Rice-milk and similar foods meant for other gods are not given into the fire. The chapter ends with the way the leaves and offerings are held between the fingers.

02-019.json.summary: Suta teaches how to make the ladle (sruva) and spoon (sruk) for the fire rite. Good woods are shriparni, shimshapa, kshiri, bilva and khadira, with dhatri, khadira and keshara praised for consecration rites. The bilva wood is taken on a day that is not an "empty" lunar day, after a fast, with no meat in mind and no sexual relations while the tools are made. The wood is divided in parts and cut to twenty finger-widths to match the pit; the bowl is hollowed like a cooking pan, like a dhatri fruit, and the altar is shaped like a winnowing basket. The ladle is cut in 24 parts and decorated, the handle is marked with a bracelet and the pattern drawn in mud. Gold or copper spoons are measured by tolas and finger-widths (a twelve-finger spoon, an eight-hand handle for rice-milk and a ten-tola one for clarifying ghee). If nothing else is at hand, a spoon of pipal wood, a clay ghee-pot or a copper vessel may be used. The chapter is short and ends abruptly.

02-020.json.summary: Suta explains the closing offering (purna) of a fire rite. If it is not done, the rite is spoiled and its glory lost. It is made with four mantras ("punatu", "saptate", "dehi me", "purna darvi"), each with its seer, meter and god (for example Kaundinya, Prajapati, Shatakratu and Pavana; the god is Agni or Prajapati). The number of closing offerings depends on the count of the main offerings: one at a hundred, two at a thousand, more for ten thousand and a lakh, and one for ordinary life-cycle rites. They are given standing, not sitting. Some fruits (such as certain citrus ones) are not to be used or counted. The number of priests is set: three for a rite to clear a debt, six for a lakh of offerings, a row of nine, five, ten or twenty-five for ten million; they should be calm and without desire or anger, and the Brahma priest honoured. A lakh of offerings gives every desire to one who wants it, and one done without desire leads to Brahman; ten million is a hundred times more. The seat must be of darbha grass, not stone, mud or cloth, and fees must be given at the end.

02-021.json.summary: Suta teaches the mandala, the drawn diagram on which the gods are worshipped. The text says the gods sit on a lotus seat; without a lotus the goddess must not be worshipped, or a yakshini takes her place. Breaking a mandala is a fault; coloured powder gives hundreds of times the fruit. Many kinds are named: the square (nine-part), krauncha, the lotus-hundred-petalled, thousand-spoked, Subhadra, Sarvatobhadra, eight-sided, six-sided and three-sided, among about forty-five. Each is matched to a rite: the square nine-part one for Vishnu rites, krauncha for the cow sacrifice, Subhadra for the horse sacrifice, a human-shaped one for the man sacrifice, a five-lion seat for Shakta rites, Harivallabha for the royal rite, and so on. Wrong use brings a fault and a low birth. Altar sizes (two hands, a few fingers high), the plastering with cow dung, the sprinkling with gold-and-gem water, the cord and pegs and their materials are described.

03-001.json.summary: The Madhyama Parva, second part, begins. Suta teaches drawing the square mandala: the ground is measured by the maker's own fingers and a cord, then enlarged step by step up to sixteen hands. A lotus is drawn in four rings: the seed-cup first, then the filaments, then the petal joints, then the petal tips. The seed-cup is yellow; the filaments are white, red and yellow from root to tip; the corners are red. The weapons and gods are drawn around: Shambhu, Gauri, Brahma, Rama and Krishna in order, with the choice of which god to begin with depending on the rite (Shiva-Vishnu rites from Shambhu, installation up to Rama, a tank up to Krishna). The nine-part lotus is then described, with spokes and "wheel" lines in several colours. The text says a Shudra, or a man who is a Brahmin only in name, must not make a mandala; it is made at river meeting-places and temples. One who draws it and does not worship it with the fire rite is born again and again "unpierced" (without initiation).

03-002.json.summary: Suta describes the krauncha (heron) mandala. A drawing is made with four rings: seed-cup, filaments, petals and sixteen petals, in a square. The bird has a red head, yellow beak, white neck, and twenty-petal tail; wings, legs and toes are given their colours, and the colours are made from powders (white from rice, yellow from turmeric, red from shell-powder and kusumba, black from burnt grain, and so on). Seeing it destroys the sin of a hundred births; one who sees it by mistake, at home, in a field or on a tree-top, and stands to bow, burns away the sin of a hundred Brahmin-killings. Living animals are also named as the forms of gods: peacock as Brahma, bull as Sadashiva, lion as Durga, krauncha as Narayana, tiger as Tripurasundari, black tiger as Kalika and spotted pigeon as Lakshmi; seeing them daily after bathing, and keeping and feeding them, keeps off the harm of planets. The chapter lists powders not to be used. It then teaches the Subhadra mandala (one and a half hands, with a lotus of eight petals and three colour rings) and the Sarvatobhadra mandala (a hand of 24 fingers, a grid of 256 cells, sixteen lines, colours by tradition: white for Vishnu rites, red for Shakti, yellow for Shiva), with decoration by a wish-vine, animals and birds (Garuda for Vishnu, a bull and monkey for Shiva, a tiger for Shakti). More mandala names follow (Shatapatra, Vajranabha, Gajahvaya, Chandrakanta, Suryakranta, Chintamani, five-lion-seat, Nrisimha, Garuda, Meru-garbha and others), then planet colours (moon white, Mercury and Jupiter yellow, Venus white, Saturn black, Rahu smoky), and the five-lotus mandala with four swastikas.

03-003.json.summary: Suta teaches that a sacrifice must have the right measure and a fee (dakshina); without them it is spoiled and all taking part may fall to hell. The priests (teacher, reciter, Brahma priest) must know the rule and no outcast may be brought in. Money units are explained: a pana is 80 cowries, and a purana, silver and gold pieces are counted from it. Fees are listed: for a sacrifice about a gold piece, two for a great garden, half for a well, one for the Tulasi or amla rite, four for a hundred thousand offerings, eighteen for ten million offerings, for installing gods and for giving up a temple; half of those for a tank or pond; eighty ratti of gold for the first hearing of the Bharata. The fee goes to the one who was chosen, not to someone else, and a householder who takes the gift becomes indebted. Fees are paid in kind where fitting: land for land, cloth for cloth, a goat for an elephant, a sheep for a horse. The fee is shared in parts among the teacher, the priests, the wife and others. Where one cannot meet the measure, the text names gifts that are priceless (an image, a book, a jewel, cows, grain, sesame, fruits and flowers) and gives values for a Shaligrama, lingams, books by verse count (a gold piece for a hundred verses of the Harivamsha), cows and bulls of different colours.

03-004.json.summary: Suta continues with measures and payments. A "handful" and a "kunchi" are measures for offerings. Fees for building fire-pits are listed by shape: a quarter gold piece for a square one in Kali, silver pieces for Sarvatobhadra, krauncha and others, a cow for the lotus or yoni pit, two mashas for a six-sided one. The text then sets daily wages in panas and kakinis for workers: digging a tank, laying brick, building a well, planting trees, working copper, bronze, lead or gold, setting gems, making cloth, barbers (ten kakinis for a shave), washers, farmers, ploughmen, porters, garland-makers and lamp-makers. The sizes of the lamp-wick and the oil are given. The lamp-stand material is rated: a gold one kills the king, silver grants all wishes, copper shortens life, iron leads to a bad birth; bronze or clay is acceptable. Wick sizes for incense and the large wick of twenty-five threads are given.

03-005.json.summary: Suta teaches the water-pot (kalasha) used at consecration. A pot filled with plain water alone does not bring success; it should have seven or five parts. Gods are called into unbroken rice and flowers and not into anything else. Five leaves (banyan, pipal, dhatri, bilva and others) go on the mouth. Pots of gold, silver, copper or clay are used according to means, free of holes and cracks; sizes are given in finger-widths, with an eight-finger mouth. The pot is set on a swastika drawn with cords; each step has its mantra, with seer, meter and god named: the earth mantra "syona prithivi", the one to smell the pot, the five-rivers mantra with Ganges water, the "yah phalinih" mantra for fruit and unbroken rice, "hiranyagarbha" for five jewels, and others for flowers, scent, grass, and five grains (sesame, urad, mung, millet and rice). Some fruits (jujube, citrus, amla and others) are not put in. A wrong order lets a demon take it.

03-006.json.summary: Suta explains the four kinds of month: the lunar (from new moon to new moon), the solar (while the sun is in one sign), the civil (30 days) and the star month. Each is used for different purposes: the civil month for sacrifices, atonements, mantra practice, a child's first feeding, the king's tax and business; the solar month for weddings and some vows; the lunar for the monthly shraddha, the eighth-day rites and vows set by the lunar day. A month is named by the full moon star (Chaitra from Chitra, and so on). The extra month (adhika) and the "dirty" month (malamasa) come when the sun does not change sign in a lunar month, and these are explained with counting of days. Rites not to be done in the extra month are listed (installations, vow starts, weddings, house-building, great gifts, pilgrimage bathing and rites for gain), while rites for the dead, the yearly rite for a husband, rites for the sacred thread of kings, pregnancy rites and similar are allowed. The setting of Venus and the old age or youth of Venus are said to stop rites in the same way. "Dvirashadha" is explained, and Vishnu is said to sleep in Karka (the sign Cancer), the god-wake being in Tula.

03-007.json.summary: Suta teaches that rites bear fruit by time, and gives rules for choosing the day (tithi) for each. Rites for gods are done in the forenoon, the rite for one person in midday, and the monthly shraddha in the afternoon. A tithi is of three kinds (short, proud, fierce) and the choice of which day to take depends on whether the moon is bright or dark. Fasts and vows are taken on the tithi that is present at sunrise or sunset, with rules for how long it must last, and certain days (second with the fire, fourth with the fifth, eleventh) are said to give merit. A tithi pierced by the next one is to be avoided for fasts, for example the sixth, eighth and fourteenth. Fasting on the eleventh is to be done with the twelfth. The text sets out rules for the seventh, the thirteenth and fourteenth, the new moon, and festival days such as Lalita seventh and the Shakra festival. Driving a plough or riding animals is forbidden on some days (bright eleventh, new moon, sankranti, shraddha days). The water-pot shraddha has its own rules. A man who has left his parents or sells oil and offerings, and a man with no son or wife, is said to have no right to the sacrifice.

03-008.json.summary: Suta describes the lunar days (tithis) and what each gives, in order. Pratipada: bathing, giving and worship of Shiva and Vishnu are tenfold in Kartika, Ashvina, Chaitra and Magha. Second: a vow kept by women so that they are not widowed, and a month of honouring a married couple with cloth, scent and flowers. Third (Vaishakha bright third and others): bathing in the Ganges frees from sin, and gifts, especially water, grow without end. Fourth: Ganesha is worshipped with sweets to remove obstacles; the three fourths (Shiva, Shanta, Sukha) are named. Fifth: in Shravana the nine Nagas are bathed with scented water, and the goddess Manasa is worshipped for safety from snakes. Sixth and seventh: bathing and gifts are said not to wear out, and the seventh is dear to the sun, best on a Sunday. Eighth: Chandika, the eighteen-armed goddess, is worshipped in Ashvina and Kartika, with fasts and night rites. Ninth and tenth: worship and fasting are advised. The eleventh and twelfth have long rules for fasting (Ekadashi) and breaking the fast on the twelfth, with what to do when the days overlap, and the "Vijaya" and "Vishnu-shrinkhala" twelfths. A king's flagpole (Indra's banner) is raised on the bright twelfth of Bhadrapada with a seven-day worship, and omens of its falling are tied to the planets, with remedies. Thirteenth: Kamadeva is worshipped, and the dark thirteenth with Shatabhisha is the great Varuni. Fourteenth: the Ananta vow with a thread of fourteen knots, and Shivaratri on the dark fourteenth of Phalguna, with a bath and worship in each watch of the night. The full-moon days are named (Maha-Chaitri, Maha-Vaishakhi and so on) with the holy places linked to each (Shaligrama, Haridwar, Puri, Kedara, Badari, Pushkara, Ayodhya, Prayaga, Naimisha), then Kaumudi, the Ashvina full moon, for Lakshmi. A rule against eating twice on the new-moon day closes the chapter.

03-009.json.summary: Suta gives the lines of "pravara", the lists of ancestor-sages that a family names at rites. For the families of Kashyapa, Gautama, Jamadagni, Shandilya, Parashara, Atri, Vatsya, Kaushika (Vishvamitra), Jaimini, Gargya, Vasishtha, Agastya, Angirasa-Bharadvaja and others, the text names the sets of three or five sage-names that form their pravara. Examples are Kashyapa-Avatsara-Naidhruva, Jamadagni-Aplavana-Cyavana, and the Kaushika group with Devarata. At the end it says that those not named, or not known, are to be counted as Kashyapa lines. The names are listed in a compressed form and some are hard to read.

03-010.json.summary: Suta teaches the Vastu rite for a site or temple. A raised square platform of three hands is made and a diagram of nine squares per side drawn on it. Forty-five Vastu gods are worshipped on it, with the central square for Brahma, and others around him, including Shikhi, Parjanya, Jayanta, Indra, Surya, Satya, Vrisha, Akasha, Vayu, Pusha, Vitatha, Yama, Gandharva, Bhringaraja, Mriga, Nirriti, Sugriva, Varuna, Pushpadanta, Asura, Shesha, Roga, Bhallata, Soma, Aditi and Diti. Outside the corners are the demonesses Charaki, Vidari, Putana and Papa-rakshasi. Lines are drawn in white, the lotus in red, and the outer rim in five colours. Each god has his colour, mount, meditation form, seer, meter and mantra, for example Aryaman red on a white-horse chariot, Vivasvan yellow on a ram, Mitra white on a swan, Indra yellow on a white Airavata, Rudra white on a bull, Yama black on a buffalo with a staff. A second form with nine squares and fifty-three gods is also given. After the offerings of cakes or rice-milk, a fire rite is done and a fee of gold given (half for a tank rite).

03-011.json.summary: Suta begins the order of worship, as taught in the Puranas and smritis, and addresses the Brahmins. He first describes how to mark out the ground by a river bank: a circle, a raised altar of set measures, a three-tiered fire pit with its lower part, and a mental resolve to be made before the rite. Worship starts with Ganesha in a pot in the north-east, then Vishnu and the guardians of the directions in the pit, and Brahma in the fire pit, each with their own mantras. After breath control and purification of the elements, the worshipper is told to picture the "lord of the house-site" as a white, four-armed figure, with many deities of the site placed on the parts of his body. The chapter then lists, deity by deity, the form to be pictured, the mantra, the seer, the metre and the offering for the site's gods and the surrounding spirits, with sacred earth, waters and plants gathered for the rite. It ends with fire offerings and a table of foods for each deity, and a hymn of praise to Vishnu said to be spoken by Shankara (Shiva), with the promise of immortality for one who reads it daily.

03-012.json.summary: Suta continues the house-site rite. The sponsor of the rite, facing north, is told to prepare a water pot with gold and silver, scented water and herbs, and to invite the water deity with a short verse, offering respectful water to him and other gods. With his wife he holds the pot, then releases pairs of fish, sheep, birds or snakes for long life, and offers a food-offering to the spirits of the directions. He gives a milch cow to the teacher and gifts of gold and cows to other Brahmins, makes the closing fire offerings, bathes, and offers water to the sun. Then he enters the new house and feeds Brahmins and the poor, and shares a meal with relatives. The chapter lists foods that are praised and avoided, and ends with rules on the measures of the house, in hands, for the first stage of building.

03-013.json.summary: Suta, addressing the Brahmins, describes the fire rite of the household tradition, which is done for sons and daughters and for the sponsor's heirs at birth ceremonies and peace rites. Each step has its own mantra with a named seer, metre and deity: taking the three-blade grass, cleansing the ground, sweeping and smearing the area, drawing lines, and bringing the fire from the proper place while setting aside the "flesh-eating" fire. The Brahma priest is seated to the south of the fire, and a water vessel is placed to the north. The chapter gives measures and materials for the spoon and vessels, where each rice, grain, cake and fruit is to be laid, and how to strain and sprinkle the clarified butter. Fire offerings are made to the directions in order, ending with the closing offering to Varuna. It is mostly a technical list of directions, mantras and sequence.

03-014.json.summary: Suta continues, naming the priest at every sacrifice and the standard offerings that must be made in all fire rites. These are the two "pouring" offerings, the two butter-portion offerings, three sacred utterances (bhur, bhuvah, svah), the five atonement mantras, the offering to Prajapati and the closing offering, fourteen in all. He then explains how the daily and occasional offerings are combined or dropped in one-day and multi-day rites, at weddings and similar events. He assigns a presiding deity to each step: Brahma at the fire, Vishnu at the praise, Maheshvara at the spoon, and others. The chapter is short and breaks off with a remark that the deities are named for the good of the twice-born.

03-015.json.summary: Suta says he will now give the best way to picture these deities, which are the tongues of the sacrificial fire; knowing them makes the rite bear fruit. Eight short verses describe each tongue in turn, by colour, number of arms, what she holds and how she sits: golden, white with water pot and grass, red with conch and discus, dark, red-hued and others, each with a prayer for her favour. The last verse turns to practical steps: looking at the place, digging it with a mantra, and laying out threads. The chapter is very short.

03-016.json.summary: Suta describes the day before the installation (pratishtha): the deities are made to "dwell" in the place, grain and the sacrificial post are set up, Ganesha is placed in a pot at night, and the guardians of the directions and planets are worshipped. Different deities are named for different works, such as Brahma for tanks and gardens and Varuna for peace rites and wells. The chapter lists the mantras used for bathing the image or post, scent, oil, flowers, fruit, grass, vermilion, eye-black, sandal, cloth and incense, and gives gifts such as a sword and a club. Priests and the sponsor eat plain food, avoiding salt and certain items. It ends with the sizes of the fire pit and hall, and the offering materials suited to each tradition, such as Vishnu, Shiva, the goddess, the sun, Gopala, Krishna and Sarasvati.

03-017.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, sets out who should serve at a dedication rite: eight fire-priests, eight door-keepers, eight other Brahmins and one chanting priest, all pure and well marked. They must be honoured with scents, gold, cloth and fees, and the text warns that without this honour the rite bears no fruit and the giver suffers in hell. Persons who may not be chosen as ritual vessels are listed, among them the childless, the diseased, the deceased wife's husband, a servant of Shudras, the greedy, the proud and the maimed. Short prayers of respect are given for the teacher and for the Yajurveda, and the priests and door-keepers are placed around the hall. The chapter then teaches that every rite needs a firm resolve (sankalpa), since desire is its root and a deed without it bears little fruit, and it lists the nine witnesses to deeds (the Ganga, sun, moon, sky, earth, night, day, Yama and the five elements). It closes with a verse describing Dharma as a white bull-shaped figure, and a rule that the same Brahmins be kept for the whole rite.

03-018.json.summary: Suta describes the time and place for installing a water-tank or similar work. The six months from Magha onward are suitable, until Vishnu sleeps; Fridays, Thursdays, Wednesdays and Mondays are good; and certain lunar days are named as auspicious, with others allowed at the equinoxes and on holy days. The hall is described: round, sixteen hands wide, with four doors at the four sides and gateways made of the fig and banyan family of trees. Flags in the colours of the guardians of the directions are to be raised, with a blue one in the centre, and the hall is ringed with reeds, grass and sugar-cane. Rules follow for the altar in the middle and the square fire pit with its tiered rim, and for the pot placed to the north-east of the pit. The chapter ends mid-description of the pot, covered with cloth and holding gold.

03-019.json.summary: Suta describes the main installation of a tank or reservoir. The sponsor performs his daily rites, makes his resolve with the Brahmins' permission, holds the growth-rite for ancestors, and chooses the teacher and priests with gifts.
