He and his wife are bathed with water from eight kinds of grain and herbs, then enter the sacrificial hall by the west door with sons and grandsons. After honouring the obstacle-remover, the Ganga and Yamuna, he sits, drives away harmful spirits, honours his seat and the Earth, and starts the worship. A long section gives the forms to be pictured and the offerings for Varuna the water god, the sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn and the two shadow planets, the guardians of the eight directions, Brahma, Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha, Lakshmi, the goddess Ambika killing the buffalo demon, Earth, Vishvakarma and Sarasvati. Chants and sacred hymns to be recited are listed, as are fire offerings. After bathing the sponsor and a sacred post, a formal gift of the water to all beings is made in a set sentence, fish and turtles are put in, and the pond is honoured and circled. The sponsor gives gold, cows and food to the priests, and returns home to feed Brahmins, children and the poor.

03-020.json.summary: Suta begins with a note that the rite just described is the best, middle and lower versions giving middle and lower fruit, and says he will now give the middle form, for those of average means. The post and other items are made ready the day before. The chapter repeats the choice of a worthy priest, lists persons to avoid (for example the wifeless, the childless and a priest who serves crowds), and gives short prayers to the teacher. The sponsor and his wife enter the hall, and the pots, altar and the nine-pot layout for Varuna, Brahma, Vasudeva and the guardians are described, with the musical measure for each deity, and the food offering for each planet. Eight great serpents, such as Ananta, Vasuki and Takshaka, are made in metals and honoured with offerings. Fire offerings, bathing of the sponsor, planting of the post, offering of gifts, and the setting of Varuna into the pond with fish, birds and turtles follow. The gift of the water to all beings is repeated, with fees to priests and a feast for Brahmins, children and the poor.

04-001.json.summary: The Madhyama Parva, third part, begins. Suta says he will now teach the special rules for gardens and similar works. A square, level area is marked out, with a pot for the god in the north-east, a middle pot for the planets, and Varuna in the centre. Vasudeva (Vishnu) is to be pictured in the centre of the lotus, four-armed with conch, discus, mace and lotus, attended by Lakshmi and Pushti, and worshipped with the usual offerings. The moon, Indra, Shiva and others are given places, and a table of fire offerings is given for each. The fire's seven tongues are named. The chapter ends with the ear-piercing of the trees with a needle (a rite for newly planted trees), gifts to the teacher and priests, and rules for bridge and causeway works, including laying five jewels in a hole and planting banana trees by the bridge. Another ritual verse notes that a person who falls from a tree is not stained by sin.

04-002.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, gives the rite for dedicating a cow-pasture (gopracara). Vishnu with Lakshmi, Brahma, Rudra, Varaha, the sun, moon and Mahadeva are worshipped, fire offerings are made, and a post with serpent hoods is planted. The giver then says the verse of gift: a jewel is placed in the ground and the land is given to the cows. The text promises freedom from sin and a stay in Vishnu's world for as many thousand years as there are blades of grass; it also says one who digs up or ploughs a pasture ruins his family and incurs the guilt of killing a Brahmin. A "cow-hide" of land is defined as the area where a hundred cows and one bull graze freely. The chapter then describes the rite for a roadside shelter (mandapa) for travellers, with prayers to the guardians of the directions, and for a well, with the eight serpent kings invoked by name. It closes with the rite for a garden, which includes piercing the trees' ears, a formal gift sentence, the same verse about falling from a tree, and gifts to priests.

04-003.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, describes the dedication of a small garden. On a level plot, a pot is set up and Vishnu and the moon are worshipped; one teacher is chosen; the trees are wrapped with thread, garlanded and given their "wish" offering, and five Brahmins are fed. The ears of the trees are pierced, the garden is formally given away, a post is set up in the middle and banana plants in the directions. Fire offerings and the fee follow. The chapter ends with the rule for a single tree: worship of Dharma, Earth, the guardians and others at its foot, a cow as fee, and water offered to the sun.

04-004.json.summary: Suta describes the rite of installing a pipal (ashvattha) tree, and, in the same chapter, a pond. A square of ground is prepared at the foot of the tree, a lotus is drawn, a pot is set up the night before, three Brahmins are fed, and the tree is wrapped in white thread. Ganesha, Brahma, the guardians of the directions and the nine planets are worshipped. Shiva is pictured as a white, two-armed figure with a trident, seated on a bull, and honoured with the usual offerings and fire offerings. The text then turns to the dedication of a pond, with the water god Varuna made in silver, a serpent figure of Ananta, and a set of fire offerings. The sponsor says a formal sentence to give the pond to Brahmins for the use of all beings, boats are used, and fish and turtles are released. Fees, milk poured round the pond, and kindness to the poor close the rite.

04-005.json.summary: Suta gives the rule for installing a lotus-pond, a step-well or a lake, and then for a garden or a single tree. The place is prepared the day before, Ganesha, Varuna, Shiva, Vishnu and others are worshipped, and fire offerings and food gifts are made. The sponsor sets up a post and gives a cow as fee, then offers water to the sun. The garden rite then begins: a round hall and a square fire pit in a forest to the west or north, with Vishvaksena and Vasudeva (Vishnu) pictured with two consorts, the moon, Vanaspati (lord of trees) and a series of fire offerings. Water is mixed with Ganga water and herbs, the sponsor is bathed with prayers, and the teacher and Brahmins are given a cow, a metal vessel and fees.

04-006.json.summary: This short chapter repeats, almost word for word, the rite for a small garden given in chapter 260: a pot is set in a prepared place, Vishnu and the moon are worshipped, trees are wrapped and garlanded, five Brahmins are fed, the ears of the trees are pierced, and the garden is formally given. A post is put in the middle with banana plants in the directions, and fire offerings and the fee follow. The chapter ends with the usual closing line giving it as the sixth chapter of the third part.

04-007.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, gives the rite for one or a few chosen trees, almost as in chapter 260. A pot is set on the west side of the tree, the tree is wrapped with thread, and Brahma, the moon, Vishnu and Vanaspati (lord of trees) are worshipped. Fire offerings of sesame and barley are made, the post is given with a banana plant, and Dharma, Earth, the guardians and attendant spirits are honoured at the tree's foot. A cow is given as fee and water is offered to the sun. This chapter is very short.

04-008.json.summary: Suta gives again the rite for installing a pipal (ashvattha) tree, a shorter form of chapter 261. A square of ground is marked with sandalwood at the foot of the tree and a lotus drawn on it. The night before, a pot is set up and three Brahmins are fed. Ganesha, Brahma, the guardians of the directions and the planets are worshipped, then Shiva is placed in the circle with his attendants Chanda, Pracanda, Nandi and Bhringi, Ananta, Kama and Ganesha, and Kartikeya in the middle. Shiva is pictured as a white two-armed figure with a trident, and Vishnu is worshipped at the foot and Brahma at the top. Food offerings and fire offerings for Rudra follow, a banana plant is set up, and the teacher is satisfied with gifts. The rite ends with milk poured in five streams and water offered to the sun.

04-009.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, gives a very short rule for dedicating a banyan tree. At its foot, on the south side, a three-hand altar is made with three pots, and Ganesha, Shiva and Vishnu are worshipped. A rice-and-milk offering is cooked, red threads and gold are used, a barley-and-milk food-offering is given, and the tree is formally given away with spoken words. The post is planted and bound with banyan roots, and the chapter ends in a list of yakshas, nagas, gandharvas, siddhas and wind-gods, apparently those to be honoured. The text is cut short.

04-010.json.summary: Suta describes the dedication of a bilva tree, the tree sacred to Shiva. The night before, a pot is set up and the tree is made ready, and the rite follows an eight-petal drawing at the foot and the binding of the tree with red threads. Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Durga, Kubera and others are worshipped, with fire offerings of sesame, food offerings to yakshas, twelve gifts of cakes and a fee including gold and a bronze vessel. Seven Brahmins and a couple are fed, the post is planted, the tree's ears are pierced, and water is offered to the sun. Suta then gives a night version of the rite, saying that one who performs the single-tree rite is not born again on earth. It ends with pots, milk and cow-products, a feast for a Brahmin couple and the fee of grain and a cow.

04-011.json.summary: Suta states a short promise: a person who makes a plot of land a hundred hands in size, planted with trees and with betel-nut and mango fruits, and worships there, lives in heaven for sixty thousand years. He then gives the rule in brief, which is to complete the daily rites, honour five Brahmins and feed them, worship Vishnu together with Prajapati, make the fire offering and give a fee to a Brahmin. The chapter is very short and gives no more detail.

04-012.json.summary: Suta gives the rite of dedicating a hall (mandapa) built of stone, wood, grass or straw. On the evening before, a pot is set up at an auspicious hour, and the sun, moon and Vishnu are worshipped in it, with sprinkling of water, scent, oil, sandal, vermilion and eye-black. At dawn the growth-rite for ancestors is done, the guardians of the directions are placed, and Ganesha, the planets and the sun are worshipped with a fire offering of milk-rice. The hall is then formally given to Brahmins and all beings, with the words of gift given in the text, and a white pot is set on top, with the hall wrapped in thread and water. A fee is given and water is offered to the sun. A further note covers a shelter for water-giving, where Varuna and Vishvakarma are worshipped, and says that the flag alone is enough when nothing else can be done.

04-013.json.summary: Suta describes the rite of consecrating a well with a great post, four hands high and sixteen hands long, over three nights. Varuna is set in a white pot on the west of the well, and the bathing, scent, oil, flower, incense, cloth and food-offering mantras are given. No ancestral rite is done at the start; it is done at the end. A couple is fed, one Brahmin is chosen, and Varuna is worshipped with Narayana, Shiva and Earth. Ten fire offerings go to Varuna and one each to the others, with the names of Shiva (Shankara, Rudra, Sharva, Pashupati, Ugra, Bhava, Mahadeva, Ishana) in a food-offering. The well is given with a spoken sentence in which the giver says he is doing it for his father, and a milch cow and fee follow. A short rule for a small well in a hall closes the chapter.

04-014.json.summary: Suta describes the dedication of a flower garden. A three-hand altar is made in the middle, a pot is set up, and the day before the Brahmins are fed. Ganesha, the sun, the moon, Agni and Narayana are worshipped. A milk-rice and honey offering is made, the post is planted in the north-east, the ears of the plants are pierced, and wheat is sprinkled. A fee of grain, barley and wheat is given to a Brahmin, and the garden is bound round with water poured in many streams. The chapter is very short.

04-015.json.summary: Suta describes the rite for installing a tulasi (holy basil) plant, to be done in the months Jyeshtha and Ashadha, on a pure day or on the eleventh lunar day. The night before, a pot is set up and Narayana, Shiva, the moon, Brahma and Indra are worshipped, with a list of mantras for scent, oil, flowers, sandal, grass, mirror, fruit and eye-black. Women who are devoted to their husbands bathe the plant. After the ancestral rite and the choice of the teacher as priest, a ten-hand hall is prepared and Narayana is worshipped with the planets, the world-guardians, Adityas, Maruts, Rudras and Vasus. A fire offering of sesame and barley is made, a post and banana plants are set up, and a fee including gold, a milch cow and a pouring of milk follows. The chapter ends with a list of trees for which this installation, or the piercing of ears, is not to be done, for example the jayanti, kadamba, neem, pipal-like trees, the shalmali and the khadira.

04-016.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, says the dedication of trees and similar works can be done in the best, middle or lower form. This chapter gives the rite for a bridge or causeway (setu). A round or square area is marked, a pot is set up the night before, and Earth and Shiva are worshipped. Scent, sandal, grass, fruit, cloth and eye-black are offered with mantras, and the ancestral rite is done the next day. A teacher and a main priest are chosen, with extra priests for large rites. Vishnu as Shesha and as the boar, Varaha, is worshipped, with fire offerings in sets and food offerings. The giver says a set sentence: he gives the bridge to Vishnu to raise twenty-one generations of his family to heaven. A verse says that if people fall in the mud or are hurt at the bridge, he is not to be stained by sin, and he gives away the merit of building it. A post and flags, a fee and a feast for relatives follow, and a shorter form for a small bridge is added.

04-017.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, goes on with the gift of grazing land. Someone who gives a square plot of sixty hands for cows to graze lives sixty thousand years in the world of Rudra, with smaller rewards for half, a quarter or an eighth, or for giving land, a maiden, a slave-girl or a bull. A cow given without ornaments earns half the fruit. The place is prepared, Brahma, Indra, Ganesha, the field guardian and the guardians of the directions are worshipped, a post is set and the ground is given with a sentence of gift. The text repeats that the giver is freed from sin, goes to Vishnu's world and stays there for as many thousand years as there are blades of grass on the land.

04-018.json.summary: Suta explains that in the present age (Kali), a person of small means can do a dedication in one day, by making the god dwell in the image at once, using clarified butter. The rite should begin after the sun turns north and after autumn, in spring. A set of thirty-two forms of Narayana and others, and images such as the elephant-faced Ganesha, may be installed. The sponsor does his daily rites, then the growth-rite, feeds Brahmins and goes to the sacrificial hall. Ganesha, the planets and the guardians are worshipped in pots, and Vishnu with his attendants on a prepared ground. The image is bathed with five kinds of water, with the five nectars, the five cow products, five kinds of earth, oils, decoctions and flower waters. The breath of life is invoked in the image, a fire offering is made, and the fee is given. This chapter is short.

04-019.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, goes on to the installation of images of the goddesses such as Kali and Tara. The place is made ready the day before, the ancestral growth-rite is done, and the goddess Durga is worshipped in a pot and then at a bilva tree, with the breath of life called into the image. The rule for images of Kali and Tara is that the image is bathed for three days, worshipped morning and night in a copper pot, and then placed in a chest with food offerings, animal gifts and fire offerings on the eighth day. Next he turns to the installation of the Shiva lingam, with the usual choices of teacher and priests, bathing, worship with attendants, and a gift of a cow of sesame or gold. Then a stone for a household shrine is installed on the twelfth lunar day and installation rules are given for images of the sun, Ganesha, Brahma, the boar-goddess and many forms of the goddess. The chapter ends with a three-day rite with girl worship, fire offerings, animal gifts where means allow, and a night of waking at the monastery festival.

04-020.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the sages, begins the teaching on bad omens and their remedies. Omens are divided into three kinds: those of the sky, of the air, and of the earth. Examples given include meteors, fire in the sky, halos, dryness of tanks, gods seen laughing or weeping or bleeding, falling stones in rain, earthquakes, comets, eclipses, birds like owls entering a house, snakes or frogs appearing in pots, lightning striking a house, strange growth of plants, and cows behaving oddly. For each, the text says what harm may follow, to the household, the king, the ministers or the country, and the remedy, a fire offering of ten thousand oblations on a day linked to the planet concerned (sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu and the comet), a cooked offering, and a gift of a cow, gold or cloth to a Brahmin. The last part gives the number of fire offerings for each planet and day in a three-day rite. The last verse gives a verse count in an unclear way and says the Bhavishya would then be complete.

05-001.json.summary: The Pratisarga Parva (the "history" part) begins with a prayer to Narayana, Nara, the goddess Sarasvati and Vyasa. Shaunaka asks Suta which kings ruled in the twenty-eighth Satya age of the Vaivasvata period, and for the length of their reigns. Suta answers with a list of the sun-line kings, beginning with Vaivasvata Manu, whose son was Ikshvaku, born after a hundred years of penance on the Sarayu river. The chapter names a long series of kings and gives each a rule of thousands of years, shortening step by step: Vikukshi, Kakutstha, Prithu, Yuvanashva, Mandhata, Purukutsa, Trishanku, Harishchandra, Rohita, Sagara and others down to Sudarshana. It notes which kings were devoted to Vishnu and which to Shiva, and mentions Sagara's sons, Bhagiratha, Ambarisha, Kalmashapada, and Khatvanga's help to Indra. Sudarshana, who is devoted to the goddess, wins the Kashi king's daughter, and rules five thousand years. Then the great goddess Mahakali tells him in a dream to go with his wife and with Vasishtha and others to the Himalaya, as a great wind will destroy the land of Bharata and its seas and islands within seven years. He goes with leading kings, merchants and Brahmins. The chapter then describes the world drying and changing over about five to ten years, until the ground appears again as dry land.

05-002.json.summary: Suta continues the story. On the third day of the bright half of Vaishakha, a Thursday, Sudarshana returns to Ayodhya with the people, and by the goddess Maya's power the city is made splendid again. After ten thousand years of rule he reaches the eternal world, and his son Dilipa follows. The sun-line then runs through Raghu, Aja, Dasharatha and Rama (called Hari himself, whose reign is given as eleven thousand years), then Kusha, Atithi, Nala and many more, down to names such as Shakyavardhana, Prasenajit, Shudraka and Suratha. The text says the sixty-five kings of the Raghu line were devoted to the goddess and to animal sacrifice, and that the sons who were born then were of mixed classes. A second line follows from Chandra, sent by Indra, who ruled at Prayaga, with Budha, Pururava and Urvashi, Ayu, Nahusha (who became Indra and was cursed to be a snake by Durvasa), Yayati and his five sons, Yadu, and Pururava's descendants down to Samvarana. Samvarana does penance in the Himalaya and the sun, pleased, gives him the maiden Tapati; the king then goes to the sun's world. The text next says that by Maya's power the age reached its end: the four seas grew, then dried, and the land became dry again through Agastya's power. Samvarana is named at the end as coming back at the sun's order with Tapati, a sage and Vasishtha. The chapter is cut off here.

05-003.json.summary: Shaunaka asks Suta, here called Lomaharshana, when King Samvarana came back and who the kings of the Dvapara age were. Suta says that on the thirteenth of the dark half of Bhadra, on a Friday, Samvarana returned with the sages to Pratishthana, a fine city five yojanas long built by Vishvakarma. Other rulers were set up: one in the Yadu line at Mathura (Satvata), and one among the mleccha line in the desert country. A very long list of kings follows, mostly giving each a rule equal to or shorter than his father's, with many names formed from the sun, Brahma and moon. It includes Dushyanta and Shakuntala's son Bharata, from whom the land is said to be named Bharata, and Hastin, who founded Hastinapura on the Ganga. Kuru makes Kurukshetra, twenty yojanas wide, and the line runs through Shantanu, Vichitravirya, Pandu, Yudhishthira and Duryodhana, who is killed at Kurukshetra. The text says the demons killed in the old war with the gods were reborn in Shantanu's time, and that the earth, burdened by their armies, went to Indra, after which Hari was born as Krishna to Vasudeva and Devaki, lived one hundred and thirty-five years and went to Goloka. Kings after Abhimanyu's son follow, ending with Kshemaka, who leaves his kingdom, is killed by mlecchas and goes to the world of Yama. By Narada's advice, his son Pradyota does a mleccha sacrifice, in which the mlecchas are destroyed. The chapter ends there; the next explains the rite.

05-004.json.summary: Shaunaka asks how Pradyota did the sacrifice. Suta says that Narada came to Pradyota at Hastinapura, told him his father had been killed by mlecchas, and said a mleccha sacrifice would bring the father to heaven. Pradyota, angry, called Vedic Brahmins to Kurukshetra, made a square fire pit of sixteen yojanas, and by Vedic mantras burnt peoples such as the Hara-Hunas, Barbaras, Shakas, Khasas, Yavanas, Pahlavas, Chinas and others. Kshemaka went to heaven, and Pradyota, called "slayer of mlecchas", ruled ten thousand years; his son Vedavan followed. Kali, in the form of a mleccha, then praises Narayana, complaining that the Vedic king had destroyed his place. Hari appears and says he will take many forms to fulfil Kali's wish, naming a man Adama and his wife Havyavati, born of Vishnu and Kardama, to increase the mleccha line. Kali goes to Nilachala; the next king, Sunanda, dies childless, and the people of the Aryan land decline while mleccha lines grow. The sages of Naimisha, eighty-eight thousand of them, go to the Himalaya to worship Vishnu. Suta then tells the story of Adam and Havyavati: Kali, as a snake, deceives the wife in a forest east of the city of Pradana, they eat the fruit against Vishnu's command, cover themselves with fig leaves, and their children are mlecchas; Adam lives nine hundred and thirty years. His descendants follow (Shveta, Anuha, Kinasha, Mahallala, Virada, Hanuka and others), described as keeping some Vedic virtues. Nyuha, a devotee of Vishnu, is warned in a dream of a flood in seven days, builds a large boat, boards it with his family and all kinds of creatures, and survives forty days of rain that cover the land. The sages praise the goddess under many names, she calms the waters, and after a year the land dries; Nyuha, with his sons Sima, Shama and Bhava, lands near the Himalaya and settles.

05-005.json.summary: Shaunaka asks what has happened since the flood up to the present. Suta says that Nyuha, a mleccha, was deluded by Vishnu's illusion and his line grew; mleccha speech, turned away from the Vedic word, was made for him, and Nyuha's three sons are named as Sima, Hama and Yakuta. Their descendants and the lands named after them are listed in a general way, including Yakuta's seven sons and the four sons of Hama. Suta then falls into yogic sleep, and wakes after two thousand one hundred years to give the line of Sima: Sima rules five hundred years, followed by a line of sons with reigns of several hundred years each, which are named only in passing. The text says mleccha speech arose through Sarasvati's curse and is very low, while Sanskrit speech stays in Bharata. The sages at Vishala meditate on Nara-Narayana for two hundred years and are woken and ask about the present king. Suta says that, three thousand years into Kali, a king named Shankha rules in Avanti, and a Shaka lord rules in the mleccha land. He says that by Kali's second thousand the land was full of mlecchas, apart from Brahmavarta, that a mleccha teacher called Musha filled the world with his teachings, and he lists four kinds of mleccha speech and sample words. He adds that the holy seven cities see violence, that in mleccha lands the wise follow mleccha ways, and that mleccha rule is found in Bharata and its islands. He advises the sage to worship Hari, and the sages weep.

05-006.json.summary: Shaunaka asks why the mlecchas did not reach Brahmavarta. Suta says it is through Sarasvati's power. A Brahmin named Kashyapa, sent from heaven at the gods' order in the first thousand years of Kali, and his wife Aryavati had ten sinless sons, named by their learning or duties (for example Upadhyaya, Dikshita, Pathaka, Agnihotri, Dvivedi, Trivedi and Chaturvedi). Kashyapa goes to Kashmir and praises Sarasvati with red flowers, incense and food, asking her to make Sanskrit the best speech and to confuse the mlecchas. She is pleased; he goes to a land called Mishra, wins over the mlecchas, and makes ten thousand of them Brahmins, two thousand Vaishyas, and the rest Shudras. They live with him in the Aryan land, grow to four crore people, and he rules a hundred and twenty years. His son Magadha is made king, and from his time the Aryan land is divided into regions around Magadha. Shaunaka rejoices and later asks about the kings after Magadha. Suta lists the kings, from Shishunaga (born from a sacrifice as part of Balabhadra) through the Nanda line and Mahananda. Then, because Kali called to mind Hari, the text says Hari was born as Gautama, who changed to the Buddhist teaching and ruled at Pattana; Shakyamuni, Shuddhodana and Shakyasimha follow. The Vedic path is said to be destroyed and all people Buddhists. Buddhasimha, Chandragupta (who married the daughter of a Yavana ruler), Bindusara and Ashoka follow. At Mount Abu a Brahmin from Kanyakubja performs a fire rite, and four Kshatriyas (Pramara, Chapahani, Shukla and Parihara) are born from it, riding elephants, who overcome Ashoka and kill four lakh Buddhists with divine weapons. Pramara settles in Avanti at the city of Ambavati.

05-007.json.summary: Suta tells where the other three fire-born kings settled: Parihara at Kalinjara near Chitrakuta, where he rules as a destroyer of Buddhists; Chapahani at Ajmer in the land of Rajputs; and Shukla at Dvaraka in Anarta. The sages, asked to say more, are told by Suta that he is going into yogic sleep, and they meditate on Vishnu. After two thousand years he resumes: in Kali year 3,710 (as stated), Pramara rules six years, followed by his descendants and by Gandharvasena, who rules fifty years and then gives the kingdom to his son Shankha. A heavenly woman, Viramati, sent by Indra, bears Gandharvasena a son, and at his birth flowers fall from the sky and drums sound. A Brahmin named Shivadrishti, with disciples, goes to the forest, practises karma-yoga with twenty others and becomes Shiva. In the three-thousandth year of Kali, by Shiva's command, one born from Kailasa, to destroy the Shakas and increase Aryan dharma, is named Vikramaditya by his father. At five he goes to the forest for twelve years of penance, then goes to Ambavati; Shiva sends him a throne with thirty-two figures, and Parvati makes a spirit (Vaitala) to guard him. At Mahakaleshvara he worships Shiva, builds a hall, installs the throne, and listens to Brahmins. Vaitala, in the form of a Brahmin, offers to tell him a great tale. The chapter ends here.

06-001.json.summary: The Pratisarga Parva, second part, begins. Suta says that Vaitala, standing at Mahakaleshvara and thinking of Shiva, tells King Vikramaditya a tale. In Varanasi, King Pratapamukuta's son Vajramukuta, with Buddhidaksha, the minister's son, rides into a forest and sees a lake and a Shiva temple. There he sees Padmavati, daughter of King Dantavaktra of Karnata, and both faint. She takes a lotus from her hair, puts it to her ear, bites it with her teeth, puts it under her foot and then on her heart, and leaves. The prince goes silent with love. Buddhidaksha learns the cause, reads the signs as a message, and with the king's leave goes with him to Karnata. Through an old woman, Buddhidaksha sends messages, she is struck in rage, but he reads the blows and finger marks as signs to come at midnight by the west window. The prince meets her and stays a month. Wishing to see his friend, he asks her leave; she poisons the minister's son's food, but he feeds it to a dog, which dies. The prince, now wary of women's tricks, leaves her, but Buddhidaksha advises him to take her ornaments while she sleeps, mark her knee with a trident, and leave. As a yogi he sells the ornament, the prince is seized as a thief, and the yogi tells the king he saw her as a pishachi in a cremation ground and marked her knee. The king drives out his daughter, and Vajramukuta takes her home. Vaitala asks who gets the great sin; Vikramaditya says the king, because the minister acted for his friend, the guards for their master, and the prince for his goal. He adds rules: a man who does not marry a daughter who has reached puberty goes to hell for sixty thousand years; one who hinders a gandharva marriage is punished by Yama; one who abandons a faultless girl goes to hell for a lakh of years.

06-002.json.summary: Suta says the pleased Vaitala tells a second tale. In Dharmasthala on the Yamuna, King Gunadhipa rules, and his priest Harisharma has a son Satyashila and a daughter Madhumati. When she is twelve, three Brahmins, Vamana, Trivikrama and Keshava, are each chosen for her by her father, brother and herself, and the wedding is fixed for the thirteenth of the dark half of Magha, on a Friday. At that time she is bitten by a snake and dies. Trivikrama becomes a wandering ascetic, Keshava gathers her bones and goes to holy sites, and Vamana stays by her pyre, taking the ashes. Trivikrama, at a house on the Sarayu, sees Ramasharma bring a dead boy back to life with a life-giving mantra, and receives the mantra. He goes to the Yamuna, revives the girl, and also the dead son of King Gunadhipa, who offers a boon; Trivikrama asks him to find Keshava, who brings the bones. When she is revived, she says she will go to the man who is right for her by dharma, and the three stand silent. Vaitala asks who is right for her. Vikramaditya answers that she is right for Vamana: the one who gave life is like a father, and the one who gave the bones is like a brother. The chapter ends on that answer.

06-003.json.summary: Vaitala tells a third tale, and Suta calls it charming. In Vardhavan, King Rupasena and Queen Vidvanmala have as servant a warrior, Viravara, who comes with his wife, son and daughter and receives a thousand gold pieces daily, half of which he spends on fire rites, holy places and Brahmins. After a year, the goddess Royal Fortune (Rajalakshmi), on Shiva's order, weeps in a cemetery at midnight to test them. The king sends Viravara to find out. She says she is Rupasena's fortune, that the king will die in a month, and that he can live long if Viravara's son's head is offered to Chandika. Viravara's wife, son and daughter all agree; the son asks to be offered, Viravara cuts off his head, and his daughter, wife and he himself die. Seeing this, the king offers his own head. The goddess, pleased, revives all and grants the king a boon, and he asks that Viravara and his family live. The king gives his daughter Kamarupini to Viravara's son. Vaitala asks who showed the best love; the answer given is that the king did, offering his body for a servant, while the servant loved gold, the wife followed duty, the sister loved her kin and the son loved his father.

06-004.json.summary: Suta tells how Vaitala continues with a fourth tale. In the city of Bhogavati, King Rupavarma keeps a wise parrot, Chudamani, who tells him, when he is thirty and asks for a bride, that Chandravati, daughter of the king of Magadha, is right for him. A Brahmin named Ganesha is sent with gifts to arrange it. He praises Shiva, and Chandravati, with her friend the female myna Madanamanjari (Menaka), prays to Durga, who confuses her parents and has the wedding done within a month. Later the king tells Menaka to marry the parrot. She refuses with a story of a wicked merchant's son, Madapala, who gambled and drank, lost everything, married the daughter of a rich man by lying, then killed his servant and abandoned his wife, and later killed her too for her ornaments; so she says some matches are unfit. The parrot in turn refuses to marry a lowly, dark female and tells a story of Jayalakshmi, wife of Shridatta, who took a lover, Homadatta, while her husband was away trading; when Homadatta died of snakebite, a spirit in a pipal tree entered his body and bit off her nose, and the thief Kaphalla saw it. The king, told by the thief, put her on a donkey and sent her to the forest. Vaitala asks who is more sinful, the woman or the man. Vikramaditya's answer, as given, is that Maya takes three forms (male, female, neuter) from Brahman, that women are bound more by action, and that action binds while knowledge frees; so he declares the woman more sinful and the man less.

06-005.json.summary: Suta tells a fifth tale from Vaitala. King Mahabala of Ujjayini has a messenger, Haridasa, a devotee of Hari, whose daughter Mahadevi asks to be given to a man better than her father. Sent to King Harishchandra of Telangana, Haridasa tells him about the coming of Kali. He says Nyuha's time came first, that Om came from Brahma's mouth and many deluding languages from the second mouth for Kali's sake, and that Kali's rule is known when Vedic dharma is turned upside down and mlecchas are loved. He describes Kali's family (Falsehood as wife, Misery as son, Bad Fate as his half), kings ruled by anger, Brahmins ruled by desire, the rich by greed, Shudras gaining greatness, shameless women and servants who kill masters, and a barren earth; he says those who take refuge in Hari are glad. Harishchandra gives him gifts. A Brahmin shows Haridasa an aerial vehicle given by the goddess, and Haridasa promises him his daughter. Mukunda, Haridasa's son, is told by his teacher to give his sister to the teacher's son. Mahadevi herself chooses Vamana, a pupil of Drona's son who shoots by sound, so three Brahmins come for her. A rakshasa carries her to the Vindhya mountain; one Brahmin (an astrologer) says where she is, one carries the other two in his vehicle, and the archer kills the rakshasa by sound. They bring her back, and then quarrel over her. Vikramaditya's answer is that the one who found her is like a father, the one who carried them like a brother, and the one who killed the rakshasa is right for the girl.

06-006.json.summary: Suta tells a sixth tale from Vaitala. In Dharmapura, the good King Dharmashila and Queen Lajjadevi have a minister, Andhaka. The king builds a temple to Durga, holds a festival for a child, and Durga appears at midnight and offers a boon; he praises her as the one eternal Prakriti by whom Vishnu, Brahma and all beings act. A voice says he will have a mighty son. A washerman, Kalibhojana, with his friend Kashidasa, sees a girl, Kamangi, walking with her father and, mad with desire, promises Chandika his head if he gets her. The goddess confuses the father and the marriage is made. After a year, Kalibhojana goes to the temple and offers his head; Kashidasa, out of love, offers his, and Kamangi, in grief, offers hers. Chandika revives all three and grants a boon: Kashidasa asks for Kamangi, Kamangi asks for her husband, and Kalibhojana asks for his friend's fine body. Vaitala asks what the goddess did; the answer given is that the heads of the two men had been cut off and she put them the wrong way round, and each received his own boon.

06-007.json.summary: Suta tells a seventh tale from Vaitala. In Champapuri, King Champakesha and Queen Sulochana have a daughter, Trilokasundari, whose beauty is praised. At her svayamvara, kings arrive, and Indra, Yama, Kubera and Varuna come in human form. Four men claim her: one says he is Indradatta, skilled in all the scriptures; another, Dharmadatta, skilled in archery; a third, Dhanapala, who knows the speech of all living things; and a fourth, skilled in the arts, who each day earns five jewels, which he gives to merit, to the fire rite, to himself, to his wife and for good food. The king is bewildered and asks his daughter, but she is shy and does not answer. Vaitala asks whom she should marry. Vikramaditya says Dharmadatta, giving the reasoning: the scripture-skilled man is a Brahmin by class, the language-knower a merchant, the arts-skilled a Shudra and the archer a king, and a girl is always fit for a man of her own class. She is then married to the good Dharmadatta.

06-008.json.summary: Suta tells an eighth tale from Vaitala. In Mithilavati in the Videha land, King Gunadhipa takes in a Kshatriya, Chiramdeva, who settles there for a living. Out hunting, the king kills a tiger and, lost in the forest, hungry and thirsty, is fed by Chiramdeva with cooked deer meat. The king offers him a boon; Chiramdeva asks that a thousand coins be given to him in turn and a hundred each month for his family. Later the king sends him to the sea, where he finds the goddess Kusumada, a gandharva's daughter at Markandeya's place, and asks to marry her. She tells him to bathe in her pool; he is swept back to Mithila and reports it to the king. The king goes to the temple, and the goddess asks him to take her in a gandharva marriage, saying she was cursed to give pleasure to a man. The king refuses, says he treats Chiramdeva like a son, and asks her to be his wife; she becomes like a daughter-in-law to him. Vaitala asks whose truth and duty was the greatest. Vikramaditya answers that Chiramdeva's was the greatest: he served the king faithfully with no other living, and the king saw it in a time of need.

06-009.json.summary: Suta tells a ninth tale from Vaitala, who finds Vikramaditya very capable. In Kamapura, King Virasimha rules justly. The merchant Hiranyadatta's daughter Kamalasa is touched by Somadatta in a forest; she says she is a maiden, promises to come to him on the tenth day after her wedding, and he lets her go. She is married to the merchant's son Madapala. On the ninth day her husband, in desire, embraces her; she weeps, tells him the promise, and he gives her leave. She goes at night; a thief stops her for her ornaments, and she promises to give them after she meets her lover. Somadatta, moved by Vishnu, honours her as a faithful wife and sends her away; the thief, too, let her keep them and returns her to her husband's house. Vaitala asks whose truthfulness was best, and Vikramaditya answers: the thief's. The merchant acted out of fear of the king, she out of fear of widowhood, her husband out of fear of dharma, and the thief out of fear of untruth.

06-010.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala goes on with the tenth tale. In Vardhana city in Gauda country the just king Gunashekhara has a minister, Nirbhayananda, who follows the Jain way. A scorpion stings the king in Shiva's temple and he faints; the minister draws out the poison and then lectures him on six inner enemies born of passion and six born of darkness. He says Vishnu, Rudra, Brahma, Indra, Yama and Kubera are each ruled by one fault and bound by illusion, so worshipping them is pointless, while the Jina who has conquered the six enemies is the one to honour. He teaches worship of the cow, no harm to living things, no meat or drink, honest earnings and feeding the hungry. The king takes up the Jain way and leaves the Vedic path; his sad queen turns to Shiva and by Rudra's boon bears a son, Dharmaraja, devoted to Vedic vows. After Gunashekhara dies and goes to hell, Dharmaraja rules justly and, by his merit, his father reaches heaven. Dharmaraja's three wives are each hurt in different ways by a lotus, the moon and a sound while on a spring outing, and Vaitala asks which is most delicate; the king says the third. Asked which is chief, the Jain or the Vedic way, the king says the Vedic way is eternal, ranks the classes and life stages, and says a householder who lives like an ascetic goes to hell, which he says Jain teaching wrongly allows.

06-011.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the eleventh tale. King Dharmavallabha of Punyapura asks his minister how many kinds of joy there are. The minister lists joy by life stage, the student stage, the householder stage (joy of the senses), the forest stage (joy of duty) and the renunciant's joy as the highest, and adds that without a wife a householder has no happiness. The king travels abroad, finds no fitting wife, and tells the minister (here named Buddhiprakasha) to find one or he will give up his life. At the sea the minister prays, and the sea shows him a golden tree with a lovely girl on it, who vanishes with the tree. The king goes there, reaches the underworld with the girl, and asks for a marriage of mutual choice; she says she will come on the dark fortnight's fourteenth day. On that day a crane-riding Rakshasa touches her and the king kills him. She says she is Madavati, a Vidyadhara's daughter, cursed by her father to be enjoyed by a Rakshasa until a hero takes her. She goes to the king's house and the town celebrates, but the minister, seeing the king with a divine wife, dies at once. Vaitala asks why, and the king says he feared the kingdom would be lost, since a king given to pleasure and pride in a woman loses his realm.

06-012.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the twelfth tale. In Chudapura, King Chudamani's guru Devasvami has a wife Vishalakshi, who by Rudra's boon bears a strong son, Harisvami. His wife Rupalavanika, a heavenly woman born on earth through a sage's curse, sleeps on a rooftop in spring and the gandharva Sukala carries her off in his air-car. Harisvami searches in vain, gives up worldly things and goes to the forest, thinking of Hari. Later he comes to a Brahmin's house, where the Brahmin cooks sweet rice and puts it under a banyan tree while he bathes; a snake poisons the food. An ascetic arrives, eats it, grows faint, and curses the Brahmin for giving poisoned food; he dies and goes to Shiva's world. Vaitala asks who among them gets the sin of killing a Brahmin. The king answers that the snake is poisonous by nature and acted without knowledge, and the Brahmin gave food to a hungry man while fate deceived him, so neither is guilty; the ascetic's death is by fate and he is not sinful either. The king says the sin falls on those who wrongly say the Brahmin did it.

06-013.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the thirteenth tale. In Chandrahridaya, King Ranadhira rules; the rich Vaishya Dharmadhvaja has a daughter, Sukhabhavini. A man devoted to a demon, a gambler who drinks and eats meat, feeds the man-eating Rakshasa Vashara and asks as a boon a hidden pit under the earth for a thief. The thief steals the king's maid and much wealth and keeps them there, in a hidden house built like a fort; the maid becomes his favourite among seven wives. The townsfolk complain, guards are posted, but the demon's illusion fools them. The king goes out at night, meets the thief and pretends to be a thief too, but the maid warns him and shows him the way home. When the king comes back with his army, the Rakshasa eats much of it; the thief tells the king that fleeing does not suit a righteous man, so the king prays to the goddess Mahakali, gets a mantra, burns the pit and the Rakshasa to ash and binds the thief. The thief is paraded on a donkey; Sukhabhavini sees him, falls for him and begs her father to free him, but the king will not take five lakh in money. The thief laughs, then weeps, at the stake and dies; she enters the fire with his body, and Durga revives both and grants a boon. Vaitala asks why the thief laughed first and then wept. The king answers that he wept because he could give nothing back to a woman ready to die for him, and laughed at the play of Krishna, who does not give heaven's fruit to the unrighteous or hell's fruit to the righteous.

06-014.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the fourteenth tale. In Pushpavati, King Suvichara and Queen Chandraprabha have a daughter, Chandravali. In a garden she sees the Brahmin Sudeva and both are struck by desire; he faints. Two learned Brahmins, Muladeva and Shashi, come; Muladeva takes Sudeva home and with a Chamunda mantra makes two pills, one that turns the taker into a twelve-year-old girl and one that makes Muladeva a very old man. They go to the king; Muladeva says his house has been plundered, and asks him to keep this woman, his son's wife, safe, so the king places her with his daughter. At night the Brahmin, in female form, takes out the charm and becomes himself again, and the two unite; the princess becomes pregnant. Meanwhile the minister's son Madanalasa desires the false Brahmin woman and is dying, so the minister gives her to him; she tells him to bathe at holy places for three months. Muladeva returns, with Shashi made a young man, demands his daughter-in-law back, and the king, afraid, explains; Muladeva then asks for the princess for Shashi, and the king marries her to him with wealth. Sudeva says she is his; Vaitala asks who rightly has her. The king answers that a girl given by her parents before the gods belongs to the one she is given to, like a field to its farmer, not the giver of seed, so she will choose Shashi. Madanalasa goes to Vrindavana, bathes at Radha Kunda, praises Krishna, is freed of desire, returns to his wife and gives his sister in marriage to Sudeva.

06-015.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the fifteenth tale. At Kanyakubja a generous Brahmin devoted to the goddess gets five coins by her grace for the Navadurga vow, fasts nine days, dies and becomes the Vidyadhara king Jimutaketu in the Himalaya. By worshipping a wish-granting tree, he has a son, Jimutavahana, who in a former life was the king Shurasena. Shurasena keeps a Rama festival on Chaitra bright ninth day, and keeps vigil at Valmiki's hut and hears Rama's story. By this merit he is born a Vidyadhara; the tree grants a boon that makes his city rich, and father and son go to practise austerity on Malaya mountain. Jimutavahana sees Kamalakshi, daughter of King Malayadhvaja, at a Shiva temple, prays to Kama, and the marriage takes place. With her brother Vishvavasu he goes to Gandhamadana and to a high place of Garuda, where the mother of the serpent Shankhachuda weeps because her son is to be Garuda's food. He gives himself to Garuda; his wife sees him carried in the sky and weeps. Garuda, shaken, learns the reason; Shankhachuda arrives and asks to be eaten instead. Garuda, pleased, promises never to eat Shankhachuda's family, and gives Jimutavahana kingdom for a long time and then Vaikuntha. Vaitala asks who got the greatest fruit; the king says Shankhachuda, who received the great fruit of life given and was fearless in offering his body.

06-016.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the sixteenth tale to the wise king. In a southern city ruled by King Chandrashekhara, the Vaishya Ratnadatta offers his beautiful daughter Kamavarudhini to the king. The king sends his minister Vidura to look at her and report. That evening the king kills a tiger attacking a cow; the tiger's body frees a demon, Mukula, who had been cursed by Prahlada, and he goes. Next day the minister sees her divine beauty, fears the king will lose his mind, and says she is not fit for him. The king gives her to his army chief Balabhadra. Later the king sees her, faints from desire, and is carried to the hall; Balabhadra says he will gladly give her up, since the minister hid her beauty from fear for the kingdom. The king refuses, saying she is rightly the commander's wife and taking her would send him to hell, and he dies of longing. His queen becomes a sati, and Balabhadra and Kamavarudhini burn their bodies; all go to heaven. Vaitala asks whose merit is greatest; the king answers that the king's is, because he held to dharma and conquered desire.

06-017.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala, in the form of a Brahmin, tells the seventeenth tale. In Ujjayini under King Mahasena, the Brahmin Devasharma's son Gunakara drinks, eats meat and gambles away his wealth, and is cast out by his kin. He comes to a holy hermitage where the yogi Kapardi offers him food from skulls; he refuses it as ghostly food, and the yogi calls a yakshini to be his guest, and he spends a joyful night with her. When she leaves for Kailasa he suffers, and Kapardi teaches him a spell to draw her. He stands in water at midnight for forty days reciting it, but she does not come; he lives for a time at home, then becomes a pupil in a forest and recites the mantra between five fires, still without success. Vaitala asks why the yakshini was not won. The king answers that action for success is of three kinds, of mind and speech, of body, and of all three together, and that all three should be done; the Brahmin did the mantra work with another's wealth, so in a later birth he became a yaksha. Vaitala is pleased and praises the king, then goes on to another tale to test him.

06-018.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the eighteenth tale. In Kambalaka under the just king Sudaksha, the Vaishya Dhanadhyaksha's daughter Dhanavati is married and has a daughter, Mohini; when Mohini is twelve her father dies. At night Dhanavati, poor and widowed, meets a Brahmin thief, Nyayasharma, left on a stake who is still alive because of his truthful name, and he offers a crore of gold for her daughter. She marries Mohini to him, digs up the gold under a banyan tree, and he dies and suffers in Yama's world. Mohini, young at her mother's house, puts a riddle in verse to the Brahmins (about pleasures, wonder, who wakes and who sleeps, sin, disease and sorrow), and only the Kashmiri Brahmin Medhavi answers, and Mohini is charmed. He gives her a child and takes gold; after ten months, told in a dream by Shiva, she leaves the baby with a thousand gold coins at the king's door. The childless king takes him, names him Haradatta, and later, ruling, offers funeral rice-balls at Gaya; three hands appear. Vaitala asks who should receive the offering. The king says it belongs to the thief, whose wife was Mohini, and Suta adds that by it the thief was freed from hell and went to heaven.

06-019.json.summary: The chapter begins in the middle of a tale, probably the nineteenth, told by Vaitala. King Rupadatta of Chitrakuta, hunting, sees a sage's daughter picking lotuses and their eyes meet. The sage arrives and the king asks about dharma; the sage says that the gift of fearlessness has no equal, and gives short rules, including punish only the unfit, be kind to cows and Brahmins, be truthful in worship and self-controlled toward the teacher. He gives the king his daughter and leaves. As the king sleeps with her under a banyan tree, a Rakshasa who wants to eat the wife wakes him; the king promises him a seven-year-old Brahmin boy as an offering. With his ministers' consent he gives the Brahmin a lakh in gold and takes the middle son. At the moment of death the boy laughs, then weeps; Vaitala asks why. The king's answer, which stops short here, says the eldest son is dear to the father and the youngest to the mother, and the middle one took refuge in the king. The boy laughed, devoted to Shiva, seeing the king with sword in hand, and wept because his body was going to a Rakshasa.

06-020.json.summary: Suta says Vaitala tells the twentieth tale. In Vishala city, King Vipulesha's village has a Vaishya, Arthadatta, whose lovely daughter Anangamanjari is given to the Vaishya Suvarna, who goes abroad to an island for wealth and stays long. The Brahmin Kamalakara comes to her house on some duty and, after a fire offering, is struck by desire for her. She promises to meet him at midnight; he thinks of her, burns with desire and falls asleep. At midnight she looks for the way to him and, when he does not come, she dies. He wakes and, seeing her dead, dies as well. At dawn her father cremates her in grief; Suvarna returns and laments, and she goes to heaven from the pyre. Vaitala asks whose love was greatest and why she went to heaven. The king answers that the woman and the Brahmin were the most loving, and that she, dying out of love for the Brahmin, went to heaven; he adds that Vaishyas should always honour a Brahmin, and that the Brahmin, thinking of Hari at death, also reached heaven.

06-021.json.summary: Vaitala tells the twenty-first tale. In Jayasthala under King Vardhamana, the Brahmin Vishnusvami, devoted to Radha and Krishna, has four sons: a gambler, a lecher, a sensualist and a non-believer. They lose their wealth and ask their father why; he says gambling wastes wealth and leads to adultery, theft and cruelty, and urges pilgrimage and vows, dropping prostitutes, giving up meat and drink, offering wealth to Vishnu, and giving up contempt for the gods, since the self and the gods dwell in every heart. They go to holy places and worship Shiva for learning; after a year Mahadeva gives them the knowledge of reviving the dead. In the forest they test it on the bones of a dead tiger: one sprinkles mantra-water to form a skeleton, the second adds flesh and blood, the third skin and breath. The non-believer sees the tiger asleep and gives it water, so it wakes and eats the Brahmins. Vaitala asks which of them is the fool, and the king answers that the one who woke the tiger is the greatest fool; Vaitala then speaks again.

06-022.json.summary: Vaitala himself now speaks to King Vikramaditya and tells his own earlier life. In a past birth he was King Kshatrasimha at Bilvati village between the Ganga and the Yamuna. The Brahmin Shambhudatta, devoted to Rudra, had two sons, the Vishnu-devoted Liladhara and the goddess-devoted Mohana. The king has a goat sacrifice performed; Liladhara objects that killing a creature leads to hell and Vishnu is not pleased by violent sacrifice. Mohana laughs and tells an old story of Brahmins in the first age, a dispute over the word for goat, and the voice of a being who said sacrifice should be with a goat. Liladhara replies that this kind of sacrifice belongs to the Treta age, that there was no violence in the first age, and that the gods are pleased by offerings, not by flesh and blood. The king frees the goat and finishes with fruit offerings. The goddess, angry in her dark form, burns the city, and Shambhudatta, made mad by Mahamaya, leaves his body and goes to heaven. The king goes to Mohana, who sings an eight-verse praise of the Mother; by it the king reaches Shiva's world and becomes Vaitala. Vaitala tells Vikramaditya to worship Durga, says Shiva sent him to test him by questions, asks to rest on the king's shoulders, and tells him to kill his enemies and restore ruined cities and fields as the scriptures say. He says Vikramaditya's time will restore dharma, that Dvapara will begin after twelve hundred years, and that Krishna's part will then be born to lift the world from Kali and to increase the Mleccha line; he adds that Suta and the sages will come to Vishala and hear the Purana. Vaitala vanishes, the king is glad, and Suta tells the sages to worship Shiva as evening comes.

06-023.json.summary: Vyasa speaks. The sages at Vishala bathe at Kedara pool, worship Shiva in their minds, and stay in meditation for a year. King Vikramaditya bows to them and praises them. The sages tell Suta this is the king of whom the tale was told and propose a horse sacrifice for him, asking Suta to stay in meditation at Chakratirtha; Suta agrees and the sacrifice is held properly. The horse roams to Kapila's place in the east, the bridge in the south, the end of the Sindhu in the west and Badari forest in the north, then reaches a river, gives up its body in fire and goes to heaven. All the gods come with their wives, but the Moon does not, and the king is sad. After the rite the king gives many gifts and goes with Vaitala to the Moon's world; the Moon says that with the terrible Kali age come he cannot come to earth, gives the king nectar water and vanishes. Indra, as a Brahmin, begs and gets the nectar; by it the king's life is made long. A Brahmin, Jayanta, gets that fruit by austerity from Indra, and offers it to Bhartrihari for a lakh of gold; Bhartrihari takes it and goes to the forest as a yogi. Vikramaditya rules without trouble for a hundred years and goes to heaven. The sages ask Suta for the chief dharma, and he recites the Puranas to them again for a hundred years, five lakh verses.

06-024.json.summary: Vyasa speaks. At Naimisha forest, Shaunaka and the sages ask Suta whom to worship in the four ages for the good of the world, and what gives wishes easily. Suta opens with praise of Satyanarayana and of Rama, then tells how the sage Narada, seeing people in sorrow and illness in the world of mortals, goes to Vishnu's world and praises Narayana. Vishnu asks why he has come and, hearing it, says that in the Kali age he, as Satyanarayana, gives visible results; dharma stands on truth, and the Satyanarayana vow is the best. Asked about fruit and method, he says the fruit is far more than Brahma could tell: the poor become rich, the childless get sons, the one who lost his kingdom regains it, the blind see, the bound are freed and the fearful become fearless. The method is: bathe in the morning and meditate on Hari holding tulsi; in the evening worship the Shalagrama stone with five pots and plantain arches, bathe it with five nectars, chant a mantra 108 times, make a fire offering of a tenth, hear the six-chapter story, share the offering among teacher, family, listeners and oneself, feed Brahmins and eat in silence. Narayana says he will make this vow known in the world that day, vanishes, and then himself comes to Kashi.

06-025.json.summary: Suta says he will tell the talk between Hari and a Brahmin. In Kashi lives the poor Brahmin Shatananda, a beggar with wife and children and devoted to Vishnu. On the road Hari, as an old Brahmin, asks where he goes; the Brahmin says he begs for his family, and Hari says the cure for this in Kali is to worship Satyanarayana, who removes poverty and grief. Asked who this is, Hari says he is many-formed and truthful and has now come as a Brahmin, and the Brahmin sees his true form and falls down in praise. Hari says worship needs little wealth, only faith, and gives the method: wheat flour, milk, sugar and ghee as an offering, bathing the Shalagrama stone with five nectars, offerings of incense, lamp and fruit, hearing the story of the king, the forest people and the merchant, bowing at its end, sharing and eating the offering. He says devotion alone pleases him and that those who worship so enjoy sons, wealth and pleasures and are with him at the end. Hari vanishes; the Brahmin begs and, without asking, receives much wealth, tells his wife, calls his kin and neighbours, and worships Satyanarayana. The god appears after the story to give a wish; the Brahmin asks for supreme devotion and long lists of wealth and blessings, and Hari grants them. The vow then spreads in the world.

06-026.json.summary: Suta tells of the righteous King Chandrachuda of Kedaramanipura, devoted to Narayana. His enemies, the Mlecchas of the Vindhya, fight him fiercely; his army is destroyed, with about a hundred chariots, a thousand elephants and five thousand foot soldiers dead, and five thousand of the enemy dead as well. Worn down by their deceitful fighters, the king leaves his kingdom alone and, under the pretext of pilgrimage, reaches Kashi, where Narayana is honoured in every house and the city is rich like Dvaravati. He sees the Brahmin Sadananda, a worshipper of Satyadeva, bows to him and asks for a vow that destroys sin. Sadananda describes the Satyanarayana vow: on any day at evening, an arch and plantain pillars, five pots and five flags, an altar with a golden Krishna stone, worship with love and sleeping on the ground for seven nights. The king worships in Kashi, and at night the god gives him a good sword that destroys enemies. He returns, kills six thousand robbers, gains wealth and worships Hari on the Narmada bank every full moon. By this vow he becomes lord of a hundred thousand villages, rules for sixty years and goes to Vishnu's city.

06-027.json.summary: Suta now tells the story of the forest people, the Bhillas, who prospered. Woodcutters of the forest go to Kashi to sell wood; one, thirsty, comes to the hermitage of Vishnudasa, sees the wealth and Brahmins serving Hari, and wonders how a beggar became rich. He asks the Brahmin, called Sadananda, who says that serving Satyanarayana gives all things, and then, asked for the method, retells how King Chandrachuda came to him and what he taught. He says to offer flour, honey and ghee as food, bathe the stone with five nectars, worship with sandal, sweet rice, fruit, flowers, incense and lamps as one can afford, and that the Lord is pleased by devotion alone, not wealth. He recalls Krishna leaving Duryodhana's royal welcome to stay at Vidura's, and taking Sudama's rice, and names others who reached Narayana, such as a cowherd, a vulture, a merchant, a hunter and Hanuman with Vibhishana. The woodcutter bows and tells his group; they agree to worship with what they earn from wood. They sell the wood for four times the usual, worship with their wives, take the offering at the story's end, and give it to their own and other communities. Prosperous with sons and wives, they enjoy life and at last go to Vishnu's abode, hard even for yogis to reach.

06-028.json.summary: Suta tells how a merchant gained by a king's teaching. King Chandrachuda of Manipura worships Satyanarayana with his people. A merchant of Ratnapura, rich in lakhs, sails along the river with loaded boats and sees a crowd with music and Vedic chanting; the people tell him the king worships Satyanarayana with his kin and gained a kingdom without trouble, and that the god gives wealth, sons, sight and fearlessness. Hearing the method, the childless merchant bows with cloth round his neck and promises a golden flag if he gets a child. His wife Lilavati bears a daughter, Kalavati, who grows up and is married to the merchant Shankhapati of Kanchanapura, who then lives in his father-in-law's house. Much later the merchant forgets his promise and sails with his son-in-law to trade, and settles at a city on the Narmada, still not worshipping. Thieves rob the king's house; the king orders his servants to find the thieves and threatens to kill them if they fail. After failing, the servants decide to die in the Narmada, but see the merchant with a pearl necklace, think he is the thief, bind him and his son-in-law and take them and their wealth to the king. The king, not asking further, has them chained in prison, and the merchant laments his past wrongs.

06-029.json.summary: Suta says those who hear Vishnu's story live in his world, and that those who go against Hari face many hells; the text gives a short list of dharma, sacrifice, king and thief as all serving Lakshmi. The merchant's wealth at home is stolen, and his wife Lilavati, in great distress, sells her clothes and ornaments to eat. Their daughter Kalavati, hungry, goes to a Brahmin's house, sees Satyanarayana worship and prays that her father and husband come home. Her mother scolds her, and she says she wants to do the worship; next morning she asks a man, Shilapala, for money, and he gives five coins. She and her mother worship and the god is pleased. In the Narmada city a Brahmin in a dream tells the king to free the two merchants, and the minister has the same dream. The king questions the merchant, who says they came to trade; the king frees and honours them and has their boats filled with coins. On the way home an ascetic, who is the god, asks what they carry; the merchant says leaves and vines, and the wealth turns into leaves. The merchant faints, then pleads, praises the god, promises a lakh in coins for worship, and is forgiven. At home Kalavati leaves the offering uneaten to see her husband, and the boat sinks with him; a voice from the sky says she must first eat the offering, and then she finds him alive. The merchant worships with a lakh of coins, enjoys sons and grandsons, and goes to heaven.

06-030.json.summary: The sages ask Suta about the work of the generative organ and what is highest of all kinds of continence. Suta tells of Pitrisharma, a Brahmin of the Kali age who fears Yama's world; he thinks that in Kali the life of the renunciant is spoiled by pretence, the forest life is gone and student life is rare, and the householder's life is best, so he needs a wife. He prays to the goddess with a hymn and she gives him Brahmacharini, the daughter of the Brahmin Vishnuyasha, and they live in Mathura. They have four sons who hold the four Vedas: Vyadi, Mimamsa, Panini and Vararuchi, the last dear to kings. The four go to the court of Chandragupta, king of Magadha, who asks what is the highest brahmacharya. Vyadi says one devoted to praising the gods; Mimamsa says one who sacrifices; Panini says one who worships by pure sounds and rules of grammar; Vararuchi says the student who lives in the teacher's house under his orders. Their father says it is the householder who honours ancestors, gods and guests and approaches his own wife only in her season, with self-control; the king agrees for the Kali age and becomes his pupil. Pitrisharma then meditates on Hari and goes to the Himalaya. Names of different ages appear together here, as the text gives them.

06-031.json.summary: The sages ask Suta which is the highest of all holy places and gifts, which brings peace in the harsh Kali age. Suta tells of Panini, son of Samana, who was beaten in debate by pupils of a teacher called Kanabhuj. Ashamed, he goes on pilgrimage, bathes at holy places, drinks water at Kedara and meditates on Shiva, living on leaves for seven days, then water, then air. On the twenty-eighth day Rudra offers a boon. Panini praises him and asks for the root of learning and for the highest holy place. Rudra gives him sutras, starting with the letters a, i, u and so on. He says the mental holy place, a pool of knowledge and true water that washes off desire and hatred, gives the fruit of all holy places. Panini goes home, composes the text of the sutras, the root list, the word-group list and the gender sutra, and attains liberation. Suta advises the listener to practise the mental holy place and says that Ganga, which is Shiva's own, is the highest water.

06-032.json.summary: Suta tells of Bopadeva, a Brahmin of Totadri, learned and devoted to Krishna. He goes to Vrindavan and worships Janardana in his mind; after a year Hari himself gives him supreme knowledge, and he receives the Bhagavata story that Shuka told to Parikshit. At its end Vishnu appears and offers a boon; Bopadeva asks for the greatness of the Bhagavata. The Lord replies with an account: when the world was under Buddhist rule and filled with pretence and heresy, Rudra saw Kashi high on the earth and praised it, saying a seven-day sacrifice had purified it. Rudra went with Shiva (the goddess) to a hidden place, with Chandisha, Ganesha, Nandi and Guha posted to guard it, and spent seven days telling the story in his mind. On the eighth day he saw that she had slept; she said she had heard up to the churning of nectar. A parrot in a hollow tree had heard the story and became long-lived, and Parvati protected it. By Rudra's order, that Shuka dwells in Bopadeva's heart, and through him Bopadeva has the Bhagavata. The Lord tells him to recite it at the Narmada bank to Gandharvasena, father of King Vikrama, and says that giving the glory of Hari is the best gift, to be given to a worthy Vishnu devotee, and that giving food to the hungry is equal. The Lord vanishes.

06-033.json.summary: The sages ask Suta which hymn gives the fruit of reciting all the Vedas, since the Vedas are many. Suta tells of a man called Vyadhakarma in King Vikramaditya's time, born of a Brahmin woman by a Shudra. His mother Kamini, wife of a Brahmin who recited the Saptashati, was lustful; when her husband was away for a month she gave five coins to a woodcutter and was with him, conceived and bore a son. At twelve the son, a rogue without Vedic learning, took up the hunter's work, and the Brahmin drove both mother and son out. The Brahmin lived in the Vindhya hills, reciting the Chandi text daily and was freed in life by the goddess. Mother and son lived in the hunter's house and Vyadhakarma lived by stealing. After hearing the original story at a Shiva temple, his mind turned to dharma; he gave his stolen wealth to a reciting Brahmin and became his pupil, repeating the letter chant, and his sin left his body as many-coloured worms. After three years he was free of sin; after twelve years he went to Kashi, praised the goddess Annapurna with an eight-line hymn, and dreamed that she gave him knowledge of the Rigveda. He became the sacrifice priest of Vikramaditya and then went to the Himalaya in yoga.

06-034.json.summary: Suta tells of Bhimavarma, a Kshatriya of Ujjayini who kills creatures, eats meat and drinks, keeps company with prostitutes and even eats human flesh. He dies young of cholera, but out of fear he had had the Chandi text recited, and by that merit he does not go to hell. He is born again in Magadha as King Mahanandi, who remembers his past life, follows Vedic dharma, and becomes the pupil of the wise goddess-devotee Katyayana. Katyayana gives him the middle section of the Chandi text with its seed syllable and returns to the Vindhya. The king recites it daily while worshipping Mahalakshmi, and by the goddess's grace his land becomes holy; the text says he gave up the Shudra state and became a Kshatriya. After twelve years his teacher returns and has a lakh-recital of the Chandi text held; the goddess appears and gives him duty, wealth, desire and liberation. He enjoys life and in the end goes to a supreme world. Suta says the way of the Yajurveda was reached by the Shudra king through the middle text.

06-035.json.summary: Suta tells of Patanjali, a teacher on Chitrakuta hill, who knows the Vedas, the Gita and the commentary tradition and is devoted to Vishnu. In Kashi he debates with Katyayana, a devotee of the goddess, and is beaten after a year. Ashamed, he praises Sarasvati, and a voice without a body tells him to recite her story attentively, saying Katyayana won by devotion to her. Patanjali goes to the Vindhyavasini temple, worships her and recites her hymn, gains knowledge that leads to Vishnu, and beats Katyayana. He sets up the upright mark, the tulsi necklace and a Krishna mantra in every house, teaches the Mahabhashya to the people, and by Vishnu's illusion gains a long life. Suta calls this the best of chants and ends with blessings: let all see good, and he who hears this collection of histories, wanting duty, desire or wealth, reaches the highest state.

07-001.json.summary: The sages ask Suta to tell what the Lord did in the time of Vikrama's tale, a time equal to a Dvapara of twelve hundred years. Suta, after salutes, tells of the end of the twenty-eighth Dvapara, when the Pandavas defeat the Kauravas at Kurukshetra on the eighteenth day. That evening Krishna, knowing the evil of the coming age, praises Shiva in his mind and asks him to protect the Pandavas; Rudra comes on Nandi with a trident to guard the camps. That night Ashvatthama, Kritavarma and Kripa praise Rudra, and Shiva gives them a way in; Ashvatthama takes a sword given by Shiva and kills Dhrishtadyumna and others. When the Pandavas learn this, they blame Shiva and strike him with their weapons, which enter his body; then they strike him with their hands and fists. Rudra curses them, saying that as Krishna's worshippers they shall be reborn in the Kali age and bear the fruit of their fault. The Pandavas take refuge in Krishna, praise Rudra without weapons, and Krishna asks Shiva to return the weapons and soften the curse. Shiva says he was deluded by Krishna's command and the curse stands, and lists their coming births: Yudhishthira as Balakhani, son of Vatsaraja; Bhima as Virana, a Mleccha king; Arjuna's part as Brahmananda, son of Parimala; Nakula as Lakshmana, Sahadeva as Devasimha, Dhritarashtra's part as Prithviraj of Ajmer, Draupadi as his daughter Vela, and Karna as Taraka. Krishna says he will protect them by a part of himself, born at Mahavati as Udayasimha, with Ahlada as a part of his abode and his teacher, and that he will destroy kings of the fire lineage and establish Kali.

07-002.json.summary: Suta says that next morning the Pandavas, grieving for their sons, perform the funeral rites and go to Bhishma, hear the teachings on kingly duty, liberation and giving, perform three horse sacrifices, rule thirty-six years and go to heaven; their parts will be born to spread Kali's dharma. Vyasa says the sages should go; he is in yoga sleep at Chakratirtha in samadhi. After twelve hundred years the sages wake, bathe, go to Suta, and ask about the kings after Vikramaditya. Suta says many kings arose in eighteen realms and lists their regions, such as Indraprastha, Panchala, Gurjara, Maharashtra, Dravida, Kalinga, Avanti, Vanga, Gauda, Magadha and Kosala. After a century the Shakas and others hear of the ruin of dharma, cross the Sindhu in many bands, defeat the Aryans, plunder them and go home with their women. Then Shalivahana, Vikramaditya's grandson, takes his father's kingdom and defeats the Shakas and other peoples such as Chinese, Bahlikas and Kamarupas, takes their treasuries, fines them, and fixes separate boundaries for Mlecchas and Aryas, making the Sindhu land the Aryan land and putting Mleccha land beyond it. One day the Shaka lord sees on a Himalayan peak in the Huna country a fair man in white, who says he is the son of Isha born of a virgin, the teacher of the Mleccha dharma, called Isha-masiha. He says his teaching is to purify the mind, repeat a chant, live with truth and one-mindedness, and worship the Lord in the sun's disc. The king bows to him, sets him up in that Mleccha land, returns, performs a horse sacrifice, rules sixty years and goes to heaven.

07-003.json.summary: Suta says that in Shalivahana's line ten kings rule five hundred years, and boundaries slowly fade. The tenth, Bhojaraja, sets out on conquest with ten thousand soldiers, the poet Kalidasa and other Brahmins, crosses the Sindhu, defeats the Mlecchas of Gandhara, Kashmir and others, and takes their treasure and fines. Meanwhile a Mleccha teacher, Mahamada, comes with his pupils. The king bathes Mahadeva, who lives in the desert, with Ganga water and five cow products and prays to him for shelter. The god answers that Bhoja should go instead to Mahakaleshwara, because the Vahika land is polluted by Mlecchas and has no Aryan dharma, and that Mahamada is an ill-willed, ghost-like follower of a demon. The king returns, and Mahamada comes to the Sindhu bank, claims the king's god is now his servant and shows a trick, and the king's mind turns toward the Mleccha dharma. Kalidasa angrily says it is an illusion, performs a nine-letter chant ten thousand times and a fire offering, and the magician turns to ash. His pupils carry the ash to Vahika and set it up in the earth, and the place becomes their holy place. At night Mahamada appears in a ghostly body and tells Bhoja, in the text's own terms, that his own people will follow a fierce ghost-like dharma with cutting, no topknot, beards, eating anything and the pestle as a rite. The king sets Sanskrit for the three upper classes and the common tongue for Shudras, rules fifty years and dies. The text then fixes Aryavarta between the Vindhya and Himalaya, with mixed classes beyond, and says the Isha-masiha teachings were set up in far lands by gods and kings.

07-004.json.summary: Suta says seven kings follow Bhojaraja in his line, short-lived, dying within three hundred years; the seventh is Virasimha. Three more follow within two hundred years, and the tenth is Gangasimha, who rules justly at Kalpakshetra. Jayachandra rules at Kanyakubja in Antarvedi, Anangapala of the Tomara line at Indraprastha, and many others as village or realm lords. The fire lineage spreads widely, with sixty lakh village lords from Kapila's place in the east to Vahika's end in the west, China's end in the north and the bridge in the south. They keep the fire rite and care for cows and Brahmins, and the time is like Dvapara everywhere; Mlecchas too take to Aryan dharma. Fearful Kali, with the Mlecchas, goes to Nila mountain and takes refuge in Hari, meditating twelve years and seeing Krishna with Radha. Kali says his four houses (gambling, drink, gold and women's laughter) were destroyed by the fire-lineage kings. Krishna smiles and says he will be born in Mahavati to protect Kali, and his part will destroy powerful rulers and set up Mleccha kings. Kali is glad. Then the text tells of the cowherd woman Vratapa of Vaksara village, who keeps the Navadurga vow nine years; Chandika offers a boon and she asks for two sons in her line equal to Rama and Krishna. King Vasuman, struck by her beauty, marries her and she bears two sons, Desharaja and Vatsaraja, each as strong as a hundred elephants, who conquer Magadha. The Mleccha Shatayatta, lord of the Vanara land, has a son Virana, a part of Bhima, and a tall, swift man Talana; the two kings fight Talana and then make friends, and three brave men come to test Jayachandra.

07-005.json.summary: Suta tells that Anangapala of Indraprastha, who has no son, holds a Shiva sacrifice and gets two daughters, Chandrakanti and Kirtimalini. He gives Chandrakanti to Devapala, king of Kanyakubja, and Kirtimalini to Someshvara of the Chahamana line, king of Ajmer. A Brahmin, Jayasharma, in meditation in the Himalaya sees a royal festival, wishes for a kingdom, gives up his body and is born as Chandrakanti's son Jayachandra, strong and self-controlled; his younger brother is Ratnabhanu. Jayachandra conquers Gauda, Vanga and desert lands and obeys his brother's word at home. In Ratnabhanu's queen Viravati, sister of Gangasimha, Nakula's part is born by Shiva's order as the swordsman Lakshana. Kirtimalini has three sons: Dhundhakara, Krishnakumara and the youngest, Prithviraj. When Prithviraj is twelve, Anangapala gives him the kingdom and goes to the Himalaya in meditation; Dhundhakara rules Mathura and Prithviraj Ajmer. Pradyota and Vidyota, moon-line ministers, have sons Parimala and Bhishmasimha as army leaders; after Anangapala dies, Prithviraj drives them out.
