In a past life Apava was a Brahmin devotee of Bhadrakali. He worshipped her with red flowers and recited the middle part of the Devi text for three years. Pleased, she asked him to choose a boon. He praised her with a hymn recalling her deeds: killing Mahishasura, Sita's defeat of the thousand-headed Ravana, and Ekadashi (Vijaya) killing the demons Mura and Naraka. Bhadrakali promised him happiness at the time of dissolution, and he became Varuna. Varuna then put forth part of himself and was born in Dehali as Namadeva, son of a widow by Hari's will, a Vishnu devotee who became Ramananda's pupil, was honoured by the Muslim ruler Sikandar, and brought dead people back to life. The next story is about the Brahmin Vishvanara, who asked for a child greater than Prakriti. Brahma replied that only the supreme Self is beyond Prakriti, so Hari himself would be his son. He was born as Agni, the Vaishvanara, and the chapter links this to Nala and Damayanti. Agni, in turn, was born as Rankana, a merchant's son in Kanchanapura, who with his wife Yankana lived poorly and served Ramananda's teaching. The text breaks off there.

08-017.json.summary: Brihaspati speaks first. Diti, mourning her sons killed by Vishnu, asked her husband Kashyapa for a son who would destroy the twelve Adityas. Kashyapa told her about dharma and adharma and said a strong son would be born if she kept a vow of purity. Indra served her in fear, found her impure in the seventh month, entered her womb and cut the child into seven parts, then each part into seven; these became the Maruts, who served Indra. The chapter then names previous births for the Vasus. The Maruts' leader Anila (Vayu) was said to be Ila, a king who was turned into a woman and bore Budha's lineage, and was later a Brahmin who lost his head to the fire god. The sixth Vasu, linked to the fire, was born as the weaver Kabir, adopted by a childless Muslim weaver in Kashi; he took Ramananda as his teacher. Dhruva, as a child, left his family, meditated at Govardhana on Narada's advice, and was given a fixed place in the sky; the text lists planets and elephants of the directions linked to him. He was reborn as Narashri, a merchant's son, who also became Ramananda's pupil. Then Atri and Anasuya are tested by Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, who behave badly towards her; she cursed them to become her sons, and they were born as Chandra, Dattatreya and Durvasa. Their parts were born as Pipa (a king who became Ramananda's pupil), Nanak (a merchant's son of the Panchala country who taught a subtle path to Muslims) and Nityananda. The Suta repeatedly relays the stories.

08-018.json.summary: Continuing, the Suta says the divine teacher turned to the two Ashvins. In the Vaivasvata age Vishvakarma, jealous of another's fine craft, praised the great goddess; part of her was born as his daughter Samjna. When she was sixteen he held a bride-choice on Meru. Gods, Yakshas, Vasus, Rudras, Adityas, demons and serpents assembled. The demon Bali seized her; gods and demons fought for a fortnight, and Vivasvan (the sun) won her and returned her to Vishvakarma. Samjna told him that a woman chooses a man of her choice, and said that Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva themselves took a daughter, a mother and a sister; the text reports this as her argument. She bore Manu Vaivasvata, Yama and Yamuna. She then left her shadow, Chhaya, in her place and went to the forest to practise austerity. Chhaya bore Savarni, Shani and Tapati. Vivasvan, finding the trick, burned Chhaya; Shani and Savarni fought him and were beaten. Samjna, as a mare in Kurukshetra, received him as a horse; the Ashvins were born. They went to the sun and were beaten when they arrived. Vivasvan blessed them, saying they would be physicians who remove troubles from planets such as Shani and Rahu. The Ashvins were then born on earth: Sadhana, a butcher's son who became Kabir's pupil, and Raidas, a cobbler's son who was defeated by Shankara and then took Ramananda as teacher.

08-019.json.summary: After Brihaspati's account, the text continues with later incarnations. Ropana, a Brahmin of Ishtika city, spread Brahma's path with a thread-and-bead garland and the mantra "Vasudeva"; he received a blanket from Krishna Chaitanya. In Chaitanya's fifth year (called a part of Yajna), the learned Brahmin Ishvara, proud of Sharada's boon, came to Shantipura and was shown by Chaitanya that his own hymn's "fault" and "ornament" could be explained; Ishvara became his follower. Shridhara, a Shiva worshipper of Pattana, was robbed and killed by seven thieves, who had sworn on Rama's name; Rama killed the thieves and revived the Brahmin, who then became a Vaishnava and wrote a commentary on the Bhagavata. Ramasharma of Kashi, on Shivaratri, asked Shiva for a boon; Shiva explained how the one Prakriti brought forth Narayana, Vishnu, the sages Nara and Narayana, Sankarshana, Rama, Lakshmana and Balabhadra, and told him to worship Rama and Lakshmana, then he joined Ramananda. Jivananda and Rupananda questioned Chaitanya, who said he was a Shakta, Shaiva and Vaishnava in turn; they became pupils, one wrote the Shat-sandarbha and the other a Krishna part of a Purana of 10,000 verses. Vishnusvami, Madhvacharya and others also came; the text records Chaitanya's views that Shiva is to be honoured by Vishnu's devotees, that animal sacrifice has merit and risk, and that Krishna lifted Govardhana by the power of Radha, so "Radha-Krishna" is the supreme form.

08-020.json.summary: Krishna Chaitanya (called Yajnamsha) is questioned by more scholars, each arguing for one deity or principle, and each time he answers with a smile and the questioner becomes his pupil. Bhattoji, a Shiva devotee, said Shiva is the teacher of all; Chaitanya replied that Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are one form in three, each giving liberation by a different path, and Bhattoji then wrote on Panini's grammar and the Siddhanta Kaumudi. Varahamihira, a sun worshipper, argued the sun is supreme; Chaitanya described higher and lower Prakriti and the gods linked with them, and Varahamihira wrote the Varahasamhita and Brihajjataka. Vanibhushana argued for the Goddess; Chaitanya answered from the Devibhagavata that the person (purusha) and Prakriti depend on each other and the purusha is greater. Dhanvantari, who was in the Brahma path, argued for the supreme person; Chaitanya said the person cannot act without Prakriti, and Dhanvantari wrote on medicine. Jayadeva, a follower of the Buddhist path, was answered with an account of creation in three kinds. Chaitanya then said he must go to Jagannath in Odisha with his pupils, and groups of followers of Shankara, Ramanuja, Nama-deva and Ramananda went with him. At the temple the deity, Jagannath, in the form of a Brahmin, said that Mlechchhas of Mishra land had been made to look like Brahmins by a Shudra, that Indra complained, and that Vishnu would be born in Kali age with the twelve Adityas as Buddhist teachers. The text continues in the next chapter.

08-021.json.summary: Krishna Chaitanya asks Jagannath to tell in full how the Buddhists arose. Jagannath tells of the sage Kanva and his wife Aryavati, who praised Sarasvati and were given ten sons and ten daughters, who married and had sixteen sons each, founding the gotras of sages. Kanva then went to the Mishra land, taught Sanskrit to ten thousand Mlechchhas, and by Sarasvati's grace they were made Shudras, craftsmen and Vaishyas, with a king set over them. After Kanva's death these people worshipped Indra with sacrifices; Indra's trouble ended when the twelve Adityas were born as Buddhist teachers at Kikata and Bodh Gaya. After 2,700 years of Kali, the demon Maya sent by Bali came as Gautama, spread a devilish doctrine and set up machines at holy places; the text says many Aryans fell into this path, ten crore became Buddhists and five lakh went to the hills. Forty warriors of the Agnivamsha cleansed and settled the rest south of the Vindhyas. Nityananda became Jagannath's pupil and received a mark of honour. The text then gives the fruit of seeing Jagannath and hearing this account. Bali again sent Maya, who taught the Mlechchhas an art with twenty-one chapters, and they placed machines in seven cities. Followers of Ramananda, Nimbaditya, Vishnusvami, Madhva, Shankara, Ramanuja, Varahamihira, Vanibhushana, Dhanvantari, Bhattoji, Ropana and Jayadeva reversed the machines in different cities, and each group took its own marks (tilaka, rosary and mantra). Shaiva, Shakta and Vaishnava groups are described, with some leaders ending at sacred places.

08-022.json.summary: This chapter is a history-in-prophecy of rulers at Delhi, told as the work of demons opposed to the gods. The demon king Bali sends Roshana to destroy the followers of the Vedic way; the chapter names a line of Muslim rulers in Delhi (Babara, his son Homayu, then Akabara) and says that the gods complained to Krishna Chaitanya, who made trouble for Homayu's rule. Mukunda, a Brahmin of Shankara's line who was burning himself in fire after Babara's wrongs, is said to be reborn as Akabara, son of Homayu in Kashmir. A heavenly voice at his birth says no such child was born before. His seven pupils, with a long list of names of earlier lives (Keshava as Gana-sena, Madhu as Haridasa, Devapi as Vira-bala, Bilvamangala and others) are linked to poets and teachers such as Tulasi-sharma (Tulasidasa), Surdasa, Mira and others, who wrote in the people's language. The text then lists later rulers (Salomas, Khurdaka, Navaranga and others) with reign lengths, a Maratha Brahmin who kills a wicked king, many small local rulers in the land, and the arrival of the Gauruna (foreign traders) said to be of Buddhist faith, who set up Kalikata (Calcutta). It also mentions an eighth ruler, Vardila, whom the monkey-faced Guruna lord Mura draws toward harm, and Krishna Chaitanya cursing them. The chapter ends with later rulers (Arjika, Devakarna, Mauryas, and a king killed by snakes), described in general terms.

08-023.json.summary: The chapter lists rulers after Vikrama's reign. Bhutananda with his Naga line took Kilkila after fighting Kubera's Yakshas and Maunas, then Shishunandi, Yashonanda and Pravira followed, and the line of Bahlika kings, said to have worshipped Nagas, ruled for 400 years. The ancestors (pitris) complained to Krishna Chaitanya that Naga kings neglected shraddha rites. Hari then had a king Pushyamitra born, who ruled for a hundred years, restored the seven holy cities and shrines, and defended Vedic dharma. Kali, in a Brahmin's form, argued that ancestor worship is useless; Pushyamitra answered with the account of how pind offerings feed the ancestors and said that those who skip the rites go to hell. Kali then made friends with him. After Pushyamitra, the text tells of a succession of rulers: Sugada of Andhra, Rakshasari of Kosala (who fixed values for coins of various metals), a Vaidarbha king, Kalamali of Nishadha who favoured ghost worship, and a long period without a ruler. The gods complained, and Krishna Chaitanya said that Vishvasphurji, son of Purañjaya and Purañjani, would be born and would reduce all classes to the Brahmin class and make them follow Vedic rites. Later the chapter tells of Somanatha, a part of Yajna born in Saurashtra, who ruled a hundred years; of Rahu, a son of Kali born to an Abhiri woman; of Muhammad's religion being introduced and spreading; and of Charvabali of Charvapuri, who began to revive the Aryan way. It ends with wars with Mlecchas and a long age of disorder.

08-024.json.summary: The Suta continues his account of Kali. Demons with Kali sail to Harikhanda, where the people, equal to gods, defeat them in war for ten years, until Indra asks Vishvakarma to make a machine that turns them away. A wind and its son Vatya then rule; the text says he honoured the three classes and made Mlechchhas into classes. Bali complains to Vamana that Kali's work was undone, and Vamana's part is born as Kamasharma's sons, Bhogasimha and Kelisimha, who build Rahah-krida-vati and each day take many women, creating a mixed population, with the text calling them Kinnara men. Krishna Chaitanya says he and the gods will leave for heaven with sages and yogis such as Ahlada, Gorakha, Shankara and Bhartrihari; Kali and the demons will then take the earth. The text then describes how, in the four quarters of Kali, creatures degrade: people with sons who are also their siblings, short life, and finally root-and-fruit eating men. It compares the worlds filled in each part of the ages. The chapter has some verse numbering errors in the source.

08-025.json.summary: Yama complains to Brahma that the hells are over-full. Brahma goes to the milk ocean and praises Vishnu. Vishnu announces that Kalki will be born at Sambhala to Vishnuyasha, a Kashyapa, and his wife Vishnukirti, on the eighth day of the dark half of Margashirsha; the gods and planets will come, and each praises the child with a verse. The text then gives the main account: the gods and planets say who they were born from, the Manus and their ages (Svayambhuva, Svarochisha, Uttama, Tamasa, Raivata, Chakshusha, Vaivasvata and the Savarnis), and human life-spans in each age of each Manu. The Purana-person's passing through the zodiac signs is linked to Vishnu's avatars: Varaha, Narasimha, Matsya, Krishna, Kurma, Parashurama, Vamana, Kalki, Buddha and Rama. The chapter explains that eighteen great cycles (kalpas), with names including Kurma, Matsya, Varaha, Bhavishya and others, exist, and that the present one is the Bhavishya kalpa. It recounts Radha and Krishna's austerity, the making of Vrindavan, the creation of Brahma from the lotus, and Vishnu's account of the world's layout with its seas, continents and upper and lower realms. The chapter ends as the gods hear Kalki's words and return home.

08-026.json.summary: This chapter, which ends the Pratisarga Parva, foretells the end of the Kali age. The Suta tells that Kalki, on a divine horse with sword and armour, will kill the Mlechchhas and the demons, then go into yoga. His yoga-fire will burn the earth for 16,000 years, then clouds will bring a flood. Kali will go to Bali, and Hari will remake the land and honour the gods with sacrifices. The four classes are said to come from Kalki's mouth, arms, thighs and feet, and Manu Vaivasvata will rule at Ayodhya, with Ikshvaku after him. The ninth day of the bright half of Karttika, a Thursday, is named Akshaya Navami, the first day of the new age: worship and shraddha under the amla (dhatri) tree are said to give great merit. Kalki then disappears. The demons of the underworld, led by Prahlada, come to war on the gods for a divine year, and Bhargava (Shukra) revives the dead demons. The gods go to the milk ocean; Hari, as a swan like a hundred suns, makes the demons retreat to Vitala under Shiva's protection. The gods place Ikshvaku as king. The Suta closes by describing the four feet of dharma (knowledge, meditation, calm and self-control), the length of each age, and that this part has 7,000 verses; the next part will follow.

09-001.json.summary: This is the opening of the Uttara Parva (Later Part). It starts with prayers to Ganesha, Sarasvati, Vasudeva, Shiva and the sun. It then sets the scene: after Yudhishthira's coronation, Vyasa and many great sages come to see him, including Markandeya, Shandilya, Gautama, Garga, Parashara, Bharadvaja, Bhrigu, Narada, Lomasha and others. He honours them and then tells Vyasa that victory brings him no joy: he killed kinsmen and Bhishma for his kingdom, and his mind is stained with guilt. He asks Vyasa to wash it with teaching and to explain the whole of dharma to him, saying he has heard other teachers but that Krishna is his best guide now that Bhishma has died. Vyasa answers that he, Bhishma, Markandeya, Dhaumya and Lomasha have already told him what there is to tell, and that Yudhishthira is wise in matters of dharma. With Krishna beside him, no one else should speak: Krishna, who creates, protects and ends the worlds and sees all, will teach him dharma. Vyasa, honoured by the Pandavas, leaves for his forest hermitage. The chapter ends with the sages waiting to hear what Yudhishthira will ask and what Krishna will say.

09-002.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks Krishna what the world rests on, how it arises and dissolves, and how many continents, oceans and mountains there are. Krishna says he will tell what Yajnavalkya taught and what he heard from sages, called the Bhavishya Uttara. He first gives a general teaching: one divine source appears in many forms like the moon in water, and Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are three names for one. A Purana has five marks: creation, re-creation, lineages, ages of the Manus, and deeds of the dynasties. Creation then goes from the unmanifest to the great principle, ego, subtle elements and the elements. A cosmic egg splits in two, one half earth and the other sky; Mount Meru is its core. Dawn, noon and evening show Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra as one. The nine sages born of Brahma, Daksha and his daughters and their marriages (to Dharma, Kashyapa, the Moon and others) are listed. The three peaks of Meru, with the homes of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, the mountains, the seven islands and oceans, the seven upper and seven lower worlds, the six past Manus and the present Vaivasvata are named. Four kinds of dissolution are described (periodic, natural, final and daily), and many universes arise and perish by the will of the Lord.

09-003.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what Vishnu's illusion (maya) is. Krishna tells how the sage Narada asked Vishnu on the White Island to show him maya. Vishnu laughed, then led Narada away in the form of a Brahmin and came to the city of Vaidisha, to the farmer Sirabhadra, who gave them hospitality. Vishnu blessed him with many sons and wealth in farming. They then visited a poor Brahmin, Gosvami, who gave them what little food he had and was blessed that he would not need to plough or grow grain. Narada asked why Vishnu gave Gosvami what sounded like a curse; Vishnu replied that farmers incur the sin of killing, so Sirabhadra would go to hell while the poor man would be freed. They then came to the lake of Vasishtha near Kanyakubja, where Vishnu bathed first. When Narada bathed he became a beautiful woman, whose body the text describes in detail. King Taladhvaja saw her, married her, and they lived happily for twelve years; in the thirteenth she bore a gourd that broke into fifty sons, who all died fighting among themselves. The woman wept bitterly, Vishnu, in Brahmin form, came and taught that grief is vain because everything passes; he told her to rise and bathe. She came out as Narada again, with all the king's household a dream. Vishnu said he had shown what maya is and vanished.

09-004.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks Krishna a string of questions: by what actions a person becomes a god, a human or an animal, what a child in the womb eats, how a person is born again and gets through the faults of life, and how one gets good family, wealth, a wife, children and an easy death. Krishna answers that good deeds give divine birth, mixed ones a human birth, and bad ones an animal birth, with the Vedas as the proof of what is right and wrong. He then describes in order how the embryo forms month by month, from the joining of seed and blood to the limbs and senses, and how it feeds through the mother's food. The unborn soul remembers its past lives and promises to seek liberation, but birth is painful and the memory is lost. The rest of the chapter is a long teaching on the suffering in every stage of life: the discomfort of the womb and of birth, the trials of childhood, youth and old age, disease, death, hunger, wealth and family cares, and even rule. The body is called impure and unreliable. The text also says the pleasure of sex is no true joy and calls women impure; this is given in the text's own words about desire, and is not the narrator's own statement. The chapter ends by saying that gifts, fasting and vows are the means by which a person gets enjoyment in this world.

09-005.json.summary: Krishna tells Yudhishthira about sin and its punishment. Wrong deeds are of the mind, speech and body, four kinds each: for example, desire for another's wife, false or harsh speech, slander, eating forbidden food, violence, stealing. The five great sins (killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, adultery with a teacher's wife, and keeping company with such people) are listed, followed by a long list of acts counted as equal to killing a Brahmin, among them harming a Brahmin's hunger, taking land given to gods, Brahmins or cows, false witness, abandoning parents or the sacred fire, and carrying tales to the king. Acts equal to lesser theft, minor sins and sins of intent (such as selling wife or children, giving a daughter late, forgetting one's vow, taking pay for teaching, harming the honest or cows, mixing castes, and unjust rulers who tax cruelly or punish the innocent) are also listed. The text says a sinner takes a new body to be punished and is led by Yama's messengers to the realm of Yama, where Dharmaraja punishes; those who show humility and do penance are led by the teacher, not by Yama. It says sin must be atoned for by penance or by suffering, and that deeds of body, speech and mind lead to many hells. Details of the hells follow in the next chapters.

09-006.json.summary: Krishna continues to Yudhishthira with an account of the journey to the realm of Yama. Every being, whatever its age or sex, must go there and have its deeds weighed by Chitragupta and others. Those who gave gifts (shoes, umbrellas, clothes, vehicles, lamps, land, food, water, medicine, shelter, a garden) travel an easy road, and the text says food is the best gift. Those who gave nothing go by a southern road filled with thorns, burning sand, wild animals, storms of stones and fire, and are dragged by Yama's messengers, hungry and thirsty. At Yama's court the good are welcomed and sent to heaven in aerial cars. The wicked see Yama as a terrible being with eighteen arms, on a buffalo; Chitragupta rebukes them, saying each person eats the fruit of his own deeds, and he scolds wicked kings in particular. The sinners are then thrown into the hells, which the text numbers in the hundreds, and it lists many punishments fitted to each sin, such as for stealing, adultery, lying, cursing one's parents or teacher, not giving to guests, and soiling or stealing from Shiva's temples and gardens. It says punishment is for a set time, tells that after hell a person is reborn through plants, insects, birds and animals before again reaching the rare human birth, and urges people to do good while the body is healthy. It adds that even a little taking of refuge in Shiva spares one from seeing Yama's face and sin cannot stain the fully devoted.

09-007.json.summary: Krishna says that the ocean of hell can be crossed by the raft of vows, fasts and rules, and that a person without vows and study is not known in this world or the next. He then tells an old story of a Brahmin of Avanti who sold roots (Mulajalika) and met an ugly siddha who had come from heaven. The Brahmin guessed where he came from by his strange look and asked him to give Rambha, the heavenly dancer, his greetings. The siddha did so; Rambha answered that she knew the Brahmin by name, because he kept the Shakata vow, lived at Mahakala forest and ate roots, although they had never met. Indra heard this, and brought the Brahmin in a heavenly car to heaven, where he enjoyed Rambha as a reward. Krishna ends by saying this was the power of the Shakata vow, and that nothing is out of reach of those firm in their vows, so one should always keep a vow. The chapter does not give the procedure of the vow.

09-008.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks Krishna for the vows of the gods, from Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu to Gauri, Ganesha, Durga, the sun, fire and moon, and for what to do on each lunar day in order. Krishna starts with the first day (pratipada) of the bright half in spring, in the month of Chaitra. A man or a woman bathes, satisfies the ancestors and gods, draws a human figure of the year in rice paste, and worships it with sandalwood, flowers, incense, lamps and food through the year, honouring the months and seasons by name with a Vedic verse. The worshipper then honours Brahmins, wraps the figure in cloth, offers seasonal fruits, roots and sweets, prays that the year be good, gives a fee to a Brahmin and puts a sandalwood mark on the forehead, which is worn daily for a year. The text says the mark makes ghosts, spirits and enemies powerless. The story told is of King Shatrunjaya and his wife Chitralekha, who took the vow in Chaitra from a Brahmin; when the king and his son were struck by an illness and Yama's messengers came to take him, they saw Chitralekha with the mark, turned back, and he recovered and enjoyed the world. Krishna says Shiva first told him this vow, and that it removes all sorrow.

09-009.json.summary: Krishna describes the Ashoka vow. On the first day of the bright half of Ashvina, at sunrise, one worships an ashoka tree with fresh shoots, using sprouted seven grains, sweets, seasonal fruits, coconuts and pomegranates, flowers and incense. The worshipper prays that the tree remove the sorrow of her parents, brothers, husband and in-laws, offers water with faith, and decorates the tree with flags and a cloth. The text says that by this vow a woman becomes dear to her husband, as Damayanti, Vedavati and Sita did. It tells how Sita in the forest, seeing an ashoka tree, worshipped it with her husband and brother-in-law with sesame, rice, lamps, food and incense and prayed with folded hands that her father-in-law, husband, Rama's brothers and Kausalya might live long. A woman who does the same, with sesame, rice, barley, wheat and mustard, bows to the tree, gives a fee to a Brahmin and returns home with her friends is said to gain joy and her husband's love, and to reach the state of Gauri.

09-010.json.summary: Krishna describes the Karavira (oleander) vow, done on the first day of the bright half of the month of Jyeshtha, at sunrise. One worships a lovely karavira tree from a garden, wrapping it in red thread, with scent, incense and ointments, sprouted seven grains, oranges, citrons, sweets and coconuts. One sprinkles it with water and rice, begs its forgiveness with a verse addressed to Karavira, the "dwelling of poison, dear to the sun", and adds a Vedic verse about the sun. After giving a fee to a Brahmin and walking around the tree, one goes home. Krishna says that Anasuya, Kshama, Savitri, Satyabhama, Damayanti, Sarasvati, Gayatri, Ganga and other women kept this vow in the human world to please the sun, and that it gives all kinds of happiness and, at the end, the sun's world.

09-011.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that gives a married woman her husband's deep love. Krishna tells how Kirtimala, wife of King Shatrughna of Mathura (a king set up by Rama), asked the sage Vasishtha how to get happiness and the "sesame" vow. Vasishtha taught the Kokila (cuckoo) vow. On the full-moon day of Ashadha, at dusk, one resolves to bathe, keep celibacy, eat only at night, sleep on the ground and be kind to creatures for the month of Shravana. With a Brahmin's leave, at dawn the vow-keeper bathes daily in a river, tank or spring, with sesame and amla paste at first, then with herbs; honours the sun and ancestors; and worships a cuckoo made of sesame paste with flowers, incense, lamps, sandalwood, sesame, rice and durva grass, using a short prayer to the cuckoo for good fortune, wealth and sons. At the end of the month a cuckoo made of sesame paste, with jewel eyes and golden wings, is placed in a copper dish with cloth, money and jaggery and given to a Brahmin, or to a mother-in-law, father-in-law or priest. The reward promised is good fortune for seven births, a loving husband with no rival wife, and a place in the world of Gauri after death. Kirtimala did all this and received sons, honour and good fortune.

09-012.json.summary: Krishna describes the Brihat-tapas (Great Penance) vow to Shiva, said to destroy sins such as killing a Brahmin. It begins at the end of the month of Ashvina, at the full moon, with a night meal of milk-rice with ghee, chewing a bilva twig, and a promise to Shiva to keep the vow for sixteen years, through all the lunar days in order. In the month of Margashirsha, on the first day, one fasts, bathes, honours Shiva at night with lamps, and invites Brahmin couples (sixteen, eight, four or one, as one can). Next morning one takes offerings to the Shiva temple, anoints the image, bathes it in the five cow products, milk, ghee, honey, curds, sugarcane juice, sesame water and warm water, puts sandalwood, camphor and flowers on it, gives a golden lotus, cloths, a flag, canopy, incense, lamps and a bell, then worships fire, feeds the teacher and Brahmin couples, and ends the fast. One repeats this each month for the first day, then the second day, and on, each lunar day in turn, for sixteen years. At the end one gives a cow with gold horns and silver hoofs to a Brahmin and honours sixteen Shiva devotees. The text says the vow removes sin, is open to men and women (including widows and wives), and that even if one dies before finishing, the fruit is gained; those who keep it pass beyond the sun to Shiva.

09-013.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a person gains memory of past lives. Krishna says by fasting for the "four Bhadras". He tells of the merchant Shubhodaya on the Yamuna, who kept them and was reborn as Svarnashthivi, son of King Sanjaya of Kushavati. When Narada and Parvata visited Sanjaya, both desired his daughter; Narada married her and gave Sanjaya a boon of a son whose bodily waste would turn to gold. Parvata cursed Narada, and Narada cursed him back; Parvata said the son would die by robbers and Narada promised to bring him back from Yama. The boy was born, remembered his past life, and understood animal speech. Robbers killed him for the gold; the gold vanished. Narada consoled Sanjaya with accounts of great kings and then brought the boy back. Krishna names the four Bhadras: Margashirsha, Phalguna, Jyeshtha and Bhadrapada, each a three-month period from the bright half, called Vishnupada, Tripushpa, Trirama and Triranga, giving different rewards. The procedure follows: on the second to fifth days of the bright half of Margashirsha, one eats once, takes a clay and cow-dung bath with prayers (mantras given only to the pure classes and to women with the husband's leave), honours Vishnu with a different name and limb each day, offers arghya to the moon, with growing offerings as the moon waxes, takes a simple meal on the ground, and feeds Brahmins. The fruits named are wealth, victory, kingship, sons, a good husband for a girl, and recall of past births.

09-014.json.summary: Krishna says there are four more second-days of the bright half, one in each of the months Shravana, Bhadrapada, Ashvina and Kartika, never told before; they are named Kaluṣā, Gīrmalā, Pretasaṃcārā and Yamā (Yama-dvitiya). Yudhishthira asks why. Krishna explains the names. After Indra killed Vritra and held the horse sacrifice, he split the sin of killing a Brahmin into six parts and put it on a tree, water, the earth, a woman and fire. So that day the woman, tree, river, earth, fire and the Brahmin-killer were made clean, and it is called Kaluṣā ("impure"). It is Gīrmalā because it carries the "stain of speech" of those who revile gods, sages and ancestors and of scholars who teach in forbidden times. It is Pretasaṃcārā because the ancestors move about in it, satisfied by the offerings of sons and grandsons. On the second of the bright half of Kartika, Yama was first fed in the house of his sister Yamuna; the beings in hell were also set free and rejoiced, so it is Yama-dvitiya. On this day one should not eat at home but at the hand of one's sister, with affection, and give her gifts of gold, ornaments and clothes. Other female relatives may take her place, and the meal is said to give strength, wealth, fame, long life and the three aims of life.

09-015.json.summary: Yudhishthira says a man without a wife and a woman without a husband cannot gain duty, wealth and desire, and asks for a vow by which a woman is not widowed and a man is not parted from his wife. Krishna teaches the Aśūnyaśayanā ("bed not empty") vow, kept on the second day of the dark half of Shravana, when Vishnu is said to sleep beside Lakshmi. One fasts, eats at night, or eats only what comes unasked. After a bath and offerings to the gods and ancestors, one makes a square clay platform, worships Vishnu with Lakshmi with food, flowers, incense and fruits, and says a prayer that one's home life, sacred fires and marriage may not be broken, and that one's bed may never be empty, as Vishnu's is not. At moonrise one bathes with the five cow products and gives the Brahmin a fee. The same is done on the second of each dark half for four months. In Kartika one gives the Brahmin a bed with an image of Vishnu, with its fittings, a water pot and grain, and offers arghya to the moon each month with a prayer. The fruit is no breaking of the home for three births, success in duty, wealth and desire, and lasting rule. A woman who keeps it will not be widowed, unlucky or left by her husband for three births.

09-016.json.summary: Krishna teaches a vow for women on the third day of the dark half of Phalguna. She fasts, keeps chastity, and in the morning, with matted hair as a crown, worships the goddess Gauri (Uma) seated on a lizard-cart, meditating on Rudra, with scents, flowers, lamps, red lac and sandal. She says the prayer asking the goddess for good fortune, to end bad luck, and for birth in a family where she is never widowed in the next life. She also honours a great tree with many offerings: cumin, salt, jaggery, ghee, fruits, flowers, saffron, red powder, cloths, cakes, sesame and rice, and sweets. She walks round it, gives the Brahmin a fee and offers arghya. The fruit is good fortune that is hard to get in the three worlds, freedom from illness, beautiful limbs, and after a hundred years a journey to Rudra's city in a swan-vehicle, enjoying divine pleasures with her husband. The text says Kashyapa first told this vow to Rukmini.

09-017.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the Meghapālī vow. Krishna says on the third day of the dark half of Ashvina, men and women should give an offering (arghya) with devotion to Meghapālī, a red creeper with betel-like leaves and flower clusters that grows in gardens, village paths and hills. The offering is sprouted wheat with seven grains, or balls of sesame and rice. Merchants also give grain, oil, jaggery and saffron. People who sinned by lying and false weights, greedy for wealth, destroy those sins at once by giving arghya to Meghapālī. She is worshipped in a clean place with fruits, flowers, dates, coconuts, pomegranates, incense and lamps, covered with a red cloth, and a learned Brahmin presents the offering with the Vedic prayer. The fruit is great wealth, a hundred years of happy life, Vishnu's world at death, and the lifting of seven generations of one's family from the lower world to heaven. The closing verse says the offering destroys sins done by false weights and measures, as the sun destroys darkness.

09-018.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that gives women a good home and great love from their husbands. Krishna tells of Shiva and Parvati on Kailasa among sages and gods. Shiva asks what good vow Parvati kept to become his beloved; she answers that she kept the Rambha vow on the third day. She says that as a girl at her father Himavan's house, her mother Mena told her to keep it for good fortune. The procedure given is: on the third day of the bright half, after a bath, sit among five fires (the three Vedic fires, a fifth fire, and the sun) facing east, with the goddess (called Mahalakshmi, Mahakali, and by the names of rivers) in front, in a flower pavilion. Brahmins make fire offerings in all directions, and the goddess is worshipped with flowers, incense and many kinds of food, including cumin, salt, sugar and jaggery. The woman sits in the lotus posture until the sun has set, bows, and says a prayer asking the goddess for a husband, a house and wealth. She then gives a fine, many-storied house, with all its fittings, to a famous Brahmin and his wife, gives the food to married women, and on the fourth day feeds married couples with sweet foods. The text says Agastya's wife Lopamudra gained her husband through it. The fruit is sons, a home, enjoyment and a growing family; beauty, skill and good fortune; and power over a rival wife. At death the keeper goes to Indra's world, then Vishnu's, then Shiva's, as Vyasa said.

09-019.json.summary: Krishna teaches the Gopada ("cow's hoof") vow, for a man or woman, kept on the third and fourth days of the bright half of Bhadrapada each year, by fasting. After a bath one honours the cows with flowers, incense, curds, rice, garlands and paste, rubs their horns, hooves and tails, and feeds them morning and evening. One eats only food not cooked on a fire and without oil or salt. When the cows go out and come back, at the village gate or the cowshed, one offers arghya at their feet with a Vedic verse addressed to the cow (the mother of the Rudras, daughter of the Vasus), and the prayer "let cows be before me, behind me, in my heart; I live among cows". On the fifth day one eats cow products and curds without anger, then sleeps controlled. In the morning one gives a golden cow-hoof to a Brahmin and asks forgiveness of Govinda. Cows and Mount Govardhana are honoured alike. The fruit is good fortune and beauty, a house full of cows and calves, wealth and grain, honoured children, divine life in heaven for a hundred ages and then Vishnu's city. The closing verse says a three-night keeper of the vow reaches the pure world of cows.

09-020.json.summary: Krishna teaches the worship of Harakali (Gauri, the beloved of Shankara) on the third day of the bright half of Bhadrapada. Sprouted grain of every kind and fresh green grass stand for her; she is worshipped with scents, flowers, fruits, incense and sweets. A night vigil with bells and songs follows, and in the morning married women carry her to a holy pond and let her go. Yudhishthira asks who Harakali is. Krishna tells of Kali, a dark daughter of Daksha with the colour of a blue lotus, who was given to Shiva and married with full rites. One day in the assembly Shiva called her playfully to come and sit near his white body. She was hurt by it and wept. Saying that because of her dark colour he had called her Harakali, she went into a blazing fire and gave up that body, leaving a green radiance on the green grass. She was born again in the house of the mountain king as Gauri and now holds half of Shiva's body. The worship prayer says "Harakali, beloved of Hara, protect me". Food is given to a Brahmin and the goddess is sent away in the morning in water with a prayer asking her to come again. The fruit for a woman who keeps it each year is a long healthy life, all enjoyments, good fortune, children and grandchildren, a hundred years on earth, and after death the knowledge of Shiva and the service of his attendants, such as Mahakala, Nandishvara and Vinayaka.

09-021.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the twelve-month Lalita vow. Krishna tells the old talk of Shiva and Parvati on Kailasa. Uma asks for the best vow on the third day by which women gain good fortune, wealth, sons, heaven, beauty and health, and explains that women suffer: some are ugly, childless, ill-treated by mothers-in-law, or unloved. Shiva says the vow is kept in the bright half of Magha, on the third day. One fasts, brushes the teeth, bathes at midday with bilva and amalaka fruits in clean water, puts on clean clothes and worships the goddess with scents, flowers, camphor, incense and sweets. A gold coin is put in a copper vessel of water and rice, and the water is poured on the head with a prayer to the goddess to wait with the water-clock. One drinks kusha water, sleeps on the ground on green grass, and on the second day bathes and worships again and feeds Brahmins. The goddess is worshipped by a different name each month: Kalika (first), Parvati, Shankara-priya, Bhavani, Skandamata, Daksha's daughter, Mainaki, Katyayani, Himadrija, the giver of good fortune, Uma and Gauri. Each month a different substance is eaten (kusha water, milk, ghee, cow urine, dung, neem leaf, curds, the five cow products and so on) and a gift is made. At the end a learned Brahmin and his wife are worshipped as Shiva and Uma, given food, a fee, and red cloths. The fruit is ten thousand years in higher worlds with her husband like Shachi with Indra, then a good rebirth, no widowhood for seven births, sons, beauty and the husband's special love.

09-022.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a woman can be with her husband and kin in this world and the next and not be parted even if widowed. Krishna gives the vow taught by Vasishtha to Arundhati. In Margashirsha, on the second of the bright half, she eats rice-milk at night, bows to Shankara, uses a tooth-stick of udumbara wood, and worships Gauri and Shambhu made of rice flour as a woman and a man, keeping a night vigil. Next day she gives the figures to the teacher and feeds Brahmins and married couples. It is done each month, with a different name and a different flower: for example Shrikantha in Shravana, Bhima with Durga in Bhadrapada, Ishana in Kartika, Sthanu in Vaishakha, Vireshvara in Jyeshtha, Pashupati in Ashadha, with flowers like blue lotus, karavira, bilva, kimshuka, jasmine and others. On the fourth day of Pausha one drinks the five cow products. At the end of the year the woman gives Shiva a canopy, incense, a bell, a banner, lamp and two cloths, and worships a golden lotus on the head of the image. She then feeds a Brahmin woman in a triangular space and twelve Brahmins and as many couples in a square. A golden Uma-Maheshvara with 64 pearls, corals and topazes on a copper plate, wrapped in cloth, goes to the teacher. Forty-eight pots, an umbrella, shoes and gifts follow, with food for the poor and blind, according to means. The fruit is no separation, beauty, good fortune, wealth, long life, sons, heaven and Shiva's world.

09-023.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what vow gives women good fortune, many sons, wealth, grain, gold, clothes and no separation from family. Krishna teaches the Umamaheshvara vow, said to have been kept first by nymphs, Vidyadharas, Kinnaras and sages' daughters, and by Rambha, Sita, Ahalya, Rohini, Damayanti and Anasuya, and brought down by Parvati for women who are unlucky, poor or childless. In Margashirsha, on the third of the bright half, the woman fasts and worships Lalita, who lives in half of Shiva's body, bathes again at dawn, says a prayer to the goddess, and worships Ishana with seasonal flowers, with Uma on the left and Maheshvara on the right, with incense, cooked food, a fire offering of sesame and ghee, and the five cow products. This is done for twelve months. At the end she makes a silver Shiva and a golden Uma seated on a silver bull, worships them with sandal and saffron, covers Shiva in white cloth and Parvati in red, feeds Shiva's devotees and Brahmins, and gives them fees. She gives the vow to a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas. The fruit is a stay in Shiva's world for the lifetime of fourteen Indras, then birth in a good family, beauty, many sons, wealth, no separation from husband or sons, and at death Shiva's city.

09-024.json.summary: Krishna teaches the Rambha-tritiya, which he says Shankara once told Parvati; it destroys sins, gives sons and good fortune, cures illness and breaks a rival wife's pride. In Margashirsha, on the third of the bright half, one rises at dawn, brushes the teeth, and promises to fast on the third of every month for a year and break the fast next day. One bathes, worships Parvati, and at night takes kusha water. In the morning one feeds Shiva's devotees and gives gold and salt. In each month a different name of the goddess is worshipped and a different thing is taken or given: Pausha gives cow urine; Magha (Sudevi) cow dung and safflower; Phalguna (Gauri) cow's milk; Chaitra (Vishalakshi) curds; Vaishakha (Shrimukhi) ghee; Ashadha (Madhavi) sesame water; Shravana (Shri) water of cow's horns; Bhadrapada (Haratali) buffalo milk; Ashvina (Giriputri) rice water; Kartika (Padmodbhava) the five cow products and a night vigil. The fruits include the merit of the Vajapeya and Atiratra sacrifices, long stays in Indra's and Vishnu's worlds, sons, good fortune and union with Shiva. At the end a golden Uma-Maheshvara, a five-coloured canopy, an umbrella, water pot, shoes, cloths, sacred threads, mirrors and lamps are given with a ceremony of conch and Vedic sound, and Brahmin couples are honoured. The text says it is called Rambha's vow because she kept it, and closes by telling the king to take refuge in Parvati, since Shiva and Gauri are one.

09-025.json.summary: Krishna teaches the Saubhagya-shayana ("bed of good fortune") vow. He tells how, when the worlds were burned, all good fortune rested in Vishnu's chest; in a quarrel between Brahma and Krishna a flame arose and good fortune dripped from Vishnu's chest and fell to the earth, taking eight forms: sugarcane, a kind of leaf, beans, cumin, milk, safflower, saffron and salt (the eight fortunes). Daksha, Brahma's son, drank the first part, and his daughter Sati was called Lalita. Shiva married her. In the spring, on the third of the bright half, one bathes with sesame, and the goddess is worshipped with Shiva with the limbs honoured one by one under different names, and the eight fortunes are set before her. A different item is taken each month (such as cow's-horn water, cow dung, curds, kusha water, milk, ghee, cow urine, black sesame, the five cow products) and a different flower is used. At the end of the year a bed with all its fittings, a golden Uma-Maheshvara and a bull and cow are given to a Brahmin couple, with other gifts, honestly and without miserliness. The fruit is every wish, good fortune, health, beauty and life with no separation for 300,000 years, or, for a twelve-year keeper, honour for three myriad ages. A woman or girl who keeps it gains the same fruit. Hearing or giving it makes one a Vidyadhara in heaven. The text says Madana, Shashabindu, Indra, Kubera, Vayu and Soma kept it before.

09-026.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that gives good fortune and health and destroys rivals. Krishna teaches the Ananta-tritiya of Gauri, in Bhadrapada, Vaishakha or Margashirsha, on the third of the bright half. The worshipper bathes with white mustard and puts a mark of cow bile, cow urine, mustard, dung, curds and sandal on the forehead; wears yellow or red cloth (widows red or yellow flowers, girls white). The image of the goddess is bathed with the five cow products, milk, honey and scented water and worshipped with white flowers, fruits and grains. Her body is honoured limb by limb with a name for each (Varada, Shri, Ashoka, Bhavani, Kamadevi, Parvati, Gauri, Katyayani and others). A twelve-petalled lotus is drawn in saffron with the goddess's forms placed in the petals. Married women are honoured with red cloths and garlands and sindura on their heads. Each month a different flower and a different thing to eat is named, and on the second of each half a Brahmin couple is fed as Shiva and Gauri. At the end a golden bed with a lotus is given, twenty-four couples are honoured once, and the teacher must be honoured, for without that all rites fail. A pregnant woman, a woman after childbirth, a girl or an ill person may have the rite done by another. A poor person may keep it by fasting for three years with flowers and leaves. The fruit is a hundred crores of ages honoured in Shiva's world. A second vow, the Rasakalyanini on the third of Magha, follows. The worshipper bathes with cow products and sesame, the goddess is honoured limb by limb, and Brahmin couples are fed. Each month one thing is given up (salt in Magha, jaggery in Phalguna, sugar in Chaitra, honey in Vaishakha, and so on), and at the end vessels with those foods, a golden lizard with five jewels, a cow and bull of gold and a bed are given. The fruit is freedom from sin at once, no sorrow for a billion births, and the merit of a thousand Agnishtomas.

09-027.json.summary: Krishna teaches the Ardrananda-kari third, a sin-removing vow of the bright third when the moon is in Ashadha or Brahma's lunar mansion. One bathes with kusha and scented water, wears white garlands and cloth and white paste, and worships Bhavani with Mahadeva seated on a fine seat, with white flowers. Their limbs are honoured one by one, with a name for each (Vasudevi, Shankara, Rambha, Pinakin, Aditi, Madhavi, Utkanthini, Nilakantha and others). Lotuses, a conch, a wheel and a svastika are made. In each month from Margashirsha one sleeps after taking a different item: cow urine, dung, milk, curds, ghee, kusha water, cow-horn water, bilva leaf, scented water, barley-flour water and sesame water. On giving, one says "may Gauri be pleased". At the end of the year the worshipper gives salt, a pot of jaggery, sandal, an eye-cloth, two white cloths, a golden Uma-Maheshvara with sugarcane and a bed with its covering to a Brahmin and his wife. The fruit is Shiva's highest place, wealth, life, health, and joy like Yama's. A woman, girl or widow gets the same fruit. Anyone who hears or recites it is honoured in Indra's world for 300 years.

09-028.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks why Krishna never told the three thirds of Chaitra, Bhadrapada and Magha, which give beauty, good fortune and sons. Krishna replies that he had not told it because it is secret, but he will, and recounts what Jaya, a companion of Uma, told the sages' daughters. On the bright third of Chaitra, after a morning fast, one makes a cloth pavilion with a water pot and a Brahmin seated on a seat, and a square fire pit. After a bath, ancestors and gods are honoured and the goddess worshipped in her temple with eight names (Parvati, Lalita, Gauri, Gandhari, Shankari, Shiva, Uma, Sati), with flowers, saffron, camphor, incense and many kinds of sweets and fruits, also household things such as a pestle, winnowing basket, mirror, and eye-salve. Girls bathe in new pots at sunset. They keep a night of music, dance and talk, give betel and saffron to married women, and in the morning bathe and worship again. The worshipper is weighed against salt, jaggery or saffron on a scale as a gift, then feeds learned Brahmins and married women and shares the food. In Bhadrapada the goddess is worshipped on a winnowing basket with seven grains, with cow urine taken; in Magha she is weighed against flowers on a bed of barley and worshipped with jasmine. The story given is of a woman of the city of Vidarbha, perfectly beautiful, who followed it on a Brahmin's word, enjoyed life and gave gifts, and was reborn as Avantisundari, a king's daughter, lovely and loved. She had sons strong as Vishnu and Indra and at death reached the worlds of the guardians and Brahma and then union with Shiva. A woman who keeps it has no unlucky daughters, no bad sons or servants, no poverty or illness in her house, and all her wishes come true.

09-029.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the Anantarya ("without break") vow of the third days of the bright half, for the good of all beings and especially women, with the name, food and offering for each month. Krishna says he will teach this vow told by Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. It starts in Margashirsha: a night meal on the second, a fast on the third, worship of Uma with flowers and scents, an offering of sugar figures, curds at night, and a couple fed in the morning, with the fruit of a horse sacrifice. Then every month, on the bright third and the dark third, the goddess is worshipped under another name (such as Katyayani, Gauri, Parvati, Bhadri, Vishalakshi, Shri, Kali, Chandika, Kalaratri, Skandamata, Kushmanda, Chanda, Rudrani, Durga, Narayani), with a set offering and a set food taken at night, then a couple fed at dawn. For each month the text names the reward, such as a horse sacrifice, a man sacrifice, a Rajasuya or the fruit of giving a thousand cows. After a year the worshipper is freed from sin. In the final rite a golden Uma and Shiva are made with jewels, set on a fine bed with canopy and flags, worshipped with a night of song and music, and given with a decorated red cow and other gifts to the teacher, with a prayer for never being parted. The fruit is the worlds of Gandharvas, Yakshas and Vishnu, then rebirth as a king; a woman who keeps it becomes a great queen who lives with her husband without parting in every birth, as Uma with Rudra, Shachi with Indra and Lakshmi with Vishnu. Krishna says to teach it only to a devoted, humble person.

09-030.json.summary: Krishna tells Yudhishthira about the third of the bright half of Vaishakha (Akshaya Tritiya), the first day of the Krita age. Bathing, gifts, prayer, fire offerings, study and offerings to ancestors done on it never decay, and it removes all sin. A merchant named Dharma of the city of Shakala, truthful and a worshipper of gods and Brahmins, heard that when this third falls on the Rohini star with Wednesday it is very fruitful. He bathed in the Ganga, honoured ancestors and gods, and gave water pots, barley, wheat, gram, flour, curds and rice, sugarcane products and gold to Brahmins, though his wife tried to stop him. He died remembering Vasudeva and was reborn as a king in Kushavati whose wealth never ran out; he did great sacrifices and gave cows, land and gold, and his riches did not decrease. The vow is to give water pots with the juices of the season, summer grain, umbrellas, sandals, cows, land, gold and clothes, and whatever one likes best, without doubt. The chapter ends by saying that what is given or offered on this day does not decay.

09-031.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that gives beauty, good fortune and happiness, and Krishna says he will tell a great secret he had not told before. He explains how Angaraka (Mars) was born: a drop of blood fell to the earth from Shiva and Parvati's great delight, and the Earth held it; from it the red child was born, named for Shiva's limb, and he gives good fortune and health. The vow is for the fourth (Chaturthi) when it falls on Angaraka's day (Tuesday), with a night meal. The text gives the rite in order: a bath with earth taken in water and prayers, touching durva grass, the shami and the ashvattha trees and a cow with prayers, then silence, a fire offering with his names (Kuja, Lohitanga and others) 108 times, and worship of a red image on a copper, gold or other vessel with red flowers and saffron. Eight limbs of the god are honoured one by one. A learned, pure Brahmin is fed and given the image, clothes, jewels and a fee; the text warns that miserliness spoils the fruit, and a poor person may do it as they can. If the day with Tuesday comes again, the vow is repeated each time. The reward is a long life with sons and grandsons, then a heavenly chariot, 36 four-age cycles among the gods, and rebirth as a handsome, wealthy and generous king, or, for a woman, a fortunate wife with children.

09-032.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks why work begun by good men does not succeed. Krishna says Vinayaka (Ganesha) was set over the troops of Rudra's followers by Rudra and Brahma to decide success. A person seized by him shows signs in dreams: bathing in water, seeing shaven men, people in red robes, flesh-eaters, riding donkeys, camels or buffaloes, going toward a cremation ground, or being smeared in oil. The text says that such a person gets no kingdom, a girl no husband, a woman no child, a teacher or pupil no learning, a merchant no profit and a farmer no crop. The remedy is a ritual bath on an auspicious day, the fourth of the bright half or Thursday, with mustard paste and all herbs and scents, in front of the one who is bathed and seated on a seat while Brahmins say blessings. Four jars of water are brought from places such as a stable, an elephant place, an anthill and a river meeting, with the prayer "Sahasraksham shatadharam" and a verse asking the waters to remove bad luck. Mustard oil is offered in the fire with the names of the Vinayaka spirits (Mita, Sammita, Shalakatankata, Kushmanda, Rajaputra). On a crossroads a winnowing basket holds rice, fish, meat, drink, sweets and other food as an offering. Then Ambika is honoured with durva, mustard and flowers and asked for beauty, victory, sons, wealth and strength. The person wears white, feeds Brahmins and gives clothes to the teacher. The reward is success in all work, fortune and, with the worship of the Sun and the planets, accomplishment.

09-033.json.summary: Krishna tells a vow that removes obstacles, kept on the fourth (Chaturthi) of Phalguna, with a night meal and a sesame-food meal to break the fast. The same sesame food is offered in the fire and given to a Brahmin. The vow-keeper worships Ganesha under names such as Shura, Vira, Gajanana, Lambodara and Ekadanta and offers fire again to remove obstacles. After keeping it through the four months and into the fifth, one makes a golden elephant-faced image and gives it to a Brahmin with four copper vessels of milk-rice and the sesame; a poor person may use clay vessels, and a silver Heramba image is also given. The text says that this frees one from all obstacles. It names those who kept it before: King Sagara, whose horse sacrifice was blocked and who got his horse back; Rudra, who destroyed the three cities; and Krishna himself, who raised the Earth with its mountains and trees when it went into the ocean (as the text has it, spoken in the Boar's words). Other kings did it too for success in sacrifice. At death the keeper goes to Rudra's city, and no obstacles come to the house of one who worships Vighnesha on the fourth with a night meal.

09-034.json.summary: Krishna teaches the Peace (Shanti) vow for householders. From the bright fifth of Kartika for one year, the keeper eats without sour food, takes a night meal, and worships Hari lying on the serpent Shesha. The serpent kings honour the limbs one by one: Ananta the feet, Dhritarashtra the waist, Padma the ears, Mahapadma the arms, Shankhapala the chest and Kulika the head. A silent bath of milk is given to Hari and milk with sesame is offered in the fire. At the end of the year Brahmins are fed, and a golden Achyuta, a cow with calf, a pair of clothes, a bronze vessel with milk-rice and gold are given to a Brahmin as one can. The reward is lasting peace in the house and freedom from fear of serpents; those who worship on the bright fifths with sweet food do not fear serpents.

09-035.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks which vow gives a sweet voice, popular favour, skill in learning, harmony between husband and wife and relatives, and long life. Krishna teaches the Sarasvata vow, whose very telling pleases Sarasvati. At the start of the year, on a Sunday with good planets and stars, the keeper feeds milk-rice to Brahmins, has blessings said, gives white cloth and gold, and worships Gayatri with white garlands and scents, with prayers asking that she never leave them and that they gain the arts, the Vedas, song and dance, and that the eight forms (Lakshmi, Medha, Vara, Arishti, Gauri, Tushti, Prabha, Mati) protect them. She is pictured with a lute, rosary, water pot and book. The keeper eats silently morning and evening, and on the fifth of the dark half feeds married women with sesame, rice, ghee, milk and gold; no food between times for thirteen months. At the end white rice food, two cloths and a cow are given, with a canopy, bell and cloths for the goddess, and the teacher is honoured honestly. The reward is learning, wealth and a good voice, poet's skill like Vyasa, and for a woman who keeps it the same; also a stay in Brahma's world for three myriad ages, and for those who hear or read it a stay in the city of the Vidyadharas.

09-036.json.summary: Krishna says the fifth (Panchami) is dear to serpents, and he names the serpents Vasuki, Takshaka, Kaliya, Manibhadra, Dhritarashtra, Raivata, Karkotaka and Dhananjaya, who give safety. Yudhishthira asks why the serpents were cursed. Krishna tells how Kadru and Vinata argued about the colour of the horse Uchchaihshravas, risking servitude: Kadru said it had a black tail, and told her serpent sons to become black hairs on it. They refused as wrong, so she cursed them to be burned in Janamejaya's serpent sacrifice. Vasuki fell in grief; Brahma comforted him, saying the sage Jaratkaru would marry his sister, and their son Astika would stop the sacrifice with his words. The serpents were glad, and the day is the bright fifth, which Brahma gave to serpents. The rite is to feed Brahmins, give a send-off with a prayer to serpents of the earth, the Himalaya, the sky, rivers and ponds, then eat. The reward is the city of the serpents, then rebirth as a king in five lives. Yudhishthira asks about those bitten; Krishna says a bitten person goes down and becomes a harmless snake, and gives a year-long vow on the fifths from Bhadrapada, with a night meal, a five-hooded serpent image in gold, silver, wood or clay, worship with flowers, and a fed Brahmin, a Narayana offering for the bitten, a bull release after a year, a gold serpent and a cow, with a different serpent each month. This frees the bitten relative. It is also said to be done with painted serpents in Bhadrapada and kusha serpents with Indrani in Ashvina, and a mantra is given. Those who worship on the fifths have no fear from serpents.

09-037.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks how Lakshmi, hard to win in the three worlds, is gained. Krishna tells that Shri, born long ago to Bhrigu and Khyati, was given by the sage to Vasudeva, and when she was in the world all was well and prosperous. The gods became proud through her favour, and truth, purity and good conduct left them; she left them for the demons, who also became arrogant and boasted that they were the Vedas, sacrifices and gods. She then entered the ocean, and the three worlds lost their wealth. Indra asked Brihaspati for a vow that wins Lakshmi and keeps her; Brihaspati taught the Shri Panchami vow, which gods, demons, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Siddhas, Vishnu, Brahmins and kings then kept, some in a pure, some in a passionate and some in a dark mood. After it they churned the ocean with Mandara and Vasuki; the moon and then Lakshmi rose, looked at all, and went to Vishnu's chest. Indra gained lordship of the three worlds, while the demons, whose mood was dark, lost their wealth. The vow: on the bright fifth of Margashirsha, make a fast and an image of Lakshmi in gold, silver or on a painted cloth, bathe, honour ancestors and gods, and worship her limbs one by one under names such as Chapala, Kamalavasini, Lalita and Madhavi, with an offering, feed married women and give a Brahmin rice and ghee. Each month she is named in turn (Shri, Lakshmi, Kamala, Sampad, Padma, Narayani, Dhriti, Sthiti, Pushti, Riddhi, Siddhi). In the twelfth month, she is placed on a bed with all its fittings in a cloth pavilion and given with a cow and calf to a Brahmin householder such as Vyasa. The fruit is Lakshmi in the house for twenty-one families, and for a woman, with her husband's leave, good fortune and many sons.

09-038.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the sixth-day vow that ends illness and gives the fruit of all acts, and for the worship of the Sun. Krishna teaches the Vishoka ("sorrowless") Shashthi. On the fifth of the bright half of Magha, one bathes with black sesame, eats lightly, fasts and keeps chastity at night. In the morning one makes a golden lotus, worships it as the Sun with red oleander and a pair of red cloths, and says a prayer for a sorrowless house and devotion in every birth. On the sixth, Brahmins are honoured, cow urine is taken, and a pot of jaggery and fine cloths go to a Brahmin; on the seventh one eats food without oil or salt, in silence, and listens to a Purana. This is done in both halves until the next bright seventh of Magha. At the end a pot with a golden lotus, a bed with its fittings and a milk cow are given. The fruit is the highest state; for as many births as a hundred crores and thousands, no sorrow, illness or bad fate; whatever is wished for is gained, and one who wishes for nothing reaches Brahman. Reading or hearing it gives Indra's world.

09-039.json.summary: Krishna tells another vow, the Padma Shashthi (also called Phala Shashthi), which frees one from sin. On the sixth of the bright half of Margashirsha, after fasting on the fifth, one makes a golden lotus and a golden fruit and gives them with sugar to a Brahmin householder in the morning, saying that the Sun be pleased. The seventh is a milk meal, and the fruit is given up on the dark seventh too. This is kept on both sixths for a year, with the Sun's names said each month in turn (Bhanu, Arka, Ravi, Brahma, Surya, Shukra, Hari, Shiva, Vibhavasu, Tvashtri, Varuna and others). At the end a Brahmin couple is honoured with clothes and ornaments, and a pot of sugar with a golden lotus and fruit is given. The fruit is freedom from all sins, even such as drinking liquor, a place in the Sun's world and the saving of twenty-one past and future men of the family. Hearing or reading it brings welfare.

09-040.json.summary: Krishna tells the Mandara Shashthi, which destroys sin and gives wishes. On the bright fifth of Magha the keeper eats lightly, cleans the teeth with a twig and fasts on the sixth, honouring Brahmins and eating a mandara flower at night. In the morning, after a bath, Brahmins are fed, and a golden man with a lotus in his hand and a lotus of black sesame with eight petals on a copper vessel are worshipped with mandara flowers. Each petal has a Sun name (Bhaskara, Surya, Arka, Aryaman, Vasudhatri, Chandabhanu, Pushan and Ananda), and the central man is honoured as the soul of all. He is wrapped in white cloth, offered food, garlands and fruit and given to a Veda-knowing Brahmin; the keeper eats in silence, facing east, without oil and salt. This is done on the seventh of each month for a year, without miserliness, and at the end it is given with cows according to means, with a prayer asking to be carried across the mud of the world. The fruit is freedom from sin and a happy stay in heaven for an age; hearing or reading it frees one from sins as well, and the text says it is better than gifts of cows, land, gold or sesame.

09-041.json.summary: Krishna tells the Lalita vow for women, on the bright sixth of Bhadrapada. A well-dressed woman bathes in a great river in the morning, takes sand in a new bamboo vessel, goes home, fasts and worships the goddess Lalita (Gauri, who lives in the penance forest) in a cloth shelter lit with lamps, with fresh flowers, champaka, oleander and others, in sets of 108 or 28, and with a prayer to Lalita as giver of comfort and good fortune. Pumpkins, gourds, bitter gourds and sweets are laid before her. The woman keeps a night of song, music and dance with her friends and must not close her eyes for the four watches, since the text says closing them brings bad luck, poverty or childlessness. On the seventh she takes the sand to the river with songs and music, gives the offerings to a Brahmin, bathes, makes a fire offering, honours gods, ancestors and a married woman, and feeds girls and fifteen Brahmins with a fee. The fruit is comfort and good fortune and the world of Gauri; the text says she shines like Lalita in the three worlds.

09-042.json.summary: Krishna speaks of the sixth of Margashirsha, dear to Kartikeya (Skanda, Guha, Gangeya), who killed Tarakasura on it. Bathing and gifts on it do not decay, and seeing Kartikeya in the south frees one from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. The keeper fasts and makes an image of gold, silver or clay, bathes in the afternoon and, sitting in a lotus posture, thinks of him while a learned Brahmin pours water from a new pot on his head from the south with a verse about the Ganga's stream. The Sun is worshipped, then Kartikeya with the names Devasenapati, Skanda, Kartikeya, Kumara, Guha, Gangeya and Shaktihasta, with fruits, offerings, sandal, and fire offerings with ghee and sesame. His goat, cock and peacock and the Krittika star-cluster are honoured. The keeper sleeps on kusha grass after eating fruits in order, and next morning gives a golden goat or cock to a Brahmin. Each month one of the twelve names of Kartikeya is said, and Brahmins are fed first. At the end of the year in Kartika he is worshipped with clothes and ornaments, and recitation and fire offerings are given to a reciter. The fruit is crossing the world, a good wish and Indra's world. The text adds that Kartikeya should always be worshipped by kings, that one who worships him on going to war wins as Indra does against demons, and that a night meal on the sixth frees from sin.

09-043.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the seventh (Saptami). Krishna says that on the bright seventh falling on a Sunday, called Vijaya, bathing, gifts, prayer, fire offering and fasting remove great sins. A person who circles the Sun with fruits and flowers gets a fine son. The fruits for each day are named: coconuts on the first, red oranges on the second, citrons on the third, bananas on the fourth, pumpkins on the fifth, ripe tendu on the sixth, and brinjals on the seventh, in sets of 108, and also jewels and many fruits. Circling is done in silence with one mind; the Sun is bathed in ghee, an umbrella is tied, he is worshipped with saffron, flowers and incense, and a prayer asks for health, life, victory and a son. The vow is kept with a fast, a night meal or food unasked. Its fruit is healing for the sick, wealth for the poor, sons for the childless and learning for the student. When it comes with a Sunday it is kept for seven sevenths, eating a night meal of mung beans, sleeping on palash leaves, and giving a golden image with mung beans to a Brahmin reciter, with a six-syllable mantra and 108 offerings. The text says gifts, ancestor rites and journeys on it succeed, and that kings who want victory should set out on it. The fruit is the Sun's world, then rebirth as a king with elephants, horses and wealth; a woman who keeps it gets the same fruit.

09-044.json.summary: Krishna tells another gift, the "Aditya-mandala" (Sun disc), which removes all bad luck. A disc like the Sun is made of white barley or wheat flour, well cooked and filled with jaggery, cow products and ghee, and the Sun is worshipped, and before him a red-sandal or saffron disc is made. It is set on red cloth, worshipped and given to a Brahmin with a prayer saying it is made of the Sun's brightness, and the Brahmin accepts it with a prayer for the wishes, wealth, duty, sons and comfort it brings. The giver shines like the Sun in heaven and becomes lord of a region. It is to be given from the Vijaya Saptami and then every day according to one's means.

09-045.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for one seventh that gives wishes, wealth and comfort. Krishna says to begin the Saptami vow on a Sunday of the bright half after the northern course of the sun has ended, under the star Pushya (Punnama). On the sixth, one avoids thirteen things, including rice, barley, sesame, beans, wheat, meat, honey, union, a bronze vessel, oil rub, eye salve and ground stone paste. The keeper pays respect with water to gods, sages and ancestors, honours the Sun, offers sesame and barley with ghee in the fire, and sleeps on the ground with the Sun in mind. Avoiding those things and keeping this for a year gives comfort and the wishes of the heart.

09-046.json.summary: Krishna says the sage Lomasha once came to Mathura, was honoured by Vasudeva and Devaki, and told Devaki, whose children had died, that she would have living sons through a vow, as Chandramukha (Chandramukhi) did after her children died. Devaki asks who she was. Lomasha tells of Queen Chandramukhi, wife of King Nahusha of Ayodhya, and the priest's wife Bhushana, close friends. At the Sarayu they saw city women worship Shiva and Uma in a drawn circle and tie a gold-thread cord on the arm, with a pledge to offer oneself to Shiva for life. The two friends took the pledge, but years later the queen forgot the cord, died, and was reborn as a monkey, and her friend as a hen; both remembered their past lives and met again. They then became Ishvari, wife of a king, and Bhushana, wife of the priest Agnimila. Bhushana had eight children, who died and came to life again; Ishvari's only son died at nine. Ishvari, jealous, plotted to kill Bhushana's sons, but they lived. Asked what merit she had, Bhushana tells of the vow: on the seventh of Bhadrapada one bathes at water, draws Shiva with Ambika, worships and ties a cord (of gold or silver) on the hand, gives a sweet cake and a roll to the mother-in-law or a Brahmin without eating it oneself, and a ring on a copper vessel to a Brahmin. She says the pledge was broken by Ishvari's pride. She offers half her merit, Ishvari accepts, becomes a mother of children and attains liberation. Krishna says Devaki will have sons and bear the Lord of the three worlds, and those who keep this vow never lose children.

09-047.json.summary: Krishna teaches a set of monthly sevenths beginning with Magha, each worshipping the Sun under a different name with the fruit of a sacrifice: Varuna (Agnishtoma), Surya in Phalguna (Vajapeya), Vedamshu in Chaitra (Ukthya), Dhata in Vaishakha (Pashubandha), Indra in Jyeshtha (Vajapeya), Divakara in Ashadha (Bahuvarna), Mitra in Shravana (Sautramani), Ravi in Bhadrapada (Tulapurusha gift), Savitri in Ashvina (a thousand cows), the sevenhorsed Sun in Kartika (a Pundarika), Bhanu in Margashirsha (Rajasuya tenfold), and Bhaskara in Pausha (man sacrifice). On the dark seventh the same is done with a fast for a year, and then the Sun sacrifice: on a clean place smeared with red sandal, a Sun disc is drawn with red lead and ochre, worshipped with red flowers, lotuses and incense and a cooked offering. Pots with rice stand before it, and a thousand fire offerings are made with arka wood, sesame, ghee and jaggery. Brahmins get a fee, red and white clothes, twelve cows with cloth, and an umbrella and sandals each. The reward is health, beauty, eloquence and long life; those who fast on the seventh and see the Sun's face reach the Sun's world. The vow is attributed to the sage Narada.

09-048.json.summary: Asked for a vow that crosses the sea of the world and gives heaven and health, Krishna teaches the Kalyana Saptami. When the bright seventh falls on a Sunday it is called Vijaya. One bathes in the morning in cow's milk, wears white and draws an eight-petalled lotus with rice, putting the Sun's names on the petals (Tapana, Martanda, Divakara, Vidhatri, Varuna, Bhaskara, Ravi and others) and a salutation to the Supreme Soul in the middle. The Sun is worshipped with white cloth, fruit, food, incense and garlands with jaggery and salt, and with fire offerings, Brahmins are fed with jaggery, milk and ghee, and a sesame vessel and gold are given to the teacher. The keeper eats ghee milk-rice with Veda-knowing Brahmins. After a year the vow is concluded with a ghee vessel and a pot of water, and a cow with clothes and ornaments and a golden face; even a poor person gives one cow, without miserliness. Reading or hearing it frees one from sins; one who worships the Sun in the lotus on the day after the sixth is said to gain good fortune.

09-049.json.summary: Krishna tells the Sugar Seventh (Sharkara Saptami), which destroys sin and gives long life, health and wealth. On the bright seventh of Vaishakha, one bathes with sesame in the morning, draws a lotus with saffron on a clean spot and offers scents and flowers to Savitri, puts a water pot with a sugar vessel and a golden horse on it, dressed in red cloth and white garlands, and worships with a prayer calling the Sun the Vedas' god and the all of nectar. One stays awake reciting the Sun hymn or hearing a Purana. On the eighth, everything is given to a Veda-knowing Brahmin, Brahmins are fed with sugar, ghee and milk-rice, and the keeper eats food without oil and salt in silence. This is done each month, and after a year a bed with cloth, a sugar pot, all its fittings and a milk cow are given, and a house can be given too; a golden horse is given with the prayer. The text warns against miserliness. It explains that drops of nectar fell from the Sun's mouth as he drank the nectar, and became rice, mung beans and sugarcane, hence sugar is dear to the Sun and ancestors. The fruit is that of a horse sacrifice, ending of all troubles, increase of children, and, for one of great devotion, the highest Brahman after a stay in heaven for an age. Those who hear, recall or read it are honoured in the world of the lord of gods.

09-050.json.summary: Krishna tells the Lotus Seventh (Kamala Saptami), whose telling pleases the Sun. In spring, on the bright seventh, one bathes with white mustard, places a golden lotus on a sesame vessel, wraps it in a pair of cloths and worships it with scents and flowers, with salutations to the Sun as the lotus-handed one, the holder of the universe and the maker of light. In the evening it is given with a water pot to a Brahmin, honoured with cloth, garlands and ornaments. On the eighth Brahmins are fed, and the keeper eats without meat or oil. It is done on every bright seventh, without miserliness, and at the end a bed with a golden lotus and a milk cow with gold and household things are given. The fruit is endless Lakshmi, joy in the Sun's world, passing through seven worlds in every age with Apsaras and then the highest state. Those who see, hear or read it are given good sense and lasting Lakshmi, and reach the worlds of the Gandharvas and Vidyadharas.

09-051.json.summary: Krishna tells the Shubha ("auspicious") Saptami, by which a person is freed from illness and sorrow. In Ashvina the keeper bathes in milk, has Brahmins say blessings and worships a tawny cow with scents and garlands, with a verse greeting her as born from the Sun. He gives a measure of sesame with a copper vessel, a golden bull, cloth, garlands and jaggery, with a prayer that Aryaman be pleased, takes the five cow products and sleeps on the ground. In the morning Brahmins are fed. Every month cloths, a golden bull and the worship of a cow are given, and at the end of the year a bed with sugarcane and jaggery, pillow, vessel, seat and a sesame measure with a golden bull go to a Veda-knowing Brahmin. The fruit is spotless wealth and fame in every birth, honour among Apsaras and Gandharvas, being a leader of the Ganas until the dissolution, then lord of the seven islands. The text says it removes the sin of a thousand killings of Brahmins and a hundred killings of unborn children. Reading, hearing or seeing it given frees one from the body and gives rank among the Vidyadharas.

09-052.json.summary: The chapter asks what to do against fear, bad luck, children who die, and bad dreams. Krishna says past sins bear fruit as illness and misfortune, and he teaches the Saptami bath (Saptami-snapana) that ends illness and the death of children.
