He tells that in the Varaha age Kritavirya of the Haihaya line ruled seven islands for 77,000 years; his hundred sons were lost through a Yavana's curse, so he worshipped the Sun with fasts and Vedic hymns. The Sun appeared, and Brihaspati told him to perform this bath. On a day chosen by the planets and stars (avoiding the child's birth star), a mother whose children have died, in the seventh month after a birth, has a Brahmin say blessings; on dung-smeared ground rice and mung offerings go to the Sun and the Mothers, and ghee, wood, barley and black sesame are offered in the fire, 108 times with the Rudra hymn. Four pots with jewels in the corners and a fifth in the middle are set up with water from tirthas, herbs and earth from places such as an elephant stable, a king's gate and a river, and a Brahmin with kusha grass says the Sun hymns. Seven women, fed and given garlands and cloth, with a priest, bathe the mother and child while a prayer asks for long life and the protection of the Sun, the Moon, Indra, Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, and that child-seizing spirits do no harm. The family worships the child in white clothes, gives a golden image of Dharmaraja on sesame with a tawny cow to the teacher, feeds Brahmins with ghee milk-rice and shares the fire remains. The text says it is also used for bad omens and trees that bear out of season, and that Kartavirya Arjuna ruled the earth for 10,000 years by it; the Sun is the one to ask for health, Agni for wealth, Shiva for knowledge, and Janardana for the path.

09-053.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what women, who cannot bear the hardship of morning baths, should do in Magha, and how they gain beauty, good fortune and children with little effort. Krishna tells a secret: the Achala Saptami (Unmoving Seventh) vow. A beautiful courtesan named Indumati of Magadha thought about the passing of life and the uselessness of days without gifts, prayer and worship, and went to the sage Vasishtha. She told him she had given nothing, made no offering, kept no fast or vow, and asked for a vow to cross the sea of life. Vasishtha told her to take a meal on the sixth and bathe on the bright seventh of Magha when the water is not stirred (before the water moves), putting a lamp on her head. She did so for three days and was reborn as the chief of the Apsaras in Indra's world. Asked for the method, Krishna says: eat once on the sixth, worship the Sun, and on the seventh go to a deep pond, river meeting or tank, undisturbed, and bathe before the water is moved, with a prayer to Varuna and to the Seventh to destroy the sins of seven births. A lamp is floated, gods are offered water, and an eight-petalled lotus is drawn with sandal, with Shiva and his wife in the middle and Sun names on the petals. A golden dish of sesame powder, ghee and jaggery with red cloth and flowers is given to a Brahmin, with a prayer for protection from bad luck and for the family. The teacher is honoured with cloth, a cow and sesame. The fruit is beauty, good fortune and every wish, and the removal of Kali's sins for one who reads or hears it.

09-054.json.summary: Krishna tells the Budha Ashtami vow, the eighth of the bright half falling on Wednesday (Budha's day), by which one never sees hell. At the start of the Krita age King Ila went into the Himalaya forest of Uma, which Mahadeva had forbidden to males; anyone who entered became a woman, and Ila became one. Budha (Mercury) found her beautiful and, on the eighth on a Wednesday, was pleased with her; she bore a son, Pururavas, who began the Moon line of kings; from then the day is honoured. A second story: Urmila, wife of a king of Mithila killed in battle, wandered poor with her children to Avanti and worked grinding grain in a Brahmin's house. She took a little wheat for her hungry children and later died. Her son took his father's seat in Videha; her daughter Shyamala, born in the Mithila line, married Dharmaraja (Yama) and was told she could run the house but never open seven cages. She opened them and saw her mother in torment in each, such as being boiled in oil, cut with saws, eaten by beasts and crushed in a press. Yama explained that stolen Brahmin grain, though taken out of love, burns a family for seven generations and had turned into worms. Shyamala said her mother could be freed, and Yama said that in a past birth as a Brahmin woman she had done a perfect Budha Ashtami with her friends; if she gave that merit to her mother, she would be freed. She gave it, and her mother was released, going to heaven in a chariot, still seen near Budha in the sky. The rite: when the bright eighth falls on a Wednesday, take a single meal, bathe in a river at morning, take a new pot of water, and make eight sets of foods in order (modaka, pheni, ghee cakes, vadas, and others); eat them with friends and kin while telling the vow's story, not eating until it ends. A golden Budha in yellow cloth is worshipped with flowers and given with gold to a Veda-knowing Brahmin, with prayers; eight Brahmins are fed and a cow with calf and ornaments given. The fruit is remembering seven births, wealth, sons, long life and, at death at a holy place, heaven; hearing it frees even one who killed a Brahmin or a cow.

09-055.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about Janmashtami. Krishna tells that after he killed Kamsa at Mathura, Devaki and Vasudeva wept for joy, and the people asked him for a day of grace on the day Devaki bore him. On his father's order the Janmashtami vow was made known: on the eighth of the dark half of Bhadrapada, with the Sun in Leo, the Moon in Taurus and the star Rohini, at midnight, he was born to Vasudeva and Devaki. The vow: fast from the morning, after cleaning the teeth, which frees one from the sins of all births; bathe at noon in a clear river and decorate a lying-in room for Devaki like Gokula, with lamps, lamp-stands, music, auspicious pots, swastikas, weapons against demons, a pestle in grain and guards. In it an image of the new mother is set on a bed in eight kinds (gold, silver, copper, brass, clay, wood, jewels or drawn) with the infant Krishna with a Shrivatsa mark; Yashoda's daughter, the gods, sages, Gandharvas and Apsaras are shown; and Vasudeva, Nanda, Gargacharya and Kamsa's guards asleep. It is worshipped with scents, flowers and fruits, with mantras naming Devaki, Vasudeva, Balabhadra, Krishna, Subhadra, Nanda and Yashoda. Women and Shudras may worship without Vedic mantras. At moonrise an offering of water is made to the Moon with a prayer naming Vishnu's many names. At midnight ghee and jaggery are poured, and the naming ceremony is held; on the ninth Brahmins are fed and given gifts. The fruit is children, health, wealth and prosperity of the land, with no foreign threat, rain on time, and no deaths, miscarriages or illness in the house; even one who keeps it only through contact reaches Vishnu's world.

09-056.json.summary: Krishna tells the Durva Ashtami, the bright eighth of Bhadrapada, which keeps a family unbroken for seven generations. Yudhishthira asks where durva grass came from. Krishna says that when Vishnu held Mount Mandara on his arms and thighs in the churning of the milk ocean, hairs from his body rubbed off and were thrown up by the waves, and became the green durva grass; the nectar placed on it and drops from the pot made it everlasting. Durva is worshipped on the eighth with fruits, flowers, dates, coconut, grapes, pomegranates, curds, rice, incense and lamps, with a prayer that the grass, spread by its shoots over the earth, give the worshipper children too. It was worshipped by the gods' wives, and later in the human world by Gauri, Lakshmi, Vedavati, Damayanti, Sita, and Apsaras such as Rambha and Menaka. Women bathe in clean clothes, give gifts to Brahmins, offer fruit and eat sesame cake, wheat and the seven grains with friends and relatives. The fruit is comfort, good fortune, children and grandchildren, a long stay on earth and then heaven with husband and kin, honoured by the gods.

09-057.json.summary: Krishna tells the Krishna Ashtami (Kala Ashtami), kept on the eighth of each dark half for a year starting in Margashirsha. Having asked the teacher, the keeper fasts or takes a night meal, avoids anger and keeps chastity, bathes in a river in the afternoon, worships the Shiva lingam with fragrant flowers and incense, and offers sesame in the fire. Each month Shiva is worshipped under a different name with a different thing taken at night: Shankara (cow urine; the fruit of Atiratra), Shambhu (ghee; Vajapeya), Maheshvara (milk; the fruit of eight cow sacrifices), Mahadeva (sesame; Rajasuya eightfold), Sthanu (barley; horse sacrifice), Shiva (kusha water; man sacrifice tenfold), Pashupati (water from a cow's horn; the gift of a hundred thousand cows), Ugra (cow dung; a million years in Rudra's world), Sharva (arka; a gold sacrifice), Tryambaka (bilva leaf), Bhava (rice water) and Rudra (curds). At the end of the year Shiva-devoted Brahmins are fed with milk-rice, honey and ghee, twelve black pots with sesame, umbrellas, sandals, gold and cloth are given, and a black milk cow is given to the Rudras. The text says the gods took their divine ranks by it: Brahma, Vishnu, Indra, Skanda and the others. The fruit is freedom from sin, lordship and joy on earth for a hundred years, and a long stay in Shiva's world in chariots, with Shiva at the end.

09-058.json.summary: Krishna tells of the sage Atri, son of Brahma, and his wife Anasuya, whose son was Datta (Dattatreya, a part of Vishnu) and whose second son Anagha married Nadi (also called Lakshmi), with eight living sons. When Shumbha's demon Jambha troubled the gods and took Amaravati, the gods fled to Anagha's hermitage in the Vindhya, and he told them to stay inside; the demons followed, wanting to seize the sage's wife, but Datta's meditation burned their strength away, and the gods, led by Indra, killed them. Anagha then did the penance called Brahmottara for three thousand divine years, and Kartavirya Arjuna, king of Mahishmati, served him by day and night. Pleased, Anagha gave him four boons: a thousand arms; stopping him from wrong; ruling the earth justly; and a death at Hari's hand in battle, with a state of yoga and an emperor's rank with the eight powers (anima, mahima, prapti, prakamya, laghima, ishitva, vashitva, kamavasayita). Arjuna conquered all seven islands, held ten thousand sacrifices with golden altars and posts, and ruled for 85,000 years. The text lists his feats, such as stopping the ocean with his arms, taming serpents, defeating Ravana and imprisoning him until Pulastya begged for his release, and giving the earth as alms to Fire. It says that Kartavirya started the vow called Anagha Ashtami (anagha: "sinless"), and that Anagha's name means he removes sins. Yudhishthira asks the method. Krishna says: on the dark eighth of Margashirsha, a couple made of kusha grass (Anagha and Anaghi, with many sons) is worshipped with flowers, with the Rigvedic Vishnu verses, and with fruits, roots, grain and incense; Brahmins and relatives are fed. A person takes the vow at the end of a year-long cycle and may not break it, with a show of dance and song, and the couple is put into water on the ninth. The fruit is a growing family, health for seven births and then the highest state.

09-059.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes another vow that gives the world of Shiva. On a Monday that falls in the bright eighth (sitashtami), a person worships Shiva with Hari imagined on the right half. The image is bathed in the five nectars, smeared with sandal, offered flowers and a lamp-waving with 25 lamps, then food. After fasting, the worshipper offers sesame-mixed ghee in the fire at dawn, feeds Brahmins and couples, and honours the ancestors. At the year's end a larger worship is done with canopies, flags, and a diagram with a triangle for Parvati and a square for Maheshvara, and a Brahmin couple is honoured with clothes and ornaments. Doing it for one year or five brings both worlds, and doing it for life frees a person from calamity, sorrow and fevers. An alternative form joins the eighth with Sunday, with the Sun worshipped as well, and the fast broken with cow products on the full day. The text promises health, wealth, sons and the world of the Sun or of Shiva.

09-060.json.summary: Shri Krishna tells how, when the ocean was churned and Janardana took a woman's form to confuse the demons, Lakshmi rested for a moment in a bilva tree. Because Shri was lodged there, it is called the Shrivriksha. The vow is on the ninth of the bright half of Bhadrapada. At early sunrise the tree is worshipped with flowers and uncooked fruit, sesame paste, grain, incense and cloth, with a mantra, and Brahmins are fed. The worshipper then eats in silence, avoiding oil and salt, with food not cooked on fire, served with curd, flowers and fruit. The text promises that a man or woman is freed from sorrow and, for seven births, has comfort, good fortune and wealth.

09-061.json.summary: Shri Krishna says that after the goddess killed Mahisha, his demon kin fought on. Raktasura, Mahisha's son, did penance for a very long time and Brahma gave him rule over the three worlds. He attacked Indra's city Amaravati and defeated the gods, who fled to the city where Shiva's beloved stays. There the nine Durgas are named (Durga with Chamunda, Mahalakshmi, Nanda, Kshemakari, Shivaduti, Maharuṇḍa, Bhramari, Rudramangala, Revati, Harasiddhi), and the gods praise each in a hymn, then ask the lion-riding goddess for protection. She came out with the Durgas and fought the demon army, naming the chief demons and their bright banners. She tore down their banners, gave them to the gods, destroyed the demons, seized Raktasura by the throat and killed him with her trident. The gods marked the ninth day with a procession of flags, and kings still keep the fast. Yudhishthira asks for the procedure. Krishna says that on the ninth of the bright half of Pausha, one bathes and worships the goddess, called Hari's sister, with flowers, flags, lamps, incense, offerings of animals, liquor and meat, and a mantra. Then the king installs flags in the goddess's temples, feeds a girl and asks pardon. The text promises protection from thieves, fire, war and danger, and says Pandu's son won on this ninth, so it is dear to her.

09-062.json.summary: Shri Krishna tells of the Ulka ninth, said to have been told by Kashyapa for Taraka's relief. On the ninth of the bright half of Ashvin, after bathing in a river and honouring the ancestors, one worships Chamunda, dear to Bhairava, with flowers, incense, food, meat, fish and liquor, then prays with folded hands: give health and victory, destroyer of Mahisha. Girls are fed and dressed in clothes and ornaments, seven, five or one as one can afford, since the goddess is pleased by faith. A circle is made with cow dung, food and sweet rice are served, and sixty straws are lit; the meal is left once the fire dies down, and one meditates on Chamunda. This is repeated every month and at the year's end girls are fed again, with gold and a cow given to a Brahmin. The text promises that enemies, thieves, ghosts and fear do not trouble the follower, and Chandika guards them like a burning torch in the hearts of rivals.

09-063.json.summary: Shri Krishna explains a curse. In the first age, while the sage Bhrigu was away to please Shiva, his wife Divya stayed in the hermitage. The demons, afraid of Vishnu, had taken shelter with her. Vishnu came, and when Divya moved to curse him, he cut off her head with his discus. Bhrigu returned and found the demons dead. He cursed Vishnu to be born ten times in the human world, which is why Vishnu takes many incarnations. Yudhishthira asks for the Dashavatara vow. On the tenth of the bright half of Bhadrapada the worshipper bathes in clean water, offers water to ancestors and gods, and prepares grain flour with ghee. Each year for ten years a different sweet is made (pastries, ghee cakes, sweet balls and so on), shared among ten cows or Brahmins, the worshipper and the family. The ten incarnations (fish, tortoise, boar, Man-lion, Trivikrama, Rama, Rama and Krishna, Buddha, Kalki) are worshipped with a mantra of refuge. The text promises relief from bad times, the world of vishnu, and then liberation, and says women who keep it get good fortune, a husband and sons.

09-064.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes the Ashadashami, the "tenth of the directions" vow. He tells of King Nala of the Nishadhas, who lost his kingdom to his brother Pushkara at dice and went to the forest with his wife Damayanti. Birds took his cloth, and he left Damayanti asleep. She wandered weeping, reached the city of Chedi and was taken in by the king's mother as a maid on stated conditions. Later a Brahmin took her to her father's house, where she still grieved and asked for a vow to be reunited with her husband. A learned Brahmin told her to keep the Ashadashami, and by its power she met her husband again. Yudhishthira asks how and when. Krishna says anyone with a wish (a prince for a kingdom, a farmer, a merchant's son, a pregnant woman, a sick person, a woman whose husband is long away) may keep it on the tenth of any bright half. The worshipper bathes, worships the ten directions at night with flowers and sandal, draws them in the courtyard with barley or flour, offers ghee food, and repeats this monthly until the wish is met. Later golden or silver images are made and each direction (east, south-east, south and so on, with above and below) is addressed in a verse. Brahmins are given gifts and kin are fed. The text promises all wishes and says women especially should keep it, since it calls their minds fickle and desire-bound.

09-065.json.summary: Yudhishthira calls himself a sinner who caused slaughter and asks for a secret vow to cross the sin of killing Bhishma and Drona. Krishna tells of King Kushadhvaja of Vidarbha, who by mistake killed a hermit while hunting, thinking him a deer. He went to hell, and was then born over twelve lives as a snake, lion, tiger, worm, bear, sea creature, flesh-eating spirit, brahma-rakshasa, and others, each time killing someone and being killed. In one life he had kept the Taraka Dvadashi, and by its power he was finally born again as a good king in Vidarbha, kept it again, ruled without trouble and reached Vishnu's city. Yudhishthira asks the method. On the twelfth of the bright half of Margashirsha one bathes in natural water in the afternoon, bows to the Sun, worships, offers a fire sacrifice until sunset, and offers water to the stars on a cow-dung circle, with a mantra, then gives a fee to a Brahmin. A different sweet or food is made each month for twelve months. At the end silver stars are made and worshipped, twelve water pots with sweets, clothes and gifts are given. The text promises the world of stars, a long stay in heaven and then Vishnu's city, and lists women and men who kept it, including Shachi, Sita, Damayanti, Rukmini, Satyabhama, Rambha and Urvashi.

09-066.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the Aranya Dvadashi, the "forest twelfth". Krishna says Sita kept it in the forest on Rama's word, and that the wives of sages once feasted at Lopamudra's house. The vow: on the eleventh of the bright half of Margashirsha one bathes, fasts, and worships Janardana through the night with scents, flowers, lamps and wakefulness. Next morning, in a forest, the worshipper feeds learned Brahmins and then eats fruit in silence, having first taken the five cow products. This is repeated for a year, with a long list of dishes. Ten or two forest-dwelling sages, ascetics, householders, and seven faithful Brahmin women are to be fed, dressed and honoured, and the twelve names of Vishnu (Vasudeva, Janardana, Damodara and so on) are used with a bow. The worshipper prays that Vishnu be pleased and then eats with family and guests. The text promises a flying chariot at death, heavenly girls, Vishnu's white island Shvetadvipa where people are four-armed and dark with conch, discus, mace and lotus, later good rebirth as a famed man, and liberation.

09-067.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what offering and which god suit the rainy season, when clouds cover the sky. Shri Krishna describes the Rohini vow on the eleventh of the dark half of Shravana. The worshipper prepares a cake of black-gram flour and five ghee-fried sweet balls, one for each person, and goes to a clean water place with no dangerous creatures. On the bank a circle is made of cow dung and flour, and the moon with Rohini is drawn and worshipped with a mantra, offered food, and the offering given to a Brahmin. The worshipper then stands in water up to the ankles, waist or neck, meditating on the moon with Rohini while the food is eaten, and then feeds a Brahmin with a fee. Kept yearly by a man, woman or girl, it is promised to bring wealth and grain, children and grandchildren, death at a holy place, and then the worlds of Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra. The last verse says this is why Rohini is the moon's favourite.

09-068.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the Aviyoga vow, the "no separation" vow. Shri Krishna says that on the twelfth of the bright half of Bhadrapada, one rises early, bathes in a pond in white clothes, and draws Hari with Lakshmi in a circle of wheat flour near a clean bank, with Shiva and Gauri, Brahma and Savitri, and the Sun with his queen. They are worshipped with scents, flowers, incense and food, in silence and with a firm wish not to be parted. Long lists of names of Vishnu, Shiva, Brahma, the Sun, Lakshmi, Parvati and Savitri are recited as prayers. After giving gifts and eating, the worshipper goes home. The text promises fame, wealth, children, freedom from sorrow, and then the worlds of Hari, Hara, Brahma and the Sun, ending in liberation. It may be kept by a couple or by either partner alone.

09-069.json.summary: Yudhishthira says the death of eighteen armies for his kingdom weighs on him, and asks for a way to wash away the sin. Krishna offers the Govatsa Dvadashi, the cow-and-calf twelfth, and tells its origin. In the first age ten million sages were doing penance at a hermitage on a hill. Shiva took the form of an old Brahmin and Uma took the form of a cow with her calf, and the text praises cows at length: the five cows from the milk-ocean, the sacred six products, and the gods said to dwell in every part of a cow's body. Shiva left the cow with the sage Bhrigu's hermitage for two days and vanished, then returned as a tiger. The sages shouted, the cow fled, and her hoof marks and the tiger's are said to be visible on a rock, with a holy place beside them. The sages rang a bell, the tiger released the cow, and Shiva appeared on his bull and was honoured. The text says the Nandini vow on the twelfth of the bright half of Kartika began then. A second story: King Uttanapada had two wives, Ruchi and Shughni; Shughni's son was Dhruva. Out of jealousy Ruchi killed the child, cut him up and cooked him, but he came back to life at mealtime. When Ruchi asked how, Shughni explained the vow, and Ruchi kept it; her sons then lived well and Dhruva is still seen among the stars. The method: on that day one eats once, honours a white, tawny or red cow with her calf at noon with scents, flowers, lamps, lentil cakes, with a mantra, and then asks her pardon. That day one avoids food cooked in a pot, sleeps on the ground and stays chaste. The text promises a stay in the cows' world for as many years as a cow has hairs.

09-070.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes the sleeping of Vishnu and the four-month vow (Chaturmasya). Vishnu is set to sleep when the Sun is in Gemini (the bright eleventh of Ashadha) and woken when it enters Libra. An image of Vishnu in yellow cloth is laid on a clean bed, bathed with curd, milk, ghee, honey and water, worshipped, and a mantra is said: when you sleep the world sleeps. The worshipper then takes vows for four months, each with a stated reward: giving up jaggery gives a sweet voice, oil gives a fine body, sweet and sour tastes give freedom from ugliness, betel gives good fortune, ghee gives beauty, fruit gives a clever mind and many sons, eating from leaves gives the merit of Kurukshetra, silence gives obeyed commands, sleeping on the ground gives rule of the earth, and so on. Praying, bowing, circling the image, singing, and reading scripture to others each bring Vishnu's world or similar. During the sleep, weddings, thread ceremonies and other rites are to be avoided. On the eleventh of Bhadrapada a great worship is done. Vishnu says he sleeps because Lakshmi, the crown, the discus and other things occupy his body, so Yoganidra took his eyes for four months, and he keeps her honour. He wakes on the bright eleventh of Kartika with the mantra "idam vishnur vicakrame"; the king takes a torchlit procession through the city, with night vigil and dance, and next day worships Vishnu, offers a fire sacrifice, feeds Brahmins, states the vows he kept and gives a fee. The text promises Vasudeva's city and no rebirth from a mother.

09-071.json.summary: Shri Krishna tells of the royal sage Ajapala, whom the people asked to end their troubles. After long thought he cared for the sick and drove out diseases, and he made the rite of peace called Nirajana (lamp-waving). In a story from that time, Ravana, lord of the demons in Lanka, set the gods to serve him: the moon as his canopy, Indra as general, Vayu as sweeper, Varuna, Kubera, Yama and others at their tasks. Kings stood in his court. Ravana asked his doorkeeper who had come, and learned that many kings were there but Ajapala was not. Angry, he sent the demon Dhumraksha to demand service or death. Dhumraksha found Ajapala with his goats, thin and dusty and surrounded by diseases, and gave the message. Ajapala answered sharply and sent Fever to Lanka. Fever shook Ravana and his people, and Ravana said he no longer needed the king's service. The rite, which cures all disease, is done at dusk on the twelfth of the bright half of Kartika, after Vishnu has woken. Vishnu is worshipped and lamps are waved before him, then Lakshmi, Brahma, Shiva, the Sun, ancestors and others. Cows and buffaloes are honoured, made to run with bells, and decorated; horses, elephants and royal signs are honoured; the king sits on his throne with priests while a woman waves a wooden vessel of lamps over his head. The text says it ends disease and brings good harvests, and should be done yearly.

09-072.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the Bhishma Panchaka, a five-day vow in Kartika. Shri Krishna says he taught it to Bhrigu and that Bhishma taught it to Yudhishthira from his bed of arrows. It is held to be the best of vows and hard to do, practised by sages in earlier ages and by Vaishyas and Shudras in the Kali age. It may be kept by Brahmins, Kshatriyas, women with their husbands' leave, and widows. For five days (the eleventh to the full moon) one bathes at dawn and noon, offers water with barley, rice and sesame to gods, sages and ancestors, avoids liquor, meat and sex, and worships Vishnu bathed with honey, milk and ghee, with a lamp, incense and the six-syllable mantra with 108 repetitions and a fire offering. Each day a different part of the image is worshipped (feet with lotus, knees with bilva leaf, navel, middle, shoulders, head with jasmine). On the successive days one eats only cow dung, cow urine, milk and curd, then fasts, and breaks the fast on the fifth with Brahmins fed. At the end an image of sin with a fierce face is made and given to a Brahmin. The text promises that this one vow removes the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft and others, and gives Vishnu's world.

09-073.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the Malla Dvadashi, the "wrestlers' twelfth". Krishna says that when he lived as an eight-year-old among the cowherds under the Bhandira banyan on the Yamuna bank, strong cowherd wrestlers (named, such as Surabhadra) and cowherd women (Gopali, Palika, Dhanya, Vishakha and others) honoured him with flowers, curd, milk and rice. Three hundred and sixty wrestlers worshipped him, and their wives did so with liquor, meat, night wakefulness and dance, with wrestling matches, food and drink, gifts of cows and bulls, and the honouring of Brahmins. The practice is to keep twelve twelfths, one a month, from the first month to Kartika, naming Vishnu by one of his twelve names each time (Keshava, Narayana, Madhava and so on), with scents, flowers, lamps, a night vigil, song, dance and mock wrestling, giving ghee and milk and seeking Krishna's pleasure. Since the wrestlers began it, it is called Malla Dvadashi. The text says that through his grace their herds multiplied and they gained strength, fame and wealth, and he promises health, strength, power and Vishnu's eternal world to those who keep it.

09-074.json.summary: Shri Krishna tells of the king of Vidarbha, Bhima, father of Damayanti, who was truthful and unbeaten in war. The sage Pulastya, son of Brahma, came to his court on a pilgrimage and was received with honour. Bhima asked what would help all beings, who suffer in hell, in the womb, in illness, in birth and from poverty, in a way that is easy and gives great reward. Pulastya replied with the best of vows, the twelfth of the bright half of Magha, kept fasting in wet clothes. It is to be shared only with devoted, calm Brahmins and not with the uninitiated, and it is said to free even a killer of a Brahmin or a teacher, a thief or a traitor. A ten-hand hall is built with a five-hand platform and coloured circle; a learned Brahmin sets up eight or four pits, and Janardana (four-armed, facing west) is placed in the middle and worshipped. A pot of water with a hole is hung over the seat, and the sponsor sits and prays, while the water falls on his head and the priests make fire offerings with palasha sticks, sesame, ghee and milk in all directions, with planets and guardians of the directions honoured. Texts such as the Harivamsha and the Bharata are recited through the night. In the morning there is a bath, an offering to the Sun, worship, a final offering, and gifts of beds, food, cows, clothes and gold to Brahmins and to the teacher, and to the poor and the helpless. The text says even a hundred Vajapeya sacrifices do not equal a sixteenth part of this, promises good fortune for seven births, years of dwelling in Vishnu's, Rudra's, Brahma's and the Sun's worlds, and then rebirth as a just king. It says Sagara, Aja, Dilipa, Yayati and others kept it, and Bhima, who fasted it, gave it the name Bhima Dvadashi.

09-075.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for one twelfth that suits those who cannot fast often. Shri Krishna names the twelfth of the bright half of Bhadrapada when it meets the star Shravana (Budha-Shravana Dvadashi). Fasting that day and bathing at a river meeting gives the merit of twelve twelfths. A water pot with five gems is set up with a golden image of Janardana on it, bathed, anointed with white sandal, covered in white cloth with an umbrella and sandals, and worshipped limb by limb with mantras, offered ghee-cooked food and new pots of water, with a night vigil. In the morning the worshipper bathes, worships again, and gives to a learned Brahmin. As an example Krishna tells of a merchant who lost his caravan in a desert, near death from thirst. He met a ghost who told him to wait under a tree, and at noon a vessel of curd and rice and water came; the merchant ate, then fed the ghosts. Asked, the ghost said he had been a merchant of Shakala who refused beggars, but his neighbour, a good Brahmin, kept this vow at the meeting of the Chandrabhaga and Toshā, and he went with him; after death he became a ghost for his unbelief. The ghost asked him to take the names and families of the other ghosts, find treasure in the Himalaya and perform funeral offerings for each at Gaya. The merchant did so, and each ghost appeared in a dream to say he was freed. He kept the vow every year and finally reached a heaven of wish-trees and rivers of sweet rice.

09-076.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes the Vijaya (victory) eleventh and twelfth. When the eleventh meets Shravana it is called Vijaya. The text tells of Bali, a mighty demon who drove the gods from heaven. Vishnu, asked by the gods, said Bali was devoted and a man of penance, so he would be reduced when the time came, and he would be born as a son of Aditi. Aditi bore Vamana, a dwarf, and the earth shook on the eleventh of Bhadrapada with Shravana. Kashyapa did his birth rites. Vamana went to Bali's sacrifice, asked for the land his three steps would cover, and Bali agreed. Vamana then grew, covered earth and heaven in two steps, and found no place for a third. The gods rejoiced. He sent Bali to the underworld Sutala, promising he would later be Indra, and returned the heavens to the gods. For the vow the worshipper fasts on the eleventh, worships Vishnu at night in a silver, gold or wooden vessel with a pot, umbrella, sandals, staff and water-pot beside it, uses given mantras for bath, sandal, flowers, incense, lamp, food and prayer, and keeps a vigil with song. In the morning he gives to a Brahmin with a mantra and eats ghee-spotted food. The text promises 72 ages in Vishnu's city, then kingship, long life and children, and says fasting the eleventh and then the twelfth together does not break the rule, since both have the same god.

09-077.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes a twelve-month vow of twelfths starting from the dark half of Pausha. Each month a different name of Krishna is used (Pundarikaksha, Madhava, Vishvarupa, Purushottama, Achyuta, Jaya and so on). For the first months the worshipper uses sesame for bathing and eating, and from Ashadha the five cow products. He worships the named god each month, gives a fee to a Brahmin, eats only at night without oil or salt, fasts on the eleventh or twelfth, and at the year's end gives wealth, grain, vessels, a seat or bed to a Brahmin. The text promises all wishes and a dwelling in the gods' abode.

09-078.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes another twelfth, the Govinda Dvadashi. On the bright twelfth of Pausha, fasting, one worships Govinda (also called Adhokshaja) with incense, flowers and food, repeating the name Govinda and giving a fee to a Brahmin. Talk with heretics and those in wrong occupations is avoided. For purification one takes cow urine, dung, curd or milk drawn from a cow. The next day one bathes, worships again, and eats food from the cow's milk. This is repeated every month, giving a day's feed for cows each month, and at the year's end Govinda is prayed to with Padma. A specially generous gift is a bull with golden horns and silver hooves with a hundred cows. The text promises the world where Govinda lives, and a shining figure like the moon.

09-079.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what follows when a fast, gift or vow is done incompletely. Shri Krishna says that a flaw in a vow or sacrifice gives a flawed result: people lose their wealth and rank, and are born one-eyed, hunchbacked, impotent or blind, or lose their spouse and have bad fortune. He then gives the Akhanda Dvadashi, "the unbroken twelfth", to repair such flaws. On the twelfth of the bright half of Margashirsha, after fasting and worshipping Janardana, one repeats Narayana's name while bathing, eating, walking and sleeping, bathes with the five cow products, gives a barley or rice vessel to a Brahmin, and prays that any broken vow of seven births be made whole. The break-fast is made after four months, with vessels of barley flour in Chaitra and following months, and ghee vessels from Shravana to Kartika. The vessels may be gold, silver, copper, clay or palasha wood. At year's end twelve Brahmins are fed with ghee and sweet rice, given clothes and ornaments, and the teacher is honoured. The text promises that it makes seven births' broken vows whole.

09-080.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes the Manoratha Dvadashi, "the wishes' twelfth". On the eleventh of the bright half of Phalguna, a man or woman worships Vishnu and keeps repeating Hari's name, then on the twelfth bathes, worships, gives a fee to a Brahmin, makes a ghee offering in the fire and prays to the lord who fulfilled the wishes of the earth. The fast is broken after four months at a time, using red flowers, guggul incense and food fit for offering in the first period; then jasmine and resin incense in Ashadha; then cow urine, fragrant incense and a water vessel in Kartika and the later months. A fee is given every month. At year's end a gold image with conch and bow is given to a Brahmin with cloth and flowers, twelve Brahmins are fed, and twelve water pots with an umbrella and sandals are given. The text says Indra, the Adityas and others won their wishes by it, and it gives sons to the childless, wealth to the poor, health to the sick, a husband to a girl, and reunion to those apart, with long stays in heaven.

09-081.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a way to remove sin with little effort or money. Shri Krishna describes the Tila Dvadashi, the sesame twelfth. It is taken in Magha, on the twelfth of the dark half when the star Ashadha or Mula is present. After bathing and worshipping Krishna on the eleventh and fasting, the worshipper worships again next day, repeating Krishna's name and giving sesame to a Brahmin with the words "may Krishna be pleased". He eats black sesame. At the end of the year black pots with sesame, cooked food, umbrella, sandals and clothes are given to Brahmins by the number of months. The text promises that for as many thousands of years as there are sesame grains that sprout, he stays in heaven, and is born healthy, not blind, deaf or leprous, and freed from sins.

09-082.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what gives merit with no harm in the next world and what the power of fasting is. Shri Krishna tells of Sirabhadra, a merchant of Vaidisha, who was absorbed in family and money and neglected rites, gifts and the next world. He died at the edge of the Vindhya forest and became a ghost scorched by the summer sun on hot sand. A Brahmin sage named Vipita, passing in a flying vehicle, saw him and asked why he burned alone. Sirabhadra listed his faults: he trusted what is passing, always planned more, bore heat and cold only for greed, never honoured ancestors, gods or Brahmins, and nursed his family on wrong earnings while they took the fruit and he alone paid. Vipita said he saw a doubt about quick relief, but that in his tenth birth before this Sirabhadra had fasted the Bhadra Dvadashi, and its power had worn down his sin in a few days, like water in an unbaked pot. The sage comforted him, and he soon reached liberation. Yudhishthira asks how such sin in hell is ended. Krishna names the Jaya Dvadashi: on the eleventh of the bright half of Phalguna one fasts, on the twelfth worships Madhusudana, repeating Vishnu's names, avoiding desire, anger, greed, pride and delusion, saying "Namo Narayanaya" while lying down, and keeping the fast-breaking rule. Four months use barley vessels, then ghee vessels, then sesame vessels from Kartika to Magha, with prayers to Vishnu. At the year's end a gold image and a cow with calf are given to a Brahmin. The text promises that fire, weapons and the guards of hell do not trouble one whose mind is on Janardana, and tells the listener to avoid heretics.

09-083.json.summary: Yudhishthira says Narayana is reached by costly sacrifices and many priests, and asks for an easy way for people of all classes. Shri Krishna tells a secret made by the gods, the Dharani Vrata, "the earth vow", which the Earth herself kept when she sank into the underworld; after long fasting, Vishnu was pleased and lifted her up. On the tenth of Margashirsha the worshipper bathes, worships and eats lightly, then on the eleventh fasts, saying that he will eat next day. At dawn he takes clean earth from a river or pond with a prayer to the Earth, bathes, worships Narayana with a mantra for each part of the body, sets four water pots (the four seas) with sesame vessels and gems, and places a golden fish-form of Vishnu with a prayer that he save the worshipper as he saved the Vedas. After a night vigil he gives the four pots to four Brahmins (Rigveda east, Samaveda south, Yajurveda west, Atharvaveda north), a Brahmin householder gets the water vessel, and then Brahmins are fed sweet rice. The text says the reward cannot be counted: the world of Brahma and the end of sins. The vow is then repeated month by month, each with another incarnation and a gold image given to a Brahmin: Kurma in Pausha, Varaha in Magha, Narasimha in Phalguna, Vamana in Chaitra, Parashurama in Vaishakha, Rama and Lakshmana in Jyeshtha (Dasharatha is said to have asked Vasishtha and so got Rama), Vasudeva and the other forms in Ashadha, Buddha-like names in Shravana (the Shravana vow gives a son), Kalki in Bhadrapada, Padmanabha in Ashvin, and Yogeshvara in Kartika, where five Brahmins are fed. A list says which incarnation to worship for which wish, such as the fish for wisdom or Kalki against enemies. The vow is said to have given Yuvanashva his son Mandhata, Kritavirya his son Kartavirya Arjuna, and Shakuntala her son. It is called Dharani Vrata because the Earth kept it, and Hari lifted her on his tusk like a boat in the water.

09-084.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that quickly removes grief at losing what one loves. Shri Krishna names the Vishoka Dvadashi, "the sorrowless twelfth", in the month of Ashvin. The worshipper eats lightly on the tenth, fasts on the eleventh, bathes with all herbs and the five cow products on the twelfth, and worships Vishnu with white flowers and cloth, with a mantra for each part of the body. A square earth platform with river sand is made and a figure of Lakshmi set on it; a winnowing tray is wrapped in cloth and worshipped with food and a gold lotus. The worshipper drinks darbha water, keeps a night of song and dance, honours Brahmin couples with clothes and garlands, bathes in the morning and feeds people as he can. This is repeated monthly, and at the end a bed with a jaggery cow is given. Yudhishthira asks about the jaggery cow. Krishna describes making a cow and calf on a black antelope skin with darbha grass, in four sizes by the weight of jaggery, adorned with silk, pearl, coral and gold horns, with prayers to Lakshmi as the cow, and giving it to a Brahmin. Ten gift-cows are named: of jaggery, ghee, sesame, honey, water, milk, sugar, curd, juice and the sacred one. The text says this vow removes sin and grief, giving good fortune, long life, health and the world of Vishnu, and a woman may keep it too.

09-085.json.summary: Shri Krishna describes the Vibhuti Dvadashi, the "prosperity twelfth", kept in Kartika, Vaishakha, Margashirsha, Phalguna or Ashadha. The worshipper eats lightly on the tenth, fasts on the eleventh, worships Vishnu on the twelfth, with a mantra for each limb, and names the ten incarnations by month. At the year's end he gives a bed with a salt mountain to his teacher, and possibly a village or field, honours Brahmins and gives clothes and cows. A poor man may do it little by little, and a very poor man for three years with flowers only. The text promises freedom from sin, the saving of a hundred ancestors, and a long stay in heaven. A story follows: King Pushpavahana, who got a golden lotus from Brahma and had a wife, Lavanyavati, and ten thousand archer sons, asked the sage Pracheta why he had such fortune. The sage said that in a former birth he was a hunter, who in a famine took lotuses to the city of Vaidisha but found no buyer. At night he and his wife heard auspicious sounds: on the twelfth of Magha a woman was giving a bed and salt mountain to a teacher. The hunter and his wife felt devotion, fasted without meaning to, and kept the vigil. A courtesan, Anangavati, offered them four kinds of food and gold, but they refused, saying they would eat next day. They gave away their lotuses at Vishnu's feet, and so gained the merit. He was reborn as king, and she as queen, and the sage said he would reach liberation. The king then kept the vow.

09-086.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the Madana Dvadashi, by which Diti once won forty-nine sons. Shri Krishna says that on the twelfth of the bright half of Chaitra, one sets up a sound pot full of white rice with fruit, sugar cane, white cloth pair and sandal, topped with a copper vessel of jaggery, and worships Vishnu in the form of Kama (Madana) with scented water, white flowers, rice and sesame, with a mantra for each limb. Next morning the pot is given to a Brahmin, Brahmins are fed, and the worshipper eats without salt. This is repeated monthly; in the thirteenth month a bed with a ghee cow, a golden Kama and a milch cow are given, with fire offering of sesame. The text promises the highest state, sons and good fortune. Then it tells how Kashyapa, pleased by the vow, made Diti young and beautiful again and gave her a son able to kill her foe (Indra). He said she should carry the child for a hundred years and gave many rules for her pregnancy, such as avoiding the twilight meal, trees, empty houses, quarrels, loose hair, bad words, fast walking, river crossing, ugly sights, heavy food and strain. She followed them, and bore forty-nine sons. The text says a woman who keeps the vow gets sons and a happy marriage.

09-087.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks which deity one should remember for protection in forests, hard places, sea crossings, gifts, battle and against thieves. Krishna answers that a person who remembers Durga, the all-auspicious goddess, meets no sorrow. He tells how, after finishing his studies with Sandipani at Avanti, he promised a fee, and the teacher asked him to bring back his son, killed at Prabhasa; Krishna fetched the boy from Yama's city and the two returned. Since then people who want sons worship Krishna, Balabhadra and Durga placed between them. The vow is kept on the 13th of the bright half of every month, with a fast, a night meal or one meal, using perfumes, flowers, honey, liquors, and a clay or gold image, with offerings that include meat and rice. The text promises freedom from all sins, and for a wife a place in heaven with her husband. A last verse says that worshipping Ambika on the tenth day with flowers, meat and liquor quickly destroys the fears of thieves, fire and the king.

09-088.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that removes bad body odour and the bad luck that comes from bitter, sour or other body faults. Krishna says the sage Jatukarnya once told this to a queen devoted to Vishnu. In the month of Jyeshtha, on the 13th of the bright half, one bathes in a holy river and worships the sun with flowers that are dear to him: white mandara, arka, red karavira and neem. Looking at the sun in the sky, one recites a short verse of homage to the sun, karavira and the neem tree, with flowers, food offerings and incense. A man or woman who does this every year is freed of body odour and bad luck. A closing verse says women who worship neem, arka and karavira with flowers, grain, incense and lamps gain all pleasures and good fortune.

09-089.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to worship Yama so as not to go to hell. Krishna says that at Dvaraka he met the sage Mudgala, who told him of a vow called Yama-darshana. Mudgala says he fell senseless and saw a thumb-sized person bound and dragged by Yama's men to Yama's court, which is described as full of diseases, fierce beings, fearsome animals, scribes like Chitragupta and hell guardians. Yama told his men they had brought the wrong person, since Mudgala was a king's son from Kaundinya who still had life left, and they let him go. Yama explained that his men do not see people who keep the 13th-day vow, or who died at Ujjayini, Prayaga or Bhairava, or who gave sesame, grain, cows or gold. The vow is kept for a year from Margashirsha on a Monday that is the 13th day, in the morning: one invites thirteen learned, pure Brahmins in Yama's name, oils and bathes them, feeds them rice, mung beans and sweet cakes, worships them with sesame and rice, and gives each a copper vessel, a fee, an umbrella, a water pot and a leather cover, reciting a verse naming Yama and Shani. The reward promised is that the doer never reaches Yama's house, goes by a heavenly chariot to Vishnu's city and then Shiva's city, and lives long in heaven; Mudgala revived and went home, and Krishna tells Yudhishthira to do the same.

09-090.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that gives beauty and good fortune. Krishna says many harsh vows are worthless and praises the single Anangatrayodashi, the 13th day vow named for Ananga (Kama), who was burned by Shiva's eye. It is kept on the 13th of the bright half in Margashirsha with a fast, a bath and worship of Shiva with incense, lamps, flowers and food offerings, a sesame fire offering, and honey taken at night. Then each month has its own form of Shiva, flower and food: Pausha, Yogeshvara with jasmine and sandal paste; Magha, Natesha with lotus and pearl; Phalguna, Hareshvara with karnikara and cardamom; Chaitra, Surupa with damana and camphor; Vaishakha, Maharupa with navamallika and nutmeg; Jyeshtha, Pradyumna with jasmine and cloves; Ashadha, Umabhartri with sesame water; Shravana, Umapati with sesame flowers and laddus; Bhadrapada, Sadyojata with saffron and aloe; Ashvina, the lord of the gods with vermilion and gold; and Kartika, Vishveshvara with all flowers. Each month's reward is beauty, good fortune, children or the merit of a named sacrifice. If the vow is blocked by weakness or birth impurity, one fasts again, makes a gold Shiva on a copper dish and a pot, wraps it in white cloth and gives it to a Shiva-devoted Brahmin, with a bed, a cow with calf, an umbrella, sandals, water pots, a fee, a five-nectar bath and a meal. A man, woman or maiden who does this gains a kingdom without enemies, fame, long life, strength and luck for a hundred births, then liberation and Shiva's world.

09-091.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks why women of good families make offerings at tanks and large waters. Krishna says that in Bhadrapada, on the bright-half day named for the spirits, a fine arghya offering is given to Varuna on the bank of a tank; Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras and women may all give it with devotion. One uses flowers, fruits, cloth, lamps, lac dye, sandal paste, uncooked food mixed with sesame and rice, dates, coconuts, citron, grapes, pomegranates and cucumbers. Varuna and his consort Varuni are drawn in a circle and worshipped with a short verse of homage, which also asks to be free of dampness, bad smell and a bad taste in the mouth. The worshipper bathes in the tank at midday, and the food offered is given to a Brahmin. The reward promised is release from all sins at once and a house where wealth is never lost.

09-092.json.summary: Krishna continues on the same day and says Devala once sang about this vow in the assembly of Brahma, having seen how empty worldly life is. On the 14th of the bright half of Bhadrapada, women make an arghya offering to the banana plant (Rambha) with fruits, sprouted seven grains, lamps, lac dye, sandal paste, curd, durva grass, rice, cloth, ghee-cooked food, nutmeg and cloves, reciting a verse asking the goddess for health and beauty. Anyone who worships in this way, man or woman, of any of the four classes, is promised that no immoral, poor, unlucky, childless or unfaithful woman will be born in the family. A woman who does not leave her husband's vow gains good fortune, children, long life and fame. The text says Gayatri, Gauri, Indrani, Lakshmi, Arundhati, Svaha, Sita, Vedavati, Bhanumati and others once kept this Rambha vow, and that women who worship the banana plant will not be troubled by sorrow.

09-093.json.summary: Krishna says the 14th day belongs to Agni. Yudhishthira asks how Agni was once lost and how he regained his nature. Krishna tells that the gods, beaten by Tarakasura, were told by Brahma that a child of Rudra, Uma, Ganga and Agni's energy would kill the demon. Shiva and Uma made love for a hundred divine years, the gods grew afraid, and they sent Wind and Fire to stop them; Uma, angry and childless, cursed the gods so that they would have no children by their own wives. Shiva told Agni to take his stored seed, and Agni then vanished; the gods searched, a bird called Jivajivaka found him, and Agni, after cursing others, blessed the bird. Then Yudhishthira asks how Agni's nature returned. Krishna tells that Utathya and Angiras, two sages, quarrelled over who was greater, and Brahma asked the gods to judge; after the sun was brought with some difficulty, Angiras was said to burn the world with his tapas, the gods sent the sun back, and asked Angiras to act as Agni for a while. When Agni was found he agreed to be Angiras's son Brihaspati and Angiras took many sons, and Agni regained his state on the 14th day. The day is called fiery or Rudra's day, and a shraddha on it is advised for those who died by poison, weapons, battle, beasts, rivers, falls, fire or suicide. The vow is a fast on the 14th, worship of Shiva with flowers, incense and food, a night vigil, five cow products, sleeping on the ground, a meal of millet without oil or salt, a sesame fire offering with 108 oblations, a morning bath of Shiva with five nectars, and a gold image of three-eyed Shiva on a bull given to a Brahmin at the year's end. The reward is a heavenly chariot and a long stay in Shiva's city, and rebirth as a generous, wealthy king or Brahmin with sons and grandsons.

09-094.json.summary: Krishna names another vow that removes sins, the Ananta vow, kept on the 14th of the bright half of Bhadrapada. Yudhishthira asks who Ananta is, and Krishna answers that Ananta is his own name, meaning Time itself, and that he came down to ease the earth's burden. Krishna then tells of Sumanta, a Brahmin of the Vasishtha line, who married Bhrigu's daughter Diksha, and their daughter was Shila, whose mother died; Sumanta married the quarrelsome Karkasha. He gave Shila to the sage Kaundinya, but Karkasha, angry at the idea of a wedding gift, shut them out with only crumbs of food for the journey. On the way Shila saw women worshipping Ananta and learned the vow: with half the food given to a Brahmin, worship at a river bank, a fourteen-knotted red thread tied on the left arm of a woman or right of a man, and a verse asking Vasudeva to lift one from the sea of worldly life. Shila kept it and prospered, but Kaundinya later angrily broke the thread, and his wealth, cattle and house were lost. He went to the forest to find Ananta and asked a mango tree, a cow, a bull, two ponds, a donkey and an elephant, and none knew. Then Ananta appeared as an old Brahmin, showed him his divine city and form, and explained that the mango was a proud Brahmin who gave no teaching, the cow the earth, the bull joy, the ponds right and wrong, the donkey anger and the elephant one who spoils right conduct. Kaundinya was told to keep the vow for fourteen years; he did, regained all, and finally became the star Punarvasu. The text promises freedom from sins to those who keep or hear this vow.

09-095.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the goddesses called Shravani and what they do. Krishna says they were made first by Brahma; they quickly hear whatever anyone says, good or bad, and report it, and can hear and see from far away. They are said to be many, like the eight kinds of god-born beings, and are to be honoured. The vow to them is strict: smelling incense, cooked food and water [as an offering], and then feeding other women. Krishna tells of King Nahusha's wife Jayashri, who met Arundhati at Vasishtha's hermitage and was told of the vow, but Arundhati only offered to let her eat there; Jayashri ate, forgot the vow, and when her death came she lay fifteen days foaming and rattling. On the sixteenth day Arundhati told Nahusha what to do; he made the offering and gave eight pots (karakas) for her, and she died at once and went to Indra's world in a shining chariot. The text gives the procedure on the 14th or 8th: invite ten women as forms of Gauri and twelve learned Brahmins, give them gifts, set twelve water pots with gold, and have the Brahmin recite a verse of passing over the Shravana month. The doer is promised an easy death, long healthy life, then Rudra's world or the moon's world; one woman fed here equals eleven in the ordinary Gauri feast.

09-096.json.summary: Krishna explains the night-meal fast (nakta). On the 14th of the bright half of any month, and on both 8th days each month, one feeds a Brahmin, worships Shiva with the mind fixed on him, and eats only at night, sitting on the ground. The text ranks fasting above begging, begging above food not asked for, and that above the night meal; it says the gods eat in the morning, sages at midday, ancestors in the afternoon and spirits in the evening. Food is simple offering food, the doer bathes, speaks truth, eats lightly, keeps a fire and sleeps on the ground. At the year's end a clay Shiva is set on a full pot with cow products, fruit, flowers, barley, milk, curd and durva, and an eightfold water offering is given. A cow or a bull is given to a learned poor Brahmin. The rewards are a bright heavenly chariot with singing nymphs, 300 crore years in Rudra's world, and rebirth as lord of a hundred thousand villages.

09-097.json.summary: Krishna describes the Shiva-chaturdashi vow. After one meal on the 13th, one fasts on the 14th, worships Shiva with Uma, gives a gold bull and eats the next day. Next morning the body of Shiva is worshipped part by part with a verse of homage for each (feet, head, forehead, eyes, face, belly, sides, waist, thighs, knees, shins, ankles, back), with Parvati also honoured. A gold bull with a water pot, white garland and cloth, adorned with five gems and with foods, is given to a Brahmin. The vow is kept on every 14th, in both fortnights, and each month a different item is eaten (cow's urine, dung, milk, curd, ghee, kusha water, the five cow products, bilva, rice gruel, sesame) and a different flower is used. In Kartika Brahmins are fed, a blue bull is released, and a gold Uma-Maheshvara with a cow and a bed with all furnishings is given to a calm Brahmin who knows the Veda and has a wife, without stinginess. The reward is the merit of a thousand horse sacrifices, destruction of sins like Brahmin-killing, long life, health, the lord of Shiva's hosts in heaven and then Shiva's place; a woman who does it with her husband's or elder's leave also reaches Shiva's state.

09-098.json.summary: Krishna describes the vow of giving up all fruits. In Margashirsha, on the 14th (and on 8th days in other months), one has Brahmins recite, feeds them sweet milk rice with a fee, and for a year gives up the eighteen grains and, apart from fruit and roots, uses medicinal foods. At the year's end, or at once if one cannot keep the vow, one makes a gold Rudra and Dharmaraja (Yama) and sixteen fruits in gold, sixteen in silver and sixteen in copper (a long list including pumpkin, citron, mango, coconut, pomegranate, grapes, dates and others). Two water pots with cloth, two dishes and a cow are given to a calm householder Brahmin with his wife, along with prayers asking for devotion to Shiva, the fruit of endless gifts and no difference seen between Shiva, Vishnu, the sun and Brahma. A bed with furnishings may be given; one who cannot may give only the fruits, or give up and give just one. The text says this is praised for vow-keepers and women alike, and that Rudra's world is gained for as many thousand ages as there are atoms in the fruits. It also promises freedom from sin, no sorrow over children or wife in later births and Vishnu's city.

09-099.json.summary: Krishna says the full-moon day (Paurnamasi) is dear to the Moon, and tells why. Tara, wife of Brihaspati (teacher of the gods), was desired by Soma the Moon, who seized her though she reminded him that Angiras had made him king and that she was like a daughter-in-law to him. Brihaspati told Indra, the gods and the Moon's side of demons fought a great war, and Vishnu came to fight with his discus. Brahma stopped him, saying Soma had been made lord of Brahmins and could not be killed; Vishnu ruled that Soma would vanish on Kuhu and Sinivali, grow again from Raka and Anumati, be fed by offerings to the ancestors, and wane in the dark half as Daksha's curse required. Soma returned Tara on Brahma's order; when both claimed the child in her womb, Tara was asked privately and said it was Soma's, and the child was Budha (Mercury). Soma took the boy home, rejoiced, and said he would honour this day. The vow is a bath on the full-moon day, offerings to ancestors and gods, Soma drawn in a circle with the stars and worshipped with flowers, ghee food, white rice and cloth, a night meal of vegetables, and a verse to the Moon; the same rule is given for the dark half, and the new-moon day (Amavasya) is described as dear to ancestors. At the year's end a gold Moon with the stars is given to a Brahmin. The promised reward is freedom from sin, a bright place in heaven, children and wealth, death at Prayaga and a very long heavenly life.

09-100.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks which days of the year give most merit for bathing and giving. Krishna names the full-moon days of Vaishakha, Kartika and Magha, which must not be passed without bathing and giving. The best places are named: a holy bathing place in Vaishakha, Pushkara forest in Kartika and Varanasi in Magha. Gifts listed are water pots with gold and food in Vaishakha, ancestor offerings and sesame, blankets, deer skins, jewels and sandals in Magha, and in Kartika the release of a bull, weddings, a lamp-waving to Hari and gifts of elephants, horses, chariots and ghee cows. Sweet-smelling fruits such as nutmeg, cloves, dates, coconut, pomegranate and cucumber are named; those who do not give on these days are said to be born sick and poor. Giving to sisters, nephews, uncles, aunts, poor relatives, a friend in trouble and a guest from afar is said to be a crore times better. Krishna tells that when Rama went to the forest with Sita and Lakshmana, Kausalya doubted until Bharata, coming from his mother's father's house, had these days told to her, and she was then comforted. The reward is Indra's world for one who gives water, food, gold, cloth and an umbrella on the full moon.

09-101.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for another great teaching, and Krishna tells a secret he has shared with no one. Four days are called the first days of the ages (Yugadi): the third of Vaishakha equals the Krita age, the ninth of the bright half of Kartika the Treta, the thirteenth of the dark half of Bhadrapada the Dvapara, and the fifteenth of Magha the Kali. Fasting, penance, gifts, prayer and fire offerings on these days are said to be worth a crore times more. On Vaishakha 3 one worships Narayana with Lakshmi and gives a salt cow (with a calf a quarter of its size) on a sheepskin, saying Shridhara be pleased, and gains ten times a thousand cows. On Kartika 9 one eats only at night after a bath, worships Shiva with Uma as Nilakantha and gives a sesame cow. On Bhadrapada dark 13 one feeds Brahmins, gives milk rice, honey and ghee to the ancestors, and a young milk cow with calf and a bell-metal milk pail. On Magha 15 one worships Brahma with Gayatri and gives a butter cow with fruit and gold. Gifts of land, gold, houses, cloth, beds, seats, umbrellas and sandals are named; even a poor person's small gift is said never to run out, and all sin of mind, body and speech is destroyed.

09-102.json.summary: At Yudhishthira's request, Krishna tells the Savitri vow. King Ashvapati of the Madras kept it with his wife, and the goddess Savitri promised him a daughter; the girl was named Savitri. When she came of age her father sent her to choose a husband herself, because a maiden who comes of age in her father's house without marriage is blamed on him. She came back and told the sage Narada, who was present, that she had chosen Satyavan, son of the blind king Dyumatsena of the Salvas. Narada said Satyavan was virtuous but would die in a year; her father asked her to choose another, but Savitri answered that a king speaks once, a scholar speaks once, a daughter is given once, and she had chosen. The wedding was held and they lived in the forest hermitage. Counting the days, Savitri fasted three days from the 12th of Bhadrapada's bright half, and on the fourth day followed Satyavan as he went to cut wood, though her in-laws first advised against it. He felt a pain in his head and lay on her lap; Yama, the Lord of Death, came, drew his thumb-sized soul out, and went off along the ancestors' road. Savitri followed, saying a wife has no refuge but her husband, and Yama, pleased, granted her boons: her father-in-law's sight and kingdom, a hundred sons for her father, a hundred sons for herself, her husband's life and lasting dharma. Savitri returned with her husband alive. The vow itself is then described: a three-night fast from the 13th of Bhadrapada, a bath on the full moon, a Savitri image with Brahma on a bamboo dish with grain and fruit, a night vigil with song and dance, and a gift of the image and the food to a learned poor Brahmin with the verse "Savitri be pleased". A woman repeats it on the full moon of Jyeshtha under the banyan tree, and the text promises sons, grandsons, long enjoyment, Brahma's world and rescue of her father's family and husband's.

09-103.json.summary: Krishna tells of the Krittika vow, kept on the Krittika star in Kartika. In the Krita age Kalingabhadra, a generous queen of King Dilipa with many sons, took the Krittika vow and kept it six months, but died by a snake bite at night and was reborn as a she-goat in the forest with memory of her past life. She kept the vow by fasting, but was caught and tied by a village herdsman for trampling a field; the sage Atri, who also remembered his past, freed her. She drank from a pond and ate a jujube leaf, completed the vow, and Atri gave her yoga. She gave up her goat body and was born as Yogalakshmi, daughter of Gautama and Ahalya, who was given in marriage to the sage Shandilya. Atri saw her pregnant, asked how many Krittikas remained, and she answered six; he gave her the vow and the mantra, and she later went to a place from which there is no return. Yudhishthira asks the method, and Krishna says it is best when the Krittika star falls on a Monday, called Maha-Kartiki. On the full moon of Kartika one fasts, bathes at a holy place, worships gods, sages and ancestors, and at sunset fills a pot with ghee or milk, jaggery and fruit, and makes six Krittika figures: gold, silver, jewelled, butter, grain and flour. They are anointed and given to a Brahmin with a verse to the seven sages' wives, the Krittikas, who are Kumara's mothers. The text promises a heavenly chariot to the star circle and a long life free of illness, and a woman reaches heaven with her husband.

09-104.json.summary: Krishna describes the Chandra (Moon) vow of Vishnu from the full moon of Phalguna. One should not speak with heretics, fallen people, outcastes, unbelievers or sinners, and keeps Narayana in mind, naming Janardana seven times while acting. Vishnu with Lakshmi is worshipped at dusk as the Moon, and at night an arghya offering is given to the Moon with a verse asking that wishes be fulfilled; then a meal is taken at night without oil or salt. The same is done in Chaitra, Vaishakha and Jyeshtha (first period), in Ashadha, Shravana, Bhadrapada and Ashvina (second), and in Kartika onward (third), with a pancha-gavya (five cow products), kusha water or sun-warmed water taken in each period, songs and Krishna's stories at night. Each month has a name of Vishnu: Keshava (Margashirsha), Narayana, Madhava, Govinda, Vishnu, Madhusudana, Trivikrama, Vamana, Shridhara, Hrishikesha, Rama, Padmanabha and Damodara. A water pot, sandals, cloth, umbrella, gold and a fee are given to a Brahmin each month with that name; one who cannot may do it all at once with a gold Moon with fruits and cloth given to a Brahmin. The promised reward is freedom from separation from loved ones, a good death, heaven and rebirth in a good family.

09-105.json.summary: Krishna names the Ashoka full moon, kept on the full moon of Phalguna, after which people never know sorrow. One bathes with earth and water, puts earth on the head, eats a little earth, makes an altar of earth, and worships the Earth by name as Ashoka with flowers and leaves. The verses ask the Earth, who was made free of sorrow by Janardana, to free the doer from every sorrow. An arghya offering is given to the Moon, and one fasts or eats at night without oil. The vow runs through the four-month periods with the names Dharani, Medini and Vasundhara, with extra worship, gifts and a night vigil at each break; pairs of Brahmins are honoured, and silk thread may stand in for cloth and milk for ghee. At the year's end a cow with calf and an image of the Earth with cloth and ornaments are given to a Brahmin. Krishna says that Earth herself kept the vow when she was lifted from the underworld by Varaha, and that he promised grace to those who worship in the same way. The reward is freedom from obstacles and sorrow in every birth.

09-106.json.summary: Yudhishthira says nothing causes more grief than childlessness or a bad son, and asks for a vow that gives a worthy son. Krishna answers with the story of King Kritavirya of the Haihayas. His queen Shiladhana, who had no son, asked the Vedic teacher Maitreyi, who told her the great Ananta vow. In Margashirsha on the Mrigashira star one takes cow's urine, bathes, fasts, and worships Ananta's left foot with flowers, incense and perfumes, giving a fee to a Brahmin and eating at night without oil. After that each month a different part of Ananta is worshipped on a different star: the waist in Pausha, the arm in Magha, the shoulders in Phalguna and Chaitra, the right arm in Vaishakha, the waist in Jyeshtha, the feet in Ashadha and Shravana, the hidden part in Bhadrapada, the heart in Ashvina and the head in Kartika, with cow's urine or the five cow products taken, sesame, gold, barley or ghee given, and fire offerings of ghee, rice or milk. At the year's end a gold Ananta with a silver pestle and plough is worshipped on a copper seat with a verse for each limb (Shesha, Vasudeva, Sankarshana and others), and twelve full water pots, cloth and gifts are given to a learned Brahmin. Shiladhana kept the vow, Vishnu was pleased, and she bore a son, born with auspicious signs, named Arjuna and known as Kartavirya. He worshipped Vishnu as Dattatreya, who gave him world rule and all weapons and, at his request, said his death would come only from Vishnu. The text says that hearing this story frees a man or woman of grief over children for seven births.

09-107.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow by which people do not lose wealth, children, heaven or what they most wish for. Krishna says to worship Vishnu as Achyuta (the Unfallen) on each month's star, with flowers, incense and water, with a different offering by season: kri sara (rice and lentil dish) in Kartika to Magha, samyava (a sweet cake) from Phalguna, and milk rice from Ashadha. The same food is given to Brahmins, one takes the five cow products, and prays with a verse asking that sin be destroyed, merit grow and wealth and children not be lost. A night meal follows; at the year's end a copper dish of ghee is given to a Brahmin with a fee. The conclusion rite is held in the seventh year with a gold Achyuta and a silver image of an elderly woman called Sambharayani, worshipped and given away with water pots, umbrella, sandals, a bed, cows and a house. Krishna then tells that Indra once asked Brihaspati about earlier Indras, and Brihaspati sent him to the ascetic Sambharayani, who knew all earlier Indras and ages. She told how the demon Shankukarna once beat the gods, entered Indra's palace and sat on his bed; when Krishna came, the demon welcomed him, embraced him, and Krishna crushed him to death. She says she has kept this vow for seven years and so lives in heaven without falling. Indra and Brihaspati then kept the vow as well.

09-108.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks by what deeds people become beautiful and well made, and why some are born blind in one eye, hunchbacked or with ear defects. Krishna says he will tell what Vasishtha told Arundhati: one must first worship Vishnu, here as the Nakshatra-purusha (the star-person). From the month of Chaitra, on each of the twenty-seven lunar stars, one bathes, fasts and worships a part of Vishnu's body: feet at Mula, shins at Rohini, knees at Ashvini, thighs at Ashadha, and then the private part, waist, sides, ankles, belly, back, arms, hands, fingers, nails, neck, ears, face, teeth, mouth, nose, eyes, forehead, head and hair at the stars that the text names in turn. The star and its deity and the Moon are also worshipped, Brahmins are fed at each star, and a gift is made to a Brahmin who knows the stars. If blocked, one fasts again on the next star; the vow ends at Magha. At the end a gold star-person, a Brahmin and his wife with cloth and ornaments, a bed, seven grains, a cow with calf, an umbrella, sandals and ghee are given with a verse asking that the bed never be empty. A person with less means gives a cow and a ghee pot. The reward is a beautiful form, health, children, sweet speech and the wishes of the heart in later births too.

09-109.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks which vow suits someone who cannot fast but is devoted to Shiva. Krishna gives the Shiva Nakshatra-purusha vow, kept with night meals, beginning when the Hasta star appears in the bright half of Phalguna. Each star's turn has a different part of Shiva and a name of homage: feet at Hasta, ankles at Chitra, Bhima at Svati, thighs at Vishakha, then the private part, waist, navel, sides, belly, chest, heart, arms, hands, nails, back, skin, lips, nose, three eyes, forehead, matted hair and the head, ending with a verse of homage to Shiva who carries noose, goad, lotus, trident, skull, snake, moon and bow. After the worship comes incense and perfume, and a night meal without oil or salt, with a measure of rice and a ghee pot given to a Brahmin at each night meal. If it is missed, one fasts at another time. At the end Brahmins are fed with jaggery, milk and ghee, and a gold Shiva with Uma on a well-made bed with furnishings is given with a kapila cow with gold horns, silver hooves and a calf, with a verse asking that Shiva's bed never be empty. The text says the vow must not be shown to the dishonest, proud or fault-finding, and may be given to a devoted, self-controlled person; it is said to destroy even great sins, and the woman who keeps it with her husband's or elder's leave is not parted from her kin or wealth. Vasishtha, Arjuna, Kubera and Indra are named as past keepers.

09-110.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what to do if one cannot finish a vow one has taken, or left it broken in the past. Krishna says there is a vow called Sampurna ("Complete") that makes any vow whole, including those broken through carelessness, pride, confusion or obstacles. One has a craftsman make a gold or silver image of the god of the broken vow, with two arms, seated on a lotus with a gentle smile, and on the same day or in the same month the Brahmin bathes it with milk, curd, ghee and water, anoints it and worships it with a water pot, incense, lamps, rice, cloth and jewels. An arghya is given with a verse asking pardon for the broken vow, and verses honour the gods of the directions and the limbs of the image from feet to hair; then the god is asked to forgive and grant both worldly and other-worldly success. While fasting, the doer faces north and gives the image to a Brahmin who knows the rite, who faces east and receives it with kusha grass in hand, with a verse saying the vow was made half before and asking that it be complete. The text praises the word of Brahmins, saying they turned the sea salty and made Agni all-devouring, and that their word removes the sin of Brahmin-killing. Krishna says Garga taught him this as a way of making amends, and he kept it as a child in Gokula. The promised rewards are a whole vow, long life, enjoyment, fame, heaven, and finally liberation.

09-111.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the conduct of courtesans (paṇyastrī): their deity, vow and fast, and how they reach heaven. Krishna tells that his sixteen thousand wives, charmed by his son Samba, grew desirous, and he foretold that after his death thieves would carry them off. They asked how they would live as slaves, and he answered that long ago, as the daughters of Agni and heavenly nymphs, they had not bowed to the sage Narada, who asked how Narayana could be their husband; Narada's curse and Krishna's own meant they would be taken by thieves and live as courtesans. Krishna also recalls that after the old war of gods and demons the god (Indra) ordered the widowed wives of dead demons to live by the courtesan's way in the houses of kings, temples and learned Brahmins. The text gives rules: not to be attached to one man without wealth, to honour and please whoever pays a fee, to take payment whether the man is handsome or not, to take it honestly and not drink, not to be unfaithful to one's master, and to give cows, land, gold and grain to Brahmins on holy days. The vow is a worship of Kamadeva (Ananga) as Vishnu on a Sunday when the Pushya or Punarvasu star falls, after a bath with all herbs, with homage to each part of his body; then a Brahmin with sound limbs is fed with rice and ghee, and, in the text's words, the woman is to satisfy him in every way he wishes, treating him as Kamadeva. This is done each Sunday for twelve months. In the thirteenth month a bed with furnishings, a gold Kamadeva with his wife on a jaggery pot, a cow and other gifts are given with a verse and the Vedic "Who gave this?" mantra. After this, any other man who comes is to be honoured like the Sunday Brahmin. The text promises freedom from the impurity of pregnancy, a place in Vishnu's world and worship by the gods, and adds that Krishna told this to the gopis before.

09-112.json.summary: The chapter describes a vow of the brinjal (vrintaka, aubergine) vow. One does not eat brinjal for a year, six months or three months, and on the Bharani or Magha star fasts one night, calls the gods on a sacred spot, and worships Yama, Kala, Nila, Chitragupta, Vaivasvata, Mrityu and Parameshthin with perfumes, incense, flowers, food and lamps. A fire offering of sesame and ghee is made to each with 108 oblations. A gold brinjal is given to a Brahmin with a black bull or cow, rings, umbrella, sandals, a black pair of cloths and a black blanket, and Brahmins are fed. The text promises the merit of a Pundarika sacrifice and of a horse sacrifice, seven thousand crore years in heaven, and not seeing Yama's world for seven births, and quotes Baudhayana for this. A closing verse says one who gives a gold brinjal with ghee and buttermilk and keeps the vow for a year or a month will never see Yama's city.

09-113.json.summary: Krishna names a secret that gives wealth and well-being and makes all planets favourable. The vow is a set of seven night meals for each planet, begun on the planet's day or star, with a gold image on a copper dish at the end and a gift to a learned Brahmin with a verse.
