The sun is taken on a Sunday: seven night meals, then a gold sun worshipped with red flowers, red cloth pair, umbrella and sandals, bathed in ghee, with laddus; the reward is health, wealth and sons. The Moon is taken on a Monday under Chitra: a gold or silver Moon in white cloth, curd rice, sandals and umbrella. Mars is taken under Svati: a gold image in red cloth with saffron and sweets. Mercury under Vishakha: white cloth and jaggery rice. Jupiter under Anuradha: a gold image in yellow cloth with sacred thread, staff and water pot. Venus under Jyeshtha: milk rice and ghee. Saturn, Rahu and Ketu together under Mula: iron images in black cloth, a fire offering of sesame and ghee with 108 or 28 pieces of each planet's wood, with black aloe incense, kri sara food and a fee. The text says that when Mars, Saturn, the sun, Rahu and Ketu trouble one, this vow ends the troubles, and that hearing it also makes the planets kind.

09-114.json.summary: Krishna tells of the sage Pippalada and Saturn. In the Treta age Indra sent no rain in a king's land through some misdeed, famine came, and the sage Kaushika left his home with wife and child and abandoned his small boy on the road. The boy ate pippala (fig) fruit under the tree, drank water at a well and practised severe austerity. Narada found him hungry, gave him the sacred thread, taught him the Vedas and gave him a twelve-syllable Vishnu mantra; Vishnu appeared on Garuda, and the boy, with Narada's leave, asked for knowledge, which Vishnu gave before vanishing. The boy asked Narada who had troubled him, and Narada said it was Saturn (Shanaishchara), whose gaze had hurt the whole land. Angry, the boy looked at Saturn in the sky and threw him down; Saturn fell from a mountain peak and broke his leg. The gods came, calmed the boy, named him Pippalada ("fig-eater") for living on pippala, and promised that those who worship him or remember his name will be free of Saturn's trouble for seven births. They said Saturn is blameless in giving good and bad fruit. The vow is to bathe on Saturdays with oil rubbed on the body, give oil to Brahmins for a year, and at the end set an iron Saturn in a pot of sesame oil with a black cloth pair, a black cow as fee, black flowers and incense, kri sara and sesame rice, and give it to a Brahmin with the verse "shan no devi". Verses of praise of Saturn, including one told to King Nala in a dream, are given. Pippalada praised Saturn, and the text says he is still seen in the sky; those who hear the story are not troubled by Saturn.

09-115.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for a vow that gives health, endless reward and destroys all sin. Krishna says the Supreme Being stands in the world as sun, fire and moon, so one should eat only at night on Sundays, once devotion to the Sun arises. At sunset one worships Brahmins, draws a twelve-petal lotus in red sandalwood paste and places Surya, Divakara, Vivasvat, Bhaga, Varuna, Mahendra, Aditya and Shanta in the petals, with the Sun's horses, Yama, Martanda, Ravi and Bhaskara around the centre. Water offering (arghya) with sesame, red sandalwood, fruit and rice is given with a mantra, and at night the vow-keeper eats food without oil, avoiding oil massage on the day before and on Saturday. After a year he has a golden lotus and a golden two-armed figure made and gives them, with a tawny cow with gold horns, silver hooves, a bronze milk-pail and a calf, to a worthy householder Brahmin. The reward is freedom from disease, wealth, sons and grandsons, and finally the Sun's world; a devoted wife who keeps it also reaches that world, and hearing or reading it gives long honour in Indra's home.

09-116.json.summary: Krishna tells of the Sankranti vow, begun on a solstice or equinox day, with a single meal the day before. On Sankranti day one bathes with sesame, draws an eight-petal lotus with sandalwood and worships the Sun in the centre and Aditya, the fire-direction deity, Savitri, Varuna, Saptasapti, Martanda and Vishnu in the petals. Worship is with scents, garlands, fruit and food, and arghya water is offered with a mantra praising the Sun as lord of the Rig, Sama and Yajur Vedas. A pot of water, a vessel of ghee and a golden lotus are given to a Brahmin, and the rite is done every month or once at the year's end. At the close one worships fire with ghee-rice, gives a Brahmin twelve cows with pots, a golden earth with crops (or silver, copper or flour if poor) together with a golden Sun, without cheating about wealth. The reward is honour in heaven, then becoming ruler of the seven continents, born in a good family with wife and descendants; hearing it with devotion also brings honour from the gods.

09-117.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks who Vishti (Bhadra) is and how she is worshipped. Krishna says she is the fearsome daughter of the Sun and Chhaya, sister of Shani, who tried to swallow the world at birth, disturbing meals, sleep, sacrifices and festivals. The Sun, unable to find a husband for her, was advised by Brahma to make her a part of the calendar divisions (karana): she is to destroy those who start journeys, entries, weddings, farming or trade during her half-day and be honoured by gods and demons in the rest of it. A verse describes her dark, long-nosed, fanged form, and the text says her mouth has five ghatikas, neck two, heart eleven, navel four, waist five and tail three; work started in her tail succeeds, while mouth, neck, heart, navel and waist give ruin, loss, death, quarrel and loss of wealth. Reciting her twelve names each morning protects from illness and brings victory. The vow is fasting on the day she falls (or one meal if she falls at night), a bath, a figure of darbha grass worshipped, 108 offerings to fire with her names, gifts of sesame and rice, and after seventeen observances a closing rite with iron seat, black cloth, iron, oil, sesame, a black cow with calf and a black blanket. The text promises no obstacles, protection from demons and spirits, no loss and the Sun's abode after death.

09-118.json.summary: Krishna tells of the Agastya vow, in answer to Yudhishthira's request for the sage's deeds, birth and the arghya offering. Mitra and Varuna, seeing the nymph Urvashi, let their seed fall in a pot, and from it came Vasishtha and then Agastya. Agastya destroyed the demons Ilvala and Vatapi, who killed Brahmins by feeding them Vatapi as a ram, by digesting Vatapi and burning Ilvala with a glance. At the gods' request he drank up the ocean so the other demons could be killed, and later the ocean refilled with Ganga's water and was churned; the Kalakuta poison arose, Shiva drank it and his throat turned blue, and Brahma sent the gods to Agastya, who sent the remaining poison to the Himalaya; a wind spread it and caused diseases for three months, from the Taurus to the Leo sign. Agastya also burned Death who had taken bodily form, gave King Shveta, who had eaten his own flesh for lack of giving food, a jewel-made funeral rite so that he reached heaven, and made the Vindhya mountain stop growing by asking it to bow until he returned, which he has not done. His wife Lopamudra asked for a rich home, which he created through Kubera. The vow is held when the Sun enters Virgo, within seven days: bathe with white sesame, set a pot with five jewels, ghee, food and seven grains, with a golden figure of the sage, worship it, and give arghya with fruits and vegetables to a Brahmin with mantras praising Agastya. It is repeated for seven years. Rewards are listed by class: learning for Brahmins, the earth for kings, long life and cattle for merchants, wealth for Shudras, sons for women, a husband for a girl, and rain and an end of disease where Agastya is honoured.

09-119.json.summary: Krishna teaches the offering of arghya (water offering) to the new moon. When the sun can be seen in the west with twelve parts of the day, on the second day of the bright half at twilight, one sets up a circle of cow dung with sandalwood and worships the moon with Rohini, using flowers, sandalwood, incense, lamp, rice, water, durva grass, curd and white cloth. A king with his priest says a mantra beginning "You are new every month" and the Vedic verse "Grow, O Soma". Done every month, it gives fame, wealth, sons and grandsons, cattle and grain, and a hundred years of life followed by the moon's world with heavenly pleasures. Krishna advises Yudhishthira to offer arghya to the newly risen moon with bowed knee, if he wants dharma and prosperity.

09-120.json.summary: Krishna describes the worship of Venus (Shukra) at the start of journeys and when Venus rises, to calm the harm of its setting. A silver Venus is placed in a silver, gold or bronze vessel filled with white rice, with white flowers, cloth and pearls, and given to a Brahmin with a cow and calf, with a mantra to the son of Bhrigu and the arghya offering. Until Venus has been worshipped with cakes and pulses, women should not give gifts. The reward is a good harvest and all wishes. Worship of Brihaspati (Jupiter) follows: a golden Jupiter with yellow flowers and cloth, a bath with mustard seed, palasha and peepal twigs and the five products of the cow, ghee offerings in fire, and giving it with a cow to a Brahmin with a mantra to the lord of the Angirases; pearls may be given instead. Doing so prevents eye defects and harm on journeys, and those who worship Venus and Jupiter at their rising meet no obstacle.

09-121.json.summary: Krishna says he will tell eighty-five vows, collected from the Bhavishya, Matsya, Martanda and Varaha Puranas, unspoken before by others. Each is a short entry: a fast or food rule, a gift, a deity and a reward. Examples: the Patra vow (gifts of sesame vessels and gold on a good day), the Shila vow (spices given to seven households on the fourth day, bringing Lakshmi's world and a clear voice), the Gaurī vow (avoiding curd, milk, ghee and cane juice in the spring month, giving fine cloth to a Brahmin couple, reaching Bhavani's world), the Kama vow (a golden Ashoka tree on the thirteenth day for Pradyumna, ending sorrow), the Pancha-ghata vow (five full pots on the full moon day), the Saubhagya vow (no salt from the third day of Phalguna, a bed given, reaching Gauri's world), the Ahimsa vow (no harming for a month or year, a golden deer and a cow given, with the reward of a horse sacrifice), the Sundara vow (seven goddesses honoured in turn for seven days with a mirror each) and the Brahma vow (a golden egg on a sesame heap, giving release). Others bring Shiva's, Vishnu's, Surya's, Indra's, Varuna's, the Moon's or Lakshmi's world, kingship after an age, health, beauty, good speech or removal of sin; the Brahmakurcha vow uses a mixture of the five cow products on the fourteenth day of Kartika and is said to destroy all sin from childhood to old age. Gifts of a daughter in marriage are called the highest gift, with the giver reaching Brahma's world with twenty-one ancestors. The chapter says hearing the eighty-five (the closing verse says "eighty-five") frees even the killers of Brahmins, cows, fathers or mothers from sin at once, and gives the hearer Indra's world.

09-122.json.summary: Krishna says the first age was of Brahmins, the second of Kshatriyas, the third of Vaishyas and the Kali age of Shudras, and that people are lax about bathing, so he teaches bathing in the month of Magha. One who controls hands, feet, speech and mind gets the fruit of a holy place, while the faithless, sinful, atheists, doubters and hair-splitters do not. Bathing at Prayaga, Pushkara or Kurukshetra, or anywhere, in Magha is advised; rivers not reaching the sea give three nights' fruit, those reaching the sea give a fortnight or month. Bathing near dawn equals the prajapatya penance. Four kinds of bath are named: by wind (cow-dust), water, mantra and divine (rain in sunshine), water being the best. All stages of life and all people may bathe in Magha, with mantras for the three upper classes and silently for Shudras and women. The month's thirty days begin from the full or new moon between Pausha and Phalguna; the rules are a morning vow, mud on the head, arghya to the Sun, offerings to ancestors, worship of Madhava with conch and discus, fire offering, one meal, sleeping on the ground and chastity if able. Sesame is used in six ways, oil and amla and fire for warmth are given at the ford, and Brahmin couples are fed and given blankets, skins, cloth and sandals with "may Madhava be pleased". The reward is freedom from sin, pleasures, twenty-one generations of family reaching Vishnu's world.

09-123.json.summary: Krishna says purity of body and mind is not possible without bathing, so a daily bath comes first. The knowing person prepares a bathing place with the root mantra "Namo Narayanaya", holding darbha grass and sipping water, and marks a square of four cubits and calls the Ganga with a verse (born from Vishnu's foot, Vaishnavi, protect us from sin). Her names such as Nandini, Nalini, Kshama and Shanta are said at the bath, and water is poured on the head three, four, five or seven times, then mud is used with a mantra to the earth asking it to remove all wrong done. After bathing and sipping water the bather puts on two clean white cloths and offers water to all beings: gods, yakshas, nagas, gandharvas, birds and others, then to the Brahma-born sages such as Sanaka and Marichi, to the ancestor groups, and to father, mother's father and others by name and gotra with sesame, with the verse that kin and non-kin may be satisfied. He then draws a lotus, offers arghya to the Sun with praise verses, circles it three times, touches a Brahmin, a cow or gold, and goes to Vishnu's house. The chapter ends saying sages praise daily bathing as removing sin and dirt, to be done in rivers, house or pond.

09-124.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the Rudra bath. Krishna reports a talk in which the sage Agastya asks Skanda, and the answer (given under Rudra's name) is that the bath is for a woman whose children died, who is unfortunate, childless, or has only daughters or is barren. It is done on the eighth or fourteenth day with a fast, on the fourth day after her period or on a Sunday, at a river meeting, Shiva temple, cow pen or quiet yard, with a calm Brahmin who keeps a sacred fire and knows Rudra rites. A square pavilion is set with cow-dung and sandalwood, a white-powder lotus is drawn with Mahadeva in the centre and the guardians of the directions, the goddess and Ganesha around, with offerings and pots at the corners, ghee and mustard offerings into the fire for the nine planets, and the priest recites the Rudra hymn eleven times, repeating. The woman, in white clothes and flowers, sits in a second circle and is washed with eleven Rudra recitations using leaves, soil from stables, anthills, river meetings, ponds, courts and cattle pens, herbs and holy water, and eight pots. She then gives a cow and gold to the one who bathed her, and gifts to Brahmins. The reward is good fortune, happiness and many sons; the text says anyone wanting sons and wealth should do it.

09-125.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the bath at an eclipse. Krishna says that for a lunar eclipse one has Brahmins speak, honours four Brahmins and sets four pots before the eclipse, filled with soil from elephant and horse stables, anthills, river meetings, ponds, cow pens and royal gates, the five cow products, five jewels, herbs, conch, crystal, white sandalwood, holy water, mustard and other things. The gods are invited into the pots with verses asking that the seas, rivers and holy places remove wrong, and that Indra, the lord of spirits and Shiva remove the eclipse's harm. After the eclipse ends the person bathes, gives a cow, gold and a white cloth to a Brahmin, and may write the mantras on gold and carry it on the head. For a solar eclipse, the Sun's name is used in the mantras. The reward is no harm from the eclipse and no loss of kin, final success, and honour in Indra's world for the one who hears this.

09-126.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a householder gives up life when death comes, and Krishna calls fasting to death the highest of such acts, giving the rule and what to recite. The wise person who knows his end is near bathes, worships Vishnu with flowers and incense, gives gifts to Brahmins and the disabled, gives up attachment to kin, wife, fields and friends, and says aloud that he gives up pleasures, food, ornaments, gifts, rites and class and life-stage duties, and that he grants fearlessness to all beings. He thinks of Vishnu alone as kin, lies on darbha grass with his head east or north, and repeats the names of Vishnu and "Om Namo Vasudevaya", picturing the four-armed form with conch, discus and mace. The text says even a very sinful person merges into Vishnu this way, as fire burns grass. Yudhishthira asks what to do if one is too old or ill to lie on grass or to fast; Krishna answers that no particular ground, grass or bed is needed, since the mind and Vishnu are the cause, and whatever one remembers at the end is what one reaches. Krishna then tells, from Markandeya, four kinds of meditation (dhyana): desire-filled, cruel, dharmic and pure white; the first two lead to bad births, the dharmic to the gods and the white to the end of birth. The chapter ends with a verse comparing fasting-death to years of staying in water, fire, wind, a cow house or a battle, and calls it an unending goal.

09-127.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the rule for dedicating (utsarga) a tank, step-well or well: the mantras, priests, posts, gifts, offerings and time. Krishna says that once a tank is finished with a firm bank, steps and stone lining and is full of water, preferably in Kartika under a steady star, the rite is done (some sages allow any time after the northern course of the sun begins). A pavilion of ten or twelve cubits with four gates and four arches of peepal, fig and banyan wood is made, with flags and a five-colour banner, and a four-cubit altar with a post: the post's wood depends on class (for a Brahmin kadamba, peepal or palasha, for a Kshatriya banyan, bilva or khadira, for a Vaishya udumbara, for a Shudra other woods). The guardians of the directions, Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Lakshmi, Ambika and Savitri are drawn and worshipped; four fire pits are made, with sixteen or eight priests, learned in the Vedas, Itihasa and Purana, wearing gold. Fire offerings follow the planets' rite, with Varuna's hymns and a cooked offering. Images of tortoise, crocodile, fish, frog and others in gold, copper, silver and tin are placed in a copper vessel. The patron, in a white head-cloth, takes water to the tank with Vedic chanting, offers it to Varuna, throws in cloth and seeds, leads a cow across, then bathes with kin and wife, gives a cow and fee to the Brahmin, and says the water is given to all beings. Water is to be given freely for three days, with up to a thousand cows given or less according to means, never cheating about wealth. Wells and step-wells follow the same rite, with pots at the corners and Shiva, Brahma and Keshava worshipped in a lotus. Rewards listed: heaven for as many years as a cow has hairs, ancestors saved from hell, seven generations lifted, lasting fame, and the maker and priest both go to heaven, while one who does it without knowing the rule goes to hell. Also praised: temples beside the tank, gifts of food and kind speech.

09-128.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks the greatness of planting trees and the closing rite. Krishna says one tree by the road is better than several sons who died or do nothing for dharma; trees feed the ancestors with leaves, flowers and fruit, give shade and shelter, and a tree planter is always as if bathing at holy places, giving gifts and doing sacrifice. Lists are given, such as one peepal, one neem, one banyan, ten tamarind, three of wood-apple, bilva and amla and five mango, which keep one out of hell. The text compares a garden to a good wife and says a person who has neither dug a pond nor planted trees has done nothing with his birth. For the closing rite (udyapana) Krishna says Parvati, being childless, once made the Ashoka tree her son at Mandara, and the tree is treated as a child: a young tree with good shade is chosen, not one with thorns or infested by insects, and a good day is chosen. The day before it is wrapped in red cloth and red thread, with four full pots, flags and fruits in a copper vessel and offerings to the guardians. In the morning a planetary fire rite is done, with four or eight Brahmins honoured with cloth, sesame and ghee offerings, then the birth rites, naming, first feeding, ear-piercing with a golden needle, hair cutting and the sacred girdle, all done to the tree with mantras. The patron then bathes, says a verse asking the trees to remove his sorrow and "you are my son", looks at his face in ghee and blesses it with a hundred years of life. A cow goes to the priest, Brahmins get fees, the poor are fed freely, and kin and workers are honoured. The reward is all wishes in this world and the next.

09-129.json.summary: Krishna lists the rewards of temple works and worship of the gods, only as given in thirteen verses. Those who build handsome temples of the gods have their glory live after death, and a high white temple gives heavenly pleasure and later a kingdom. Those who set up images of gold, silver, iron, stone or copper shine on thrones in heaven. Those who bathe the gods with the five nectars, anoint them with sandalwood and saffron, worship them daily with fragrant flowers, burn incense, wave fans and give cloth reach heaven or become rulers on earth. Lighting a lamp in a temple, keeping a night vigil with music at spring and other festivals, sweeping and cleaning the temple floor, and giving bells, canopies, whisks and umbrellas all give heavenly palaces, divine company and in some verses rule over the earth. The text ends with worship and bowing to the gods bringing the fruit of the three worlds. The chapter has no story and no speaker besides Krishna.

09-130.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks what gives a body of great brightness. Krishna says the ascetic Pingala once came to Mathura and Krishna's wife Jambavati honoured him, and what he said is repeated here. On holy occasions (Sankranti, eclipses, new and full moons, the two solstices, equinoxes, the eleventh day of the bright half, the fourteenth day, the seventh and eighth days) one bathes, keeps the vow and gives a lighted lamp in a ghee pot to Brahmins, called "gods on earth". Asked why, Krishna tells how King Trishanku, wanting to reach heaven in his body, was made an outcaste by Vasishtha, and how Vishvamitra, angry, held a sacrifice whose offerings the gods refused and so created other gods, plants and beings; Indra appeased him, and the gods now live in images in temples, bound by mantras, giving boons to devotees. Lamps are therefore given before them, with different cloth for each: red for the Sun, yellow for Krishna, white for Shiva, safflower for Gauri, blue for Kama, black for the Nagas and so on, with a Vedic verse. The rewards: Brahma's world in a sun-bright aircraft until the end of the age, good eyesight, and the lamp giver's path always upward; lamps are to be of ghee or oil, never of fat or marrow, and putting out or stealing a lamp brings blindness or loss of an eye. A story is told of Lalita, daughter of the Vidarbha king Chitraratha and chief queen of Charudharma of Kashi, who lit a thousand lamps in Vishnu's temple every day in Kartika. Asked by her co-wives, she tells that in a past life she was a mouse who, in a temple of Vishnu on the Devika river, took a lamp wick, was frightened by a cat, and while escaping pushed the lamp so that it blazed again; for that she was reborn a princess with memory of her birth. She ends by saying she keeps giving lamps, and that she and the king reached Vishnu's world. The chapter closes saying lamp-giving also guides a person safely through darkness.

09-131.json.summary: Krishna teaches the bull release (vrisha-utsarga), on a full-moon day of Kartika or Magha, or on the third day of Chaitra or the twelfth day of Vaishakha, a rite the sage Garga taught in Gokula. A blue-grey bull with white feet and a mark is chosen, with four young cows. The mother-ancestors are worshipped and a mother rite (shraddha) is done, a pot is set with peepal leaves, a learned Brahmin sets Rudra and offers six fire oblations with Pushan mantras. The bull, well-formed and of one or two colours, is branded with a trident on the left and discus on the right, marked with conch and discus, given a garland and white cloth, and let go with four calves in a temple, cow pen or at a river meeting, with a mantra naming him lord of the calves. The reward: it purifies ten earlier and ten later generations; whatever water the bull touches with tail or horns, and whatever earth he scratches, becomes unending for the ancestors, better than a thousand tanks. The text says a man should want many sons because one might go to Gaya, do a horse sacrifice or release a blue bull, and a son who does not release a bull or give water offerings is called his father's dirt.

09-132.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks why a festival is held at village and town on the full moon at the end of Phalguna, why children shout, why the Holika fire is lit, what "Adada" means, and who is worshipped. Krishna tells of King Raghu in the first age, whose people complained of a demoness called Dhundha who troubled children day and night and could not be stopped by guards, spells or medicine. The priest explains she is the daughter of Malin, who got a boon from Shiva after harsh penance that gods, humans and weapons could not kill her and that she would be safe in cold, heat and rain, day or night, but with a limit: she would fear mad people and children, and she was told to bear this in each season. Using Shiva's words, she seizes children, and the cry "Adada" came from a householder chanting a spell against her. The cure is to act on the fifteenth day of Phalguna, when winter ends: children come out like soldiers with sticks, dry wood and dung cakes are piled, and fire is lit with mantras that destroy demons; people go round it three times, laughing, singing and talking freely, and the noise and the fire drive her away. The fire (holika) rite also removes disease. Children are guarded that night in a dung-smeared yard, and men with sticks touch them with wood, with songs, and are given jaggery and cooked food. Next morning, on the first day of spring, one honours the fire ash, a woman anoints a seated person with sandalwood, and mango flowers with sandalwood are eaten, as worship of Kama; gifts are given with "may Kama be pleased". The reward is wishes fulfilled, no ills, sons and grandsons.

09-133.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks why the damana plant is offered to gods though it is fragrant, and asks for the greatness of the swing festival and the chariot festival. Krishna tells that in the Mandara mountain the damana tree, loved by bees, drove the gods' wives and the sages mad with desire by its smell, so that sages dropped their rules and study. Brahma, angry, said it was born to subdue the world (damana) and rebuked it, but the tree answered that it acts by its own nature, which Brahma made. Brahma then granted that for one day in spring it will stand above the gods' heads, and those who offer it with gifts will be happy; the fourteenth day of the spring month will be known as Damana and be dear to Shiva. The text then describes the swing festival: a god in the grove swings, and Parvati asks Shiva for a swing; he has demons build one with two posts, with Vasuki as the rope and a jewelled seat. When Shiva and Parvati swing, the mountains shake and the seas churn, and the gods ask him to stop. Shiva declares that from now on those who hold a spring swing at a pond, with a decorated swing and fire rite, offering to the directions, and who put the god on it with the root mantra, will be free of disease for a hundred years, with sons, wealth and then reach his city. People play with coloured water and saffron.

09-134.json.summary: Krishna tells the chariot festival (ratha-yatra). In Chaitra, when spring was at the Malaya mountain, the sage Narada came to Shiva's world and said Kama, though burned, rules through Spring, his friend: with the wind from the Malaya, the cuckoo and mango, all beings sing, dance and laugh, even the old. Curious, Shiva rode out in his chariot, and Vishnu, Brahma, the Sun, Parvati and Ganesha came in chariots to see; Shiva's attendants sang, rolled, played and laughed. Seeing the gods stirred, Shiva thought it needed care, called Spring and told him to stay one month in the bright half, adding that each year the god will come in the same chariot-form, and those who hold the chariot festival will enjoy heavenly pleasures and be free of disease. Yudhishthira asks how to make the chariot; Krishna says a fine strong wooden or bamboo chariot with good wheels, covered in cloth, with garlands, two white oxen, an umbrella and whisks, set in the courtyard, a planetary fire rite is done, and the god is placed with the root mantra and led around with conch, drums, torches and music. Betel and flowers are given, any who come to watch may take what is offered, and if an axle, flag or yoke breaks, a fire offering with sesame, ghee and milk repairs it. The festival goes on over several days with vigils, the chariot placed at the south and north on set days and taken home on the sixth. The text adds this is also the setting of the Ratha-saptami, and lists the gods to worship on each tithi: Gauri on the third, Ganesha on the fourth, Sarasvati on the fifth, Skanda on the sixth, the Sun on the seventh, Shiva on the eighth and fourteenth, Chandi on the ninth, the sages on the tenth, Vishnu on the eleventh or twelfth. The spring festival gives peace of mind.

09-135.json.summary: Krishna tells of the worship of Kama (Madana). After marrying Gauri, Shiva took the Pashupata vow and sat in meditation, and the gods, wanting a son for Gauri, sent Kama with Spring, Rati, Priti and his companions to disturb him. Kama shot his flower arrow, but Shiva, angry, opened his third eye and burned Kama to ash; Rati and Priti wept, and Gauri asked Shiva to bring him back. Shiva said Kama, as a bodied being, had troubled the whole world, but to honour her he would let Kama take a body again on the thirteenth day of the bright half in spring, and that he would be the seed of the whole world's growth. For the worship, on that day one bathes and draws or makes a figure called Ashoka-nagara, a golden, wooden or painted Kama with Spring, Rati and Priti, with nymphs and musicians, feeds Brahmins at midday with incense, garlands and clothes, and says a mantra bowing to Kama who disturbs Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and Indra. Sweets are placed before the god with "may Kama be pleased", a Brahmin couple is given a pair of cloths with a fee, a wife honours her husband as Kama with cloth, garlands and ornaments, and the host keeps a night vigil with a festival, lamps, dancing and shows. The reward is a year free of disease, good harvests, safety, fame and rain in the kingdom, and the pleasure of the gods and all beings.

09-136.json.summary: Yudhishthira describes the "Bhutamata" festival in which people run through every village and town singing, dancing, laughing, talking wildly, falling, rolling in mud and smearing themselves with ash, and asks whether it is scripture or custom. Krishna says he believes Yudhishthira is a believer and tells a story. Shiva and Parvati were at play at Mandara, and after a hundred divine years a dark, fierce woman rose from their union (as a result of Parvati's pressure), with skull garlands, a staff and a tiger skin, with her followers, and a male like her came from Shiva, followed by fearsome spirits. Shiva called them brother and sister, named them "Bhutamata", "Bhratribhanda" and "Udakasevika", and granted a boon: those who serve her under an old tree with water-filled pots, anoint her with sandalwood, worship her with flowers and incense and feed her with rice, cakes and sweet rice get sons, cattle, health, and no harm from female spirits, ghouls or demons, and their children thrive. She is worshipped everywhere under various names and times, from the first to the fifteenth day of Jyeshtha, with shows. The chapter then gives the text of the mock-plays and jeering cries used in the show (for example, jeers at a thief, an old man who does not support his wife, a hunter and a dancing "yogini"), ending with a figure carried to the foot of a tree, and the promise of no poverty or sorrow.

09-137.json.summary: Krishna tells of Raksha-bandhan, the tying of a protection thread. In an old war between gods and demons the defeated demons went with their king Bali to Shukra, who told them not to despair, since victory and defeat come in time, to make a pact with Indra for two half-years, because Indra was made unconquerable by Shachi's protection thread. He told them to wait a year, and they waited. Asked about the rite, Krishna says that on the full moon of Shravana, at sunrise under clouds, one bathes, offers water to gods and ancestors, and Brahmins do the Vedic upakarma, with a rite for the sages; for Shudras a bath and gift with a mantra is said to be good. In the afternoon, protection packets are made of rice, white mustard and gold wrapped in clean cloth, house protection is made with dung-free round lumps and durva grass, and the king, with his ministers, priest and friends, sits on a seat in the cleaned house. Women and prostitutes honour him, and the priest ties the thread on the king with a mantra (the thread that bound Bali, the strong demon king; "O protection, do not move"). Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras and others should all tie it after honouring Brahmins. The text promises a year free of faults and happy, with sons and friends.

09-138.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the Mahanavami (Great Ninth Day): since when it has been kept, whether before Krishna's birth from Yashoda's womb, and what fate awaits living beings killed in it, whether the killer, the one who gets it done or the one who approves. Krishna says the highest power, called by names such as Kali, Sarvamangala, Maya, Katyayani, Durga, Chamunda and Bhavani, is worshipped on the eighth and ninth days by all kinds of beings. When the eighth day of the bright half of Ashvin falls with the Mula star it is called Mahanavami; worshipping the mother of the world on both days frees one from sorrow and defeats enemies. Buffaloes and other animals offered to her on that day go to heaven and there is no sin for those who kill them; the goddess is pleased more by buffaloes than by flowers or incense. She was born as Yashoda's daughter, put her foot on Kamsa's head and went away, and was set up at the Vindhya hill. The rite for a king who wants victory runs from the first day to the eighth: a pavilion with a fire pit on the south-east, weapons, royal insignia, horses, elephants and the white umbrella are blessed, with mantras for each (the umbrella, horse, banner, elephant, sword, armour, drum, bow, conch, whisk, dagger, golden rod and throne). On the eighth day a golden, silver, brass, wooden or copper Durga is bathed and worshipped with bilva leaves, a hymn is said, and there is a night vigil with dance and song. At dawn, a hundred or fifty buffaloes and rams are cut down before the goddess, and wine jars are offered; shares go to Kapalikas, servants and kin. On the ninth day at the afternoon the king, with his army, takes the goddess round the kingdom in a chariot, with swords, elephants, conches and dancers, and gives an offering of meat, blood, rice and water to the spirits with a mantra to all gods and beings. The reward is freedom from sin, going to the goddess's city, no harm from fire, thieves or obstacles, and passing hard places.

09-139.json.summary: Krishna tells of the Indra banner (Indradhvaja) festival. In an old war between gods and demons, a banner pole was set on Meru for Indra's victory, worshipped and decorated, and the demons, seeing it, were frightened and destroyed or fled to the underworld. Later King Vasu, who went to Indra's world, was given the pole by Indra and set it up with other kings in the rainy season on earth, and Indra, pleased, gave Vasu a boon: in places where people worship the banner at the end of the rains there will be no disease, plenty of food and festivals. The rite: in the month of Shravana a twenty-cubit pole of good wood is bathed, dressed in cloth and fitted with thirteen boxes or discs in set shapes and colours (with the guardians of the directions, Chandika, Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, Yama and the nine planets), with flags, bells, garlands and whisks, tied with ropes and raised slowly after a fire offering. Brahmins are honoured with fees and sweet cakes, and a festival of seven or nine days follows with shows, songs, wrestling, gifts and gambling, and a night vigil to keep crows, owls and pigeons away, since they are said to bring famine, the king's death and the people's ruin. Omens are listed for a break in the umbrella, banner, top, rope or posts. If it falls or breaks, a gold or silver one is raised and a peace rite done; if it is not raised, it must be done in the twelfth year. At the end, from Shravana to Bharani, the pole is released at night with a mantra. The reward is rain on demand, no plague or fear of death, victory over enemies and rule on earth, then honour in Indra's world.

09-140.json.summary: Krishna tells of Kaumudi, the festival of the day of Bali. He recalls that Vishnu, as the dwarf, begged the earth from Bali with three steps, gave the kingdom to Indra and sent Bali to the underworld, but allowed him one day and night, on the new moon night of Kartika, when the demons act freely. Yudhishthira asks the name, the deity, the gifts and the joys. Krishna says that on the fourteenth day of the dark half people who fear hell must bathe at dawn, wave apamarga twigs over the head with a mantra, offer water to Yama with his names, and give a lamp for Naraka; at dusk lamps are lit in temples, houses, streets, gardens, wells, stables and on rivers. On the new moon day one bathes, honours gods and ancestors, does the new-moon shraddha, feeds Brahmins, and in the afternoon the king has it announced that this is Bali's kingdom and all may enjoy themselves. People dress, gamble, drink, dance, play music, put lamps on tree branches (the lamp-waving, nirajana, for victory), and the king walks his city at midnight. At dawn women drive out ill fortune with winnowing baskets and drums, prostitutes and women go house to house, the king gives gifts and honours to servants, kin, wrestlers and actors, and watches animal fights and shows. In the afternoon a "road-guard" (margapali) rope of kusha grass is tied to a tall post in the east, animals are led under it, and anyone who passes under it is free of disease. At night a figure of Bali is drawn on the ground in five colours with Vindhyavali and demons, and worshipped with flowers, food, meat, liquor and lamps, with a mantra to Bali, son of Virochana, and a vigil. The text says gifts on that day are never lost, that the festival is called Kaumudi because people rejoice (mud) on earth (kau), that a person's mood that day sets the year's, so one should be happy, and it ends with lamp-day verses.

09-141.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks the rite for peace and prosperity, and Krishna gives the rite for the nine planets (graha-yajna) in three forms, by ten thousand, a hundred thousand or ten million offerings. For the ten-thousand rite a square altar is made in a pit's north-east, and the planets are set in the right places on rice: the Sun in the centre, Mars south, Jupiter north, Mercury north-east, Venus east, the Moon south-east and Ketu north-west, each of the right metal or stone (copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver and iron), with their ruling and joint deities (Shiva, Uma, Skanda, Vishnu, Brahma, Indra, Yama, Kala, Chitragupta and others). Each gets its colour of cloth and flowers and its own food (jaggery rice for the Sun, ghee milk-rice for the Moon, goat meat for Rahu, and so on). A pot with five jewels is set with Varuna and holy waters. Offerings of twigs of arka, palasha, khadira, apamarga, peepal, udumbara, shami, durva and kusha, with ghee, barley, rice, sesame, honey, curd, are made with each planet's own Vedic verse, followed by offerings to the other gods; the patron is bathed with a verse naming all beings and rivers, and fees are given for each planet (a tawny cow to the Sun, a conch to the Moon, a red ox to Mars, gold to Mercury, a yellow cloth pair to Jupiter, a white horse to Venus, a black cow to Saturn, iron to Rahu, a goat to Ketu), with verses for each gift. The forms of the planets are described (the Sun on a lotus with seven horses, the Moon white with a mace, Mars red with sword, shield and mace, and so on). The text says to worship specially the planet that is troubling one, that planets, cows, kings and Brahmins punish if slighted, and a fee must not be skipped. The hundred-thousand rite uses a bigger pavilion and pit, ten times the offerings and fees, with four to ten priests, and the text says one without wealth should not do it, and it grants whatever is wished for: sons, wealth, a wife, a husband, a lost kingdom. The ten-thousand rite is also done at weddings, installations and omens.

09-142.json.summary: Krishna tells that King Samvarana of Pratishthana, learned, strong and devoted to the gods, once received the great yogi Sanatkumara (son of Brahma), honoured him and asked what to do in earthquakes, meteors, dust-rain, house collapses, drought, fever, bad planets, famine, war and illness. Sanatkumara teaches the Koti-homa, the "ten million offerings" rite. It is done in a temple, at a river, in a forest or on a hill, on a good day and star, with a Brahmin priest honoured and asked to lead. A pavilion (up to a hundred cubits), an eight-cubit fire pit with three girdles, a four-cubit altar, fourteen water pots with leaf mouths, arches in the directions, and Vishnu in the centre, Brahma east, Rudra west, the Vasus north, the planets north-east, the Maruts south-east and the guardians of the directions are set. A hundred learned Brahmins are chosen; the fire is called up and described, black sesame with ghee and a little barley, with palasha twigs, is offered, and each thousand ends with a full offering. Samvarana says it is very hard for so many priests over so long, and asks for a short form. Sanatkumara names four forms: with a hundred mouths (a hundred pits, each with a hundred Brahmins, done together, or a thousand Brahmins at once), ten mouths (two hundred Brahmins over a month or two), two mouths (two pits) and one mouth (one pit, free of count or time). Since life and wealth are unsteady, the short form is advised. At the end, there is a festival, priests receive gifts (a hundred cows, a hundred horses, a thousand gold coins, villages, elephants, chariots), the poor are given cloth, and the patron bathes with the earlier pots. The reward is health, wealth, sons, growth of the state, end of sin, and an end of drought, omens, famine and planet harm.

09-143.json.summary: Krishna gives the Maha-shanti, the great peace rite taught by Mahadeva for the good of kings. It is done at a king's coronation or before a campaign, after bad dreams and evil omens, when planets are unfavourable, after lightning, meteors, a comet, thunder from a clear sky or an earthquake, at a birth under Mula or a junction star, at the birth of twins, when umbrellas or flags fall, when crows, owls or pigeons enter the house, when harsh planets turn back in the 1st, 4th, 8th or 12th house of the birth chart, in planetary wars, at the loss of clothes, weapons, cattle, horses, jewels or hair, a rainbow at night, a broken house beam, a she-mule giving birth, and at eclipses of sun and moon. Five Brahmins of good family, learned in the Vedas (especially the Atharva) and purified by fasting, perform it. A pavilion of ten or twelve cubits is built with a four-cubit altar and a one-cubit fire pit in the south-east with three girdles, sandal garlands and arches. Five pots are set on the altar, at the corners and in the middle, holding herbs, five jewels, gorochana, sandal, white mustard, shami, durva, kusha, rice, barley, twigs of the sacred trees and earth dug by an elephant's tusk, with holy water, grain and cow products in the middle pot, each pot blessed with its own Vedic verse. The fire is laid with verses, milk-rice is cooked with the Purusha hymn, and shami and palasha twigs are offered, then offerings with verses to Jatavedas, Yama and Vishnu, twenty-seven to the stars, sesame with ghee to the planets, and an expiation offering. To the sound of drums and conches the patron, seated on a seat of kashmarya wood in the middle of the altar, is bathed from the five pots with Vedic verses; food is offered to the directions, the Brahmins recite the peace verses, and the rite ends with the declaration of an auspicious day. Land, gold, clothes, beds and seats are given to the Brahmins, and the poor and learned are fed. The rite brings long life, quick victory over enemies, success in taking forts and good sons: as armour stops the blows of weapons, so the peace rite stops the blows of fate, and the planets are kind to one who is gentle, self-controlled, kind and earns his wealth rightly.

09-144.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the peace rite of Ganesha, the lord of the ganas, and Krishna gives the rite of Vinayaka, which removes obstacles to every work. A person troubled by Vinayaka dreams of plunging into deep water, of shaven heads and ochre robes, of riding flesh-eating animals and of being among outcasts and corpses; awake, he feels followed, is downcast and fails without cause. A prince does not win his kingdom, a maiden finds no husband, a pregnant woman no child, a scholar no teaching post, a student no learning, a merchant no profit and a farmer no harvest. On an auspicious day he is rubbed with white mustard paste and ghee, anointed with perfume and saffron, and seated on a good seat while Brahmins say blessings. Earth from a horse stable, an elephant stable, an anthill, a river meeting and a lake, with gorochana, perfumes and guggulu, is put in water drawn from a lake in four pots, and he is bathed on a red bull's hide with verses: "I bathe you with the thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed water", "Varuna, the Sun, Brihaspati, Indra, Vayu and the seven sages give you good fortune", and "whatever misfortune is in your hair, parting, head, forehead, ears and eyes, may the waters destroy it". Mustard oil is then offered on his head with an udumbara ladle to the names Mita, Sammita, Shala, Katankata, Kushmanda and Rajaputra, and at a crossroads, on kusha grass in a winnowing basket, offerings are laid out: cooked and raw rice, sesame rice, cooked and raw fish, meat, coloured fragrant flowers, three kinds of liquor, radish, puris, cakes and a garland. He then prays to Ambika, Vinayaka's mother, for beauty, fame, fortune, sons, wealth and all wishes, feeds Brahmins and gives his teacher a pair of cloths. Worship of the Sun and of Mahaganapati also brings success; a Mahaganapati carved from the root of the white arka plant is especially powerful, and even an unlucky man or king who worships it gains every success and is always victorious.

09-145.json.summary: Krishna tells how Garga asked the sage Kaushika, seated at his fire rite, how a person held in chains, imprisoned or struck by illness is set free, and which illnesses can be cured. Kaushika says an illness that begins under one's birth star or other harmful stars brings suffering or death, and how long it lasts depends on the star under which it starts: nine nights for Krittika, three for Rohini, five for Mrigashira, while Ardra takes life; seven nights for Punarvasu and Pushya, nine for Ashlesha, while Magha lasts until the cremation ground; two months for Purva Phalguni, three fortnights for Uttara Phalguni, a light illness for Hasta, half a month for Chitra, two months for Swati, twenty days for Vishakha, ten for Anuradha, half a month for Jyeshtha; under Mula comes release; fifteen days for the Ashadhas, two months for Shravana, half a month for Dhanishtha, ten days for Shatabhisha, nine for Purva Bhadrapada, fifteen for Uttara Bhadrapada, ten nights for Revati and a day and a night for Ashvini. An astrologer should learn the star at birth as well. For each star an offering to its ruling deity is named: twigs of milky trees for Ashvini, sesame with honey for Bharani, barley for Krittika, rice and other grains, ghee, milk-rice, curd, priyangu grain, red rice and parijata flowers for the others, and whole fruits a hundred and eight times for Revati. Last, it gives the single offering with the Savitri verse that Brahma once taught, which quickly cures every fever.

09-146.json.summary: Vasishtha tells King Ikshvaku of the Aparadha-shata vow, the vow of the hundred offences, which burns away even heavy sin like a heap of cotton and brings both what one desires and liberation. He lists the offences: not living by an ashrama, keeping no sacred fire or vows, not giving, impurity, cruelty, greed, impatience, harming people, deceit, disbelief, mocking the Vedas, harshness, lies, violence, theft, uncontrolled senses and mind, anger, envy, pride, cunning and harsh words; leaving one's wife, mother or son, honouring the unworthy, neglecting ancestor rites, prayer, the five daily offerings, the twilight prayers and the sacred fire; sex out of season or on festival days, slander, adultery, visiting prostitutes, gifts to the unworthy, forbidden food, selling one's wife or children, cutting trees for firewood, selling learning, begging, bad friends, killing women, cows or friends, abortion, eating others' food, and above all the great sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold and violating the teacher's wife. There are countless more, but all are destroyed by worshipping Satyesha, the Lord of Truth: Vishnu with Lakshmi, with five faces (Vamadeva east, Narasimha south, Kapila west, Varaha north and Achyuta upward), seated on a lotus on a half-moon in the milk ocean, holding lotus, mace, conch and discus, with the Ganga flowing from his feet and his eight powers, Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanti, Papanashini, Unmilini, Vanjuli, Trisprisha and Vivardhana. The vow is kept each month from Margashirsha, fasting on the twelfth, the new moon or the eighth of both halves. A gold image of one pala is placed on a golden lotus above a pot of milk and worshipped with mantras for bathing, clothing, the sacred thread and sandal paste, with salutations to Vasudeva, Narasimha, Kapila, Varaha, Achyuta, Sankarshana, Aniruddha and Govinda, and the prayer "Krishna, Krishna, Rama, Rama, Hari, protect me from all sorrows". Money is quietly given to one Brahmin over the year. When the year ends the closing rite is done, the Brahmin says "may your sins be destroyed", and everything is given to him. The fruit is ten million times that of all the Vedas and holy places: wealth, grain, sons, friends, learning and health in this world, and dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation, for whoever does it, reads it or hears it.

09-147.json.summary: Krishna tells that in the White Island Lakshmi, pressing Vishnu's feet, asked him for a vow that gives beauty and good fortune and the fruit of all holy places. Vishnu says this vow is the best, as the householder is among the ashramas and the Ganga among rivers; it was kept by Gauri with Shiva, by Rama with Sita after he won his kingdom, by Nala when parted from Damayanti, by the Pandavas with Draupadi in the forest, and by Rambha, Mena, Shachi, Satyabhama, Arundhati, Urvashi, the naga maidens, Gayatri, Sarasvati and Savitri, and it frees men and women even from the great sins. It is the Kanchana-puri vow, the gift of a golden city, made on the third or eleventh day, the full or new moon, the eighth, a sun's entry into a sign or another holy day. The keeper bathes in a river with verses to the earth (raised by Vishnu as the boar) and to the waters, goes home without speaking to slanderers, heretics or cheats, fasts or eats once at night, and drinks water from a gold-set conch blessed with the twelve-syllable mantra. An altar of shami wood with four pillars is built, hung with cloth, a canopy, flowers and incense, with a lotus pattern in the middle and Vishnu with Lakshmi on a seat. A pot called the Milk Ocean, with five jewels, carries the golden city of four, two or one pala, ringed with sweets and an arch of banana stems; Brahmins install in it a gold Vishnu with Lakshmi, with jewel eyes, diamond teeth, pearl ornaments, conch, discus and mace. He is bathed with the five nectars and each limb is worshipped by a name, from the feet (Vasudeva) to the head (Sarvatman), Brahmins with Vedic verses and others with Puranic ones; Lakshmi, the guardians of the directions, the nine planets and Ganesha are also honoured, with offerings of milk-rice, ghee cakes, sweets and fruit and ten lamps. Sixteen Brahmin couples are honoured as Vishnu and Lakshmi with clothes, umbrellas, sandals, rings, seven grains and food, with the words "may Krishna be pleased", and a furnished bed and, at the end, a cow are given. The city is covered with cloth, the patron's eyes are bound, and a learned teacher says "see this golden city that grants all wishes"; the patron uncovers his eyes, throws flowers to the teacher, sees the city, and on his knees offers water with five jewels, Ganga water, fruit, mustard, rice, gorochana and curd to Krishna and to Lakshmi, praying for good fortune, sons and wealth. He keeps a night vigil with songs, dances and Vaishnava stories, worth a hundred sacrifices, and next morning honours the ancestors, feeds and gives gifts to the Brahmin couples, pleases the poor, blind, deaf and lame, and breaks his fast with sweet milk food among friends. The merit cannot be told: he lives in the worlds of Brahma, Rudra and Vishnu and is then born an emperor on earth, and one who hears it lifts up seven generations. Vishnu ends by telling Lakshmi that she herself once kept this vow, and by its merit won him as her husband.

09-148.json.summary: Krishna praises the gift of a daughter in marriage. One who adorns his daughter and gives her in the Brahma form of marriage lifts up seven generations before him and seven after, reaches the worlds of Daksha Prajapati, and by the Prajapatya form saves himself as well and goes to heaven. Giving land, cows, horses or elephants to a man of low caste sinks the giver into deep darkness, where he eats crows' filth for thousands of years, and one who takes a bride-price for his daughter goes to a terrible hell. A daughter should be given by the rules to a man of her own class, or to one of higher class. One who performs the rites (tonsure, sacred thread and the rest) for an orphaned Brahmin boy wins the fruit of a horse sacrifice, and one who gives an orphan girl in marriage is honoured in heaven. Gold given with the bride doubles the fruit. Honouring a maiden equals worshipping Vishnu, and the giver rides a lovely aerial chariot, filled with the songs of heavenly women, to the world of the best of the gods.

09-149.json.summary: Krishna praises the Brahmins. They are gods on earth and gods in heaven, and nothing in the three worlds is higher; they can make a god of what is not a god and unmake a god. The gods were born from Brahmins in the beginning and the whole world comes from them, and through their mouths the gods, ancestors, sages and nagas eat. Whatever a person gives to Brahmins with devotion comes back to him birth after birth. Even by fanning a tired Brahmin with a palm leaf, rubbing his limbs, washing and bathing his feet and serving him as he wishes, a person reaches the everlasting heaven without any sacrifice. What contented Brahmins speak, being the visible gods among whom the unseen gods dwell, surely comes true for that person, so one should always serve them.

09-150.json.summary: Yudhishthira says he never tires of Krishna's nectar-like words, and since Govinda is famed as the lord of cattle and is pleased by the gift of a bull, he asks for the rite of giving a bull. Krishna says a single strong draught ox equals ten milk cows, and is even better than the gift of ten cows. It should be a good carrier with a fine back, healthy, young, gentle, well tempered and without faults; such a bull alone upholds a great family and saves the giver from the round of rebirth. On an auspicious day the calm bull is adorned, given a silver tail ornament and given to a Brahmin with the prayer "You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the joy of the world and the seat of the eight-formed Shiva; protect me, eternal one", together with a fee, and the Brahmin is bowed to and sent off. The sin of seven births, in word, mind and body, is destroyed; the giver rides a shining chariot yoked to bulls to heaven and lives in the world of cattle for as many thousands of years as the bull has hairs, and is then reborn as a great Brahmin who performs sacrifices and is honoured by all. The right receivers are householders whose ears are full of the Veda, who have mastered their senses, do not kill living beings and are slow to accept gifts; giving a strong, sturdy, well-horned bull to such a Brahmin truly brings the fruit of ten cows.

09-151.json.summary: Yudhishthira, having heard of the Puranas, the emptiness of worldly life and the many vows, asks about the greatness of gifts: what to give, when and how, since he thinks nothing is higher than giving and only that wealth cannot be taken by kings and thieves. Krishna says wealth placed in a Brahmin's hand is a treasure that grows without being invested and goes with one on the last road. A strong, long-lived body is useless if it does not help others; why not give even half a mouthful to the needy, since wealth as large as one's wishes never comes? A day without giving is like being robbed, and a man whose days pass without dharma, wealth or pleasure breathes like a blacksmith's bellows but does not live. Those who never gave, offered, died at a holy place or gave gold, food and water to Brahmins are seen reborn poor, hungry, rough-skinned and begging with a skull bowl. Wealth won with great effort has only one good path, giving; the others are disasters. Riches are not used up by enjoyment or by giving, only by the end of past merit, so even one who has not seen the highest truth should give to worthy people, since nothing goes with the dead. Asked which gifts please Brahmins, Vishnu and Shiva, Krishna names the three great gifts, cows, land and learning, which purify seven generations through milk, ploughing and knowledge, and begins with the cow. A cow to be given is young, beautiful, gentle, in milk, rightly earned and with her calf, and goes to a learned Brahmin; an old, sick, maimed, barren, vicious or calf-less cow, one far away or wrongly gained, must never be given, nor to a man of low birth, a fool, a greedy man, a slanderer or one who neglects offerings to gods and ancestors. On a holy day, after bathing, offering water to the ancestors and bathing Vishnu and Shiva with ghee and milk, the giver faces the cow north or east, with her calf, covered with cloth and a white sacred thread, with gold horns, silver hooves and a bronze milking pail, and gives her to the Brahmin with a fee, saying "May cows be before me, cows behind me, cows in my heart; I live among cows", walks around her, says "accept this cow I give you", treats the Brahmin as a god and follows him eight steps as he leaves. Such a giver goes to heaven with all wishes fulfilled, frees seven generations before and after and himself from the sins of seven births, and wins at every step the fruit of a horse sacrifice and of a hundred cows; the cow takes away sin for as long as fourteen Indras reign. It is the expiation for all sins, even those done knowingly, when joined with repentance, and people of every class have reached the worlds they wished for by it. The learned say no gift in the world is holier than cows.

09-152.json.summary: Krishna now gives the "cow" gifts made of other materials for those who seek special wishes, warning that a gift is fruitful only when complete: a gift without its fee or done wrongly serves only pride, loses money and brings no fruit. He begins with the sesame cow (tila-dhenu), taught long ago by Varaha, which frees even the killer of a Brahmin, a cow or a father, one who violated his teacher's bed, an arsonist and a poisoner from all great and lesser sins and sends him to heaven. On ground smeared with cow dung and covered with a black antelope skin and darbha grass, a cow is made of white, black and brownish sesame, four adhakas for the cow and one drona for the calf, with gold horns, silver hooves, a sugar tongue, a jaggery mouth and dewlap, sugarcane legs, a copper back, eyes of pearl shell, ears of fine leaves, teeth of fruit, a garland tail, udders of fresh butter, a white cloth on the head, hairs of white mustard, and fruits, grains, gems and pearls, with a bronze milking pail. It is given on a holy day with the prayer "May the goddess Lakshmi, who lives in all beings and in the gods, in the form of a cow remove my sin", walked around, worshipped and given with a fee. The giver is freed from all sin and reaches the highest Brahman, and the receiver and those who gladly praise the gift also reach Brahma's world. Living on sesame for three days, or one, before giving it is better than the chandrayana fast, and it destroys the sins of childhood, youth and age, of word, mind and deed, of spitting into water, bathing naked, threatening a Brahmin with a pestle, going to a low woman or the teacher's wife, drinking liquor and eating forbidden food. The giver passes over the terrible road of Yama, the Vaitarani river, the burning sands, the iron-beaked crows and fierce dogs that tear the flesh of sinners, the sword-leaf forest and the iron-thorned silk-cotton tree, and rides a golden chariot to the highest state. It must not be given to a man without virtue, a rich man, one born of adultery or a greedy man, and one cow goes to one receiver only, as the sages taught at Naimisha; cows, houses, beds and wives must not be shared among many, and a sesame cow that is sold burns seven generations. It is best given on the full moons of Magha, Kartika, Vaishakha and Margashirsha, at eclipses, equinoxes, solstices, vyatipata and the gajachchhaya day, and the giver lives in heaven for as many thousands of years as the cow has hairs. The receiver says "I accept you, goddess, to support my family; you are always kind to us".

09-153.json.summary: Krishna gives the water cow (jala-dhenu), whose gift pleases Vishnu. A water pot holding jewels and village grains is set up, wrapped in a pair of white cloths and decorated with durva, fragrant herbs (kushtha, jatamansi, usira, valaka), amalaka and priyangu leaves, with a white sacred thread, sandals and an umbrella, on a seat of darbha grass, with four silver bowls of sesame around it and its mouth closed with a bowl of curd, ghee and honey; a calf is set beside it, with a garland tail and a copper milking pail. After worshipping Vasudeva, the giver blesses the pot with the prayer "May the Lakshmi on Vishnu's breast, the Svaha of Agni and the power of the Moon, Indra and the Sun be my cow", and, dressed in white, calm and free of envy, gives it to a Brahmin with the words "May Keshava, who sleeps on the waters on the serpent bed, be pleased with me", and keeps the cow vow that day. He gains all the joys of gods and men, health beyond compare, lasting peace and every wish. Krishna then tells what the sage Mudgala, who remembered his past births, sang. Mudgala once went to Yama's world and saw the tortures of sinners: burning machines, boiling oil, rivers of hot lye, the pot of cooking (kumbhipaka) and more. Out of his pity the sinners felt sudden relief, and Yama told him the reason: three births before, Mudgala had given a water cow after worshipping Vishnu, and its fruit now gives joy to all who see, hear or think of him. No gift brings such joy: for nineteen births its givers know no fault, fever, pain or weariness. Yama adds that those who take refuge in Krishna, worship him, fast for him, remember him, say "Namo Krishna, Achyuta, Ananta, Vasudeva" or give gifts saying "may Achyuta be pleased" are outside his rule, for Hari is lord even of Yama. Hearing this, the sinners praised Krishna with many names (Hari, Vishnu, Hrishikesha, Janardana, Govinda, Narasimha, Vamana, Varaha, Ananta, Vasudeva); at once the weapons blunted, the fire grew cool, the hot lye rivers dried up, the thorny tree fell, light filled the hell, the sword-leaf forest grew still, Yama's servants lost their strength, the rivers of pus and blood ran with Ganga water, and sweet breezes and music arose. Yama honoured them, bowed to Krishna and to all who bow to him, and the sinners rode chariots to heaven. Mudgala, reborn in the Kanva family remembering all this, sang of how hard Vishnu's maya is to cross, how the soul passes through insects, plants, birds and beasts before reaching human birth, and how one who enjoys the world without breaking dharma but rests in Vishnu crosses it. Days, months and years spent without worshipping Hari are wasted; with arms raised, having seen both worlds, he cries out: worship Govinda and give the water cow, for even one water cow given to a Brahmin brings comfort in Yama's house, more than a hundred hard sacrifices.

09-154.json.summary: Krishna gives the ghee cow (ghrita-dhenu). Pots of cow's ghee, decorated with perfume and garlands, with a bronze milking pail and covered with white cloth, form the cow; it has legs of sugarcane, silver hooves, gold eyes, horns of agaru wood, sides of the seven grains, a dewlap of woollen cloth, a nose of incense and camphor, udders of fruit, a sugar tongue, a mouth of jaggery and milk, a silk-thread tail, hairs of white mustard and a back of a copper plate, with a calf made the same way. It is worshipped with the prayer "Ghee is brilliance, the highest remover of sin and the food of the gods; everything rests on ghee. You, goddess, made of ghee, remove all my sins and give me happiness", and given with a fee to a Brahmin, whom the giver thinks of as shining like a ghee flame, saying "take this cow for my good". The giver lives on ghee for one night with self-restraint. A butter cow (navanita-dhenu) is given the same way. Givers of the ghee cow go to worlds with great rivers of ghee and milk and banks of milk-rice, taking with them seven generations above and below, freed of sin; this is the fruit for those who give with desire, while those who give without desire reach the sinless state. Agni and Soma are ghee and all the gods are made of it, and the gods themselves stand in awe of those who give ghee. Holding the tail of the ghee cow, the meritorious cross the endless ocean of worldly life, whose waters are illusion, whose waves are children and wives, and whose crocodiles are greed.

09-155.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the best of gifts, by which all gifts are given, all wishes fulfilled, all sins destroyed and all expiations done. Krishna names the salt cow (lavana-dhenu), which frees even the killer of a Brahmin, a cow or a father, one who violated his teacher's bed, a betrayer of trust and any cruel sinner, sends him to Shiva's world and makes him fortunate, rich, long-lived, unconquered and blessed with all wishes. On ground smeared with cow dung and spread with darbha grass, a sheepskin is laid facing east and covered with cloth, and a cow is made of one adhaka of salt, whatever one's wealth, with gold horns, silver hooves, sugarcane legs, fruit udders, a sugar tongue, perfumes for the nose, sea shells for ears, a silk dewlap, a bell at the neck, horns of sandalwood, pearl eyes, cheeks of barley-flour balls, barley in the mouth, sesame and wheat on the sides and the seven grains as available, a copper plate on the back, a lump of jaggery at the rear, a woollen tail, grapes at the udder and honey with all good things below; a calf is made of a quarter of the salt. Adorned with garlands, clothes and ornaments, it is walked around with wife and sons and given on any holy day to a well-behaved Brahmin of good conduct with the prayer "All tastes are in salt and all gods are in salt; homage to you, goddess called salt, made of all the gods", together with a fee. By this the giver has, as it were, walked around the whole earth, given every gift and won the fruit of every sacrifice; all tastes, all food, the moving and unmoving world, good fortune, wisdom, health and wealth are his, and he lives in heaven until the dissolution of beings and then in the world of cows with every comfort.

09-156.json.summary: Krishna gives the gold cow (kanchana-dhenu), whose gift frees from every sin, even drinking liquor, killing a Brahmin or a cow, cowardice, a broken vow, killing one's teacher, incest and adultery. A tawny cow of fifty palas of pure gold, or half that, or whatever one can afford, is made with full belly and udders, well-shaped limbs, a fine rump and lovely ears, set with jewels all over; its calf is of a quarter of the gold. It has a silver bell, a silk wrap, copper horns, a dewlap of cat's-eye gem, pearl eyes and a coral tongue. It stands on a prastha of jaggery on a black antelope skin, with eight pots, many fruits, the eighteen grains, an umbrella, a pair of sandals, a vessel, cloth, a copper milking pail, lamps, food, salt, sugar and coriander. After bathing, the giver walks around it, invokes and worships it with the verses of the jaggery cow and with praises: "You are the jewel of the temple of all the gods, of Shiva, the Ganga, the ocean and the mountains; bowing to you, one whose sins are cut to pieces by the sharp water of faith reaches the highest peace. Who that reaches you, giver of every wish, can know fear? The knowers of the Veda call you the wish-fulfilling cow." It is then given with a fee and its furnishings to a Brahmin, who is bowed to and asked for pardon. At the moment of giving, all gods, holy places and Manus live in the cow's body: the Sun and Moon in her eyes, Sarasvati on her tongue, the Maruts in her teeth, the Ashvins in her ears, Rudra and Brahma at her horn tips, gandharvas and apsaras on her hump, the four oceans in her belly, the Ganga in her womb, the sages in her hair pores, the earth at her rear, the nagas in her entrails, the mountains in her bones, dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation in her feet, the four Vedas in her lowing, the Rudras in her throat, Meru on her back and Vishnu throughout her body. So the gold cow is made of all the gods, and its giver has given every gift. This rare gift purifies, saves and brings fame and peace; the giver, man or woman, lives in heaven for over a hundred crore years, honoured by the gods on a fine chariot amid songs and garlands, and is then reborn on earth handsome and free of sorrow and disease, gaining every wish birth after birth, and reaches the world of Shiva, filled with siddhas, sages, kinnaras and gods and surrounded by a hundred maidens.

09-157.json.summary: Krishna gives another rare gift, the jewel cow (ratna-dhenu), which brings the fruit of the world of cows. On a holy day, on ground smeared with cow dung, a cow is made of jewels: eighty-one rubies in the mouth, a hundred topazes in the feet, a gold mark on the forehead, a hundred pearls for the eyes, a hundred corals for the brows, shells for the ears, gold horns, a hundred diamonds on the head, a hundred zircons on the neck and eyelids, a hundred sapphires on the back, a hundred cat's-eyes on the sides, a belly of crystal, a hundred saugandhika gems on the hips, gold hooves, a tail of strings of pearls, sunstone and moonstone for the nostrils with camphor and sandal, saffron hair, a silver navel, a hundred emeralds at the rear and other jewels at every joint, with a sugar tongue, dung of jaggery, urine of ghee and curd and milk, a whisk at the tail tip and a copper pail at the udders; a calf is made of a quarter of the same. With fruits all around, it is invoked like the jaggery cow and praised: "Rudra, Indra, the Moon, Brahma and Vasudeva praise you as the home of all the gods; so, goddess, whose body holds the three worlds, quickly save me, sunk in the ocean of rebirth." It is then given to a learned Brahmin versed in the Vedas, honoured with clothes and ornaments, with a fee, and he is bowed to and asked for pardon. The giver lives happily in Shiva's world for more than a hundred crore kalpas, then becomes a king of kings on earth, rich in every wish and the destroyer of his enemies; free of all sin, he rides a shining chariot with his kin, sons and grandsons, beautiful as Kama, to the abode of Shambhu.

09-158.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to give a cow that is in the act of calving, and its fruit. Krishna says such a cow is won only by great merit. While the calf's feet are in the birth passage and its head can be seen, until the calf is born, the cow is the earth itself; while she is "two-faced" she is the earth with all its mountains, woods and forests. The merit of giving such a two-faced cow cannot be told by any one mouth: why perform many sacrifices and gifts? Give one calving cow. That one alone saves from hell and brings happiness. She is given to a fine Brahmin adorned with gold horns, silver hooves, a pearl-decked tail and a bronze milking pail. The giver lives in heaven for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on the cow and calf, and, giving a rich fee, surely lifts his father, grandfather and great-grandfather out of hell, going himself where rivers run with ghee and milk, the banks are curd and milk-rice and the wish-granting tree grows. One who gives her with much gold easily reaches the world of cows and Brahma's world. A weak cow or a small fee must never be given; this rite is for one who seeks a wish and bears fruit only when done by the rules, and moon-faced, golden-skinned, lotus-eyed women serve the giver forever.

09-159.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks how and when to give a thousand cows (go-sahasra). Krishna says cows are holy and the refuge of the worlds; Brahma created them first, for the good of the three worlds and for people's livelihood. Even temples are purified by their urine and dung, Lakshmi lives in cow dung, they are the root of sacrifice and made of all gods, and Brahmins and cows are one family split in two, one holding the mantras and the other the offering. One good cow, beautiful, gentle, young, rich in milk and with a good calf, saves a whole family, so what of ten, a hundred or a thousand? King Nahusha and the wise Yayati gave a thousand cows and went to Brahma's world, and Aditi gave them on the Ganga bank and won Narayana as her son. The ancestors sing that if anyone in their family, son or daughter, gives a thousand cows, they will reach the highest state. For the rite a pavilion of ten or twelve cubits with four doors and arches is built at a holy place, cow pen or home, with a four-cubit altar, a planet altar in the north-east where the planets are worshipped as in the planet sacrifice, worship first of Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra, sixteen, eight or four priests and a teacher adorned with earrings, rings and umbrellas, a fire pit for Shiva, two pots with five jewels at each door, and offerings to the guardians of the directions as in the gift of a man's weight in gold. Ten cows with calves are taken out of the thousand, adorned with cloth and garlands, gold bells, copper pails, gold forehead marks, silver hooves, horns of gold and jewels and whisks; some sages add a gold Nandikeshvara on a peak of a drona of salt, others one real bull. After a bath in water with all herbs, amid music and song, the giver holds flowers and prays: "Homage to you, the forms of the universe and mothers of the world; the twenty-one worlds and Brahma and the gods stand in your limbs; may the mother cows protect me. May cows be before me, behind me and all around me; I live among cows." He gives the Nandikeshvara with the bull prayer to his teacher, and gives the cows, a hundred, fifty, twenty, ten or five to each of many Brahmins; one cow must never be shared among many, but many may go to one. He keeps a milk fast and celibacy for a day. No weak, low-milk, sick or old cow, nor one with worn cloth or grieving for her calf, may be given. The giver is freed from all sin, served by siddhas and charanas, rides a sun-bright chariot with bells to the worlds of all the guardians and lifts up seven generations below, seven above and seven more; a woman who gives it is a queen for seven births. Not the gift alone, but the receiver, the time, the kind of cow and the rite all count; even one virtuous cow given to a worthy man purifies three generations, and the fruit of a thousand given with faith cannot be told.

09-160.json.summary: Yudhishthira again says he never tires of Krishna's words and asks the fruit of giving a bull, since Govinda, lord of cattle, is pleased by it. Krishna repeats the teaching on the bull gift: one strong draught ox equals ten milk cows and is even better than them; it should be healthy, well fed, young, gentle and faultless, and such a bull alone upholds a great family and saves the giver in the round of rebirth. At a holy time the calm bull is adorned, given a silver tail ornament and given to a Brahmin with the prayer "You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the joy of the world and the seat of the eight-formed Shiva; protect me, eternal one", with a fee, and the Brahmin is bowed to and sent off. The sins of seven births in word, mind and body are destroyed; the giver rides a shining bull-drawn chariot to heaven, lives in the world of cows for as many thousands of years as the bull has hairs, and is reborn a great, honoured Brahmin who performs sacrifices. The right receivers are patient, self-controlled householders whose ears are full of the Veda, who have mastered the senses, do not kill living beings and are slow to accept gifts; giving them a strong, sturdy-necked bull brings the merit of ten cows.

09-161.json.summary: Yudhishthira asks the greatness of giving a kapila, a tawny cow, and Krishna repeats what Vinatashva told, as the Boar (Varaha) once taught it to the Earth. Brahma made the kapila long ago from the essence of all brilliance, for the fire rite and for sacrifice; she is the holiest of holy things, the most auspicious and meritorious, the best penance, vow and gift, and her gift never decays. Fire offerings made twice a day with her ghee or milk carry the offerers in sun-coloured chariots to the sun's disc, and all holy places live always in her head and neck. Whoever rises at dawn and puts on his head, with devotion, the water that drips from a kapila's neck and head burns away twenty years of sin, and walking around kapila cows at dawn equals walking around the earth and destroys ten years of sin; bathing in her urine equals bathing in the Ganga and all holy places and frees one from a lifetime's sin. Brahma said giving one kapila equals giving a thousand cows, and one who kills a kapila has killed a thousand. Scratching cows, guarding them from fear and disease and giving land for their grazing all bring heaven. There are ten kinds of kapila: golden, pale yellow, Asha, fire-flame, ladle-coloured, ghee-yellow, white-yellow, milk-yellow, rose-coloured and flower-yellow, all saving their givers, and the fiery Asha cow should be given in the south-east. The text holds that a kapila must be received only by Brahmins: it says Shudras who take one or live on its milk, ghee or butter fall like outcastes and go through the Raurava hell and then births as dogs and worms in filth, and a Brahmin who takes gifts from them is to be shunned. Giving one kapila to a poor, learned Brahmin of good conduct who keeps the sacred fire frees one from all sins, and it is better than countless other gifts. A cow due to calve within the month should be kept for giving, and best of all is a kapila given while calving: while the calf's face shows at the birth passage she is the earth itself, with its oceans, mountains, forests and jewels, and her giver lives in Brahma's world for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on cow and calf, specks of dust on earth or stars in the sky. With gold horns, silver hooves, a bronze pail, cloth, bell and ornaments, she is given with gold, from a thousand gold pieces down to what one can afford, with water poured in the Brahmin's hand and verses ("Iravati dhenumati", "Syona prithivi" and others); even the stealer of a Brahmin's wealth, the killer of a cow, an embryo or a Brahmin should give such a two-faced cow with gold, after a fire offering on a dung-smeared circle, and live on milk that day. The giver says "Take this great cow and be my brother; destroy my sins and bless me", the Brahmin answers with the "Ko 'dat" verse, and the giver, freed with his ancestors, goes to Vishnu's highest abode, while the gods always serve the golden, half-calved, two-faced kapila. Reading this rite at dawn, three times a day, at an ancestor rite or before Brahmins on the new moon destroys a hundred years of sin, satisfies the ancestors for a hundred years, and hearing it frees one from a year's sin; it is the secret Varaha told the Earth.

09-162.json.summary: Krishna tells the greatness of giving a she-buffalo, which removes sin and grants long life and every wish. It is given at eclipses of the sun and moon, on the Kartika full moon, at the solstices, on the fourteenth of the bright half, on the day the sun enters a sign, or whenever the heart is willing and the means are there, by one who fears the round of rebirth. She should have fine udders, good horns and hooves, be young, in her first calving, gentle and faultless; she is adorned with gold horn tips and a forehead mark, bells and ornaments, covered with red cloth and given with a bronze milking pail, a basket of oil cake, gold as one can afford and the seven grains, to a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas, reads the Puranas or knows astronomy, never to one without Vedic learning or with bad vows. On a holy day she is walked around and given with the prayer "May the fair queen-buffalo of Indra and the other world guardians, and the mother of Mahishasura, whose son stands as the helper of Yama, grant me every wish"; the receiver takes her by the back, and the giver has her led to the Brahmin's house, honours him with clothes and ornaments and says "I have brought her to you; be pleased with me". The giver gains every wish here and hereafter: a woman who gives a she-buffalo becomes a chief queen and a man a great king, as Vyasa said; a Brahmin becomes a performer of sacrifices, a Kshatriya victorious, a Vaishya wealthy and a Shudra rich in all things, so one with means should give one for the good of sons, grandsons and great-grandsons. Narada said a she-buffalo equals ten cows, Vyasa twenty, and the Sun called it the best of all gifts; Sagara, Kakutstha, Dhundhumara and Gadhi gave them. Whoever hears this is freed of all sin and honoured in Shiva's world, and one who gives a rain-cloud-dark, milk-rich buffalo with a gold mark to a fine Brahmin wins both worlds.
